meta.title: Meteorology
meta.intro: Read the data, name the hazard, pick the safe action.

notes.title: Observation tools
notes.html:
On the ground: ASOS (automated airport stations), mesonets (dense local stations), buoys (water). Aloft: radiosondes on balloons, aircraft reports.

Radar productShows
ReflectivityHow much precipitation, and where
Base velocityMotion toward or away from the radar
Correlation coefficient (CC)How alike the targets are. Rain is high. Debris is low
Storm relative motionWinds with the storm's own movement removed. Shows rotation
Composite reflectivityStrongest echo at any height
Wind profileWinds at each height over the radar

Satellite: visible needs daylight. Infrared (IR) works day and night: cold cloud tops are bright, so tall storms stand out. Water vapor shows moisture in the middle and upper air.

Velocity: toward the radar is NEGATIVE (green). Away is POSITIVE (red). Think "red = run away".

notes.title: Station models and METAR
notes.html:
A station model packs temperature, dew point, pressure, wind and sky cover into one symbol.

SpotMeans
Upper leftTemperature
Lower leftDew point
Upper rightPressure, last 3 digits (tenths of mb)
Lower right3-hour pressure change
Center circleSky cover (more filled = cloudier)
Barb staffPoints toward where wind COMES FROM
Half flag / full / pennant5 kt / 10 kt / 50 kt
Pressure: 500 or more → put 9 in front. Less than 500 → put 10.132 → 1013.2 mb 987 → 998.7 mb 047 → 1004.7 mb

METAR example: KOKC 202153Z 18018G28KT 6SM TSRA BKN040CB 27/22 A2985

PartMeaning
KOKCStation
202153ZDay 20, 21:53 UTC
18018G28KTFrom 180° at 18 kt, gusts 28 kt
6SMVisibility 6 statute miles
TSRAThunderstorm with rain
BKN040CBBroken clouds at 4,000 ft, cumulonimbus
27/22Temp 27°C, dew point 22°C
A2985Altimeter 29.85 inHg

Sky: FEW 1–2/8, SCT 3–4/8, BKN 5–7/8, OVC 8/8. Height × 100 ft. Negative temps start with M (M05 = −5°C).

notes.title: Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
notes.html:
Standard levels: 850 mb (low moisture), 700 mb (steering), 500 mb (troughs and ridges), 300 mb (jet stream).

Hodograph: plots the wind at each height as a point, then connects them. A long, curving path means strong shear. Curving clockwise with height (veering) favors supercells.

Stüve / Skew-T: temperature (solid) and dew point (dashed) against pressure. Lines close together = moist or cloudy. Far apart = dry. A layer where temperature rises with height is an inversion (very stable, a "cap").

States/Nationals:

LCL (m) ≈ 125 × (T − Td in °C)Dry parcel cools 10 °C per km. Typical air cools about 6.5 °C per km.
CAPE (J/kg)Instability
Under 1,000Marginal
1,000–2,500Moderate
2,500–4,000Strong
Over 4,000Extreme
Low LCL (low cloud base) raises tornado risk. CAPE alone is not enough: you also need shear and a lift trigger.

notes.title: Setup for severe weather
notes.html:
Recipe: moisture + instability + lift + wind shear.

IngredientRole
Jet streamSteers storms, adds energy aloft
Cold frontCold air pushes in. Fast, sharp storms
Warm frontWarm air slides over cold. Wide, steady precipitation
StationaryStalled boundary
OccludedCold front catches warm front
DrylineMoisture boundary (moist east, dry west on the Plains). Not a temperature boundary
Atmospheric riverNarrow stream of heavy water vapor. Extreme rain at landfall
Wind shearWind changes with height. Organizes storms; directional shear starts rotation
FetchDistance wind blows over water
Ocean heat contentWarm deep water fuels hurricanes. Storm wakes are cooler

Mountains lift air (trigger storms), and can block, weaken or redirect storms.

notes.title: Severe-weather clouds
notes.html:
CloudSignal
CumulonimbusThe thunderstorm cloud
Wall cloudLowered, often rotating base under the updraft. Tornado warning sign
Shelf cloudWedge at the leading edge. Marks the gust front
Funnel cloudRotating cone not touching ground
MammatusPouches under an anvil. Often a storm weakening
Funnel cloud = not on the ground. Once it touches down it is a tornado.

notes.title: Drought and heat waves
notes.html:
Drought: long stretch with too little precipitation. Heat wave: long stretch of abnormal heat. Both are often caused by a blocking high-pressure ridge that sits in place and steers storms away.

Effects: crop loss, water limits, wildfire, heat illness, power demand.

notes.title: Precipitation, flooding, IDF
notes.html:
How it forms:

ProcessResult
Collision-coalescenceDrops merge into bigger drops (warm clouds)
Bergeron processIce crystals grow while supercooled drops shrink (cold clouds)
RimingSupercooled drops freeze onto ice (builds graupel and hail)
AggregationIce crystals stick together (snowflakes)
TypeLayers it fell through
SnowCold all the way down
SleetSnow melts, then refreezes as ice pellets in a cold layer near the ground
Freezing rainRain falls on a surface below 0 °C and freezes on contact
HailStrong updraft keeps stones aloft, they grow by riming
RainWarm all the way down

Flood types: flash (minutes to hours), stream/river (rises over days), urban (drains overwhelmed). Burn scars and steep land produce debris flows and mudslides.

Hail: pea ¼ in, penny ¾ in, quarter 1 in (severe), golf ball 1¾ in, baseball 2¾ in.

States/Nationals: an IDF curve shows rainfall intensity versus duration for a return period. Longer duration = lower intensity. Rarer storms (100-yr) plot higher. Chance in any year = 1 ÷ return period.

notes.title: Lightning
notes.html:
Ice and graupel collide in the cloud. Smaller, lighter ice rises with positive charge. Heavier graupel falls with negative charge. The cloud base is mostly negative. The ground below turns positive.

TypePath
Cloud-to-groundCloud to the surface
IntracloudInside one cloud
Cloud-to-cloudBetween two clouds
Cloud-to-airCloud into clear air

Lightning detection systems locate strikes using sensors across a network (they time the signal at each sensor).

Miles = seconds between flash and thunder ÷ 5

notes.title: Severe thunderstorms
notes.html:
NWS "severe": hail ≥ 1 inch, wind ≥ 58 mph, or a tornado.

TypeKey trait
Single-cellOne short-lived cell
MulticellCluster or line at different stages
SupercellOne long-lived storm with a rotating updraft (mesocyclone). Makes the strongest tornadoes
MCCLarge round long-lived cluster

Life cycle: cumulus (updraft only) → mature (updraft + downdraft, worst weather) → dissipating (downdraft only).

notes.title: Winds from storms
notes.html:
Straight-line winds = damage not from rotation. Damage is spread out in one direction.

TermMeaning
DowndraftSinking air
DownburstDowndraft that hits the ground and spreads out
MicroburstDownburst under 4 km wide. Brief, intense
MacroburstDownburst 4 km or wider. Longer lasting
Gust frontLeading edge of cool outflow
Squall lineOrganized line of storms
DerechoLong-lived, widespread windstorm. Track of hundreds of miles
Downslope windAir accelerating down a mountain slope

On radar: bow echo (derecho/damaging wind), fine line (gust front), bowing segment on a squall line.

notes.title: Tornadoes, scales, radar
notes.html:
Tornado = violently rotating column touching the ground and a cloud base. Waterspout = same over water. Peak: late afternoon, spring, Plains and Southeast.

EF scale3-second gust
EF065–85 mph
EF186–110 mph
EF2111–135 mph
EF3136–165 mph
EF4166–200 mph
EF5over 200 mph
F scale = before 1 Feb 2007. EF scale = on or after. Both rate DAMAGE, not measured wind.
SignatureMeans
Hook echoRain/debris wrapping a mesocyclone (reflectivity)
TVSTight inbound-outbound velocity pair = intense rotation
Debris ballLow CC inside the hook = debris in the air
Bow echoStraight-line wind; may hide small tornadoes

notes.title: Hurricanes
notes.html:
Hurricane = typhoon = cyclone (same storm, different ocean). Needs warm water (about 26.5 °C or more), moisture, low shear, and distance from the equator.

Life cycle: Invest → Depression (under 39 mph) → Tropical Storm (39–73) → Hurricane (74+) → Major (Cat 3+).

Saffir-SimpsonSustained wind
Cat 174–95 mph
Cat 296–110 mph
Cat 3111–129 mph (major)
Cat 4130–156 mph (major)
Cat 5157+ mph (major)

Parts: eye (calm, 20–40 mi), eyewall (worst winds and rain), spiral bands (can spawn tornadoes).

Storm surge = water pushed onshore. Biggest with strong wind, large size, slow movement, and shallow, funnel-shaped coasts. Often the deadliest hazard.

Land cuts off the heat source, so storms weaken. Shear and dry air weaken them. El Niño tends to raise shear in the Atlantic and quiet it.

Atlantic season: June 1 – Nov 30.

notes.title: Severe winter storms
notes.html:
StormKey facts
BlizzardWind or gusts ≥ 35 mph + falling/blowing snow + visibility under ¼ mile, all for 3+ hours
Nor'easterStrong East Coast storm; northeast winds; snow, coastal flooding, wind
Lake effectCold air over warm open lake water, narrow heavy snow bands downwind
Ice stormFreezing rain builds up ice. ¼ inch can bring down lines
A blizzard does not need new snow. Wind can blow old snow.

notes.title: Hazards and safety
notes.html:
StormMain hazard
TornadoViolent wind, debris
HurricaneStorm surge, wind, inland flooding
Severe thunderstormHail, wind, lightning
Flash floodRapid water rise
LightningDirect strike, fires
Winter stormSnow/ice load, low visibility, cold
Drought/heatWater shortage, heat illness
AlertMeans
WatchConditions favorable. Get ready
WarningHappening or about to. Act now
AdvisoryLess serious but still disruptive

Actions: tornado = lowest floor, interior room, no windows. Hurricane = follow evacuation orders. Flash flood = go high, never drive through water. Lightning = indoors or hard-topped car. Generators outside only (carbon monoxide).

Reliable sources: weather.gov, spc.noaa.gov (storms), nhc.noaa.gov (tropics).

notes.html:
EventKnow the type
Galveston 1900Hurricane, huge storm surge, deadliest US natural disaster

Katrina 2005Hurricane, surge and levee failures, Gulf Coast
Sandy 2012Hurricane turned post-tropical, giant size, surge in NY/NJ
Ida 2021Hurricane, Louisiana landfall, then remnant flash flooding in the Northeast
Ian 2022Hurricane, southwest Florida, large surge
Hilary 2023Pacific hurricane, rare Southern California tropical storm rain
Helene 2024Hurricane, Florida Big Bend, deadly inland flooding in the Appalachians
Erin 2025Atlantic hurricane that intensified rapidly to a major hurricane
Melissa 2025Very intense hurricane that hit Jamaica
Blizzard of March 1888East Coast blizzard
Dust Bowl 1930sDrought, plowed soil, dust storms on the Plains
Xenia 1974Violent tornado in an outbreak (Ohio)

Great Flood 1993Mississippi/Missouri river flooding after months of rain
Storm of the Century 1993Huge March storm: blizzard, tornadoes, surge

You will get data. Case method: 1) name the storm type, 2) list the clues, 3) apply the scale or signature, 4) check dates (EF cutoff 1 Feb 2007).

cards: To where the wind comes FROM
Low correlation coefficient in a hook
35 mph wind, under ¼ mi visibility, 3+ hours
Narrow stream of heavy water vapor
Pouches under an anvil, storm weakening
Water pushed onshore, often deadliest hurricane hazard

written: A radar velocity image shows a bright inbound patch right next to a bright outbound patch inside a hook echo. A low correlation coefficient spot sits at the tip of the hook. What is happening and what should be issued?

A tornado is likely on the ground (tornadic vortex signature) and lofting debris (debris ball). The NWS should issue a Tornado Warning and people should shelter in an interior room on the lowest floor.
Explain why a hurricane's storm surge is often more deadly than its wind.

Surge pushes a wall of ocean water inland. Water is heavy and drowns people, destroys buildings, and floods large low areas quickly. Wind damage covers a smaller zone, and surge height depends on size, speed, wind and coast shape.
A town reports sustained 40 mph winds, heavy blowing snow, and 1/8 mile visibility for 4 hours with no new snowfall. Is it a blizzard? Explain.
Yes. Wind of at least 35 mph, snow in the air (blowing snow counts), visibility under ¼ mile, all for at least 3 hours. New snow is not required.
Describe the three ingredients that must come together for a supercell-producing environment.

Instability (CAPE) plus moisture to fuel the updraft, a lifting trigger such as a front, dryline or terrain, and strong wind shear, especially with direction change, to organize and rotate the updraft.
An observer counts 20 seconds between a flash and the thunder. How far away is the strike and what should they do?
About 4 miles (20 ÷ 5). Lightning can strike miles from the storm. Go indoors or into a hard-topped vehicle now.
bench: Given a printed station model: write temperature, dew point, dew point depression, pressure in mb (use the 9 or 10 rule), wind direction and speed, and sky cover. Then predict: fog, rain, or clear?
Decode a 4-line METAR set. Make a table: station, time, wind (with gusts), visibility, weather, clouds with heights, temperature, dew point, altimeter.
Given reflectivity, velocity and correlation coefficient images, name the signature (hook, TVS, debris ball, bow echo, fine line), the hazard, and the NWS product you would expect.
Station 4: Read a sounding or hodograph
Mark where temperature and dew point nearly touch, any inversion, and the strongest shear layer. State if storms are likely to be strong and why. (Skew-T for States/Nationals.)
Given wind or damage data and a date, rate it with Fujita/EF or Saffir-Simpson and state which scale applies and why.
Given a data packet for a historic event, identify the storm type, three clues, the main hazard, and the safety action.
safety: Use only reliable sources: weather.gov, spc.noaa.gov, nhc.noaa.gov.
During real watches or warnings, follow official instructions, not this app.
Never chase storms or drive through flood water for practice.
checklist: Binder: three-ring, tabbed by topic number (i to xv), one summary page per tab.
Station model, METAR, EF and Saffir-Simpson charts as one-page tabs.
Radar signature page with sketches and a velocity color key.
Read the whole test. Do the data-interpretation questions first (at least half of the test).
Show reasoning in words when asked. Use the proper term.

questions.w: In the Northern Hemisphere that turn is counterclockwise.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, winds around a high-pressure center spin clockwise or counterclockwise?
sol: Highs spin the opposite way from lows.
In the Northern Hemisphere highs spin clockwise.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR
questions.w: In the Northern Hemisphere highs spin clockwise.

questions.q: A station model shows the pressure code 132. Add a leading 10 and put a decimal before the last digit. What is the pressure in hPa?
sol: For codes starting with 0, 1 or 2, put 10 in front.
132 becomes 1013.2 hPa.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR
questions.w: 132 becomes 1013.2 hPa.

questions.q: A station model shows the pressure code 987. For codes starting with 5 to 9, put a 9 in front and a decimal before the last digit. What is the pressure in hPa?
sol: The code starts with 9, so put a 9 in front: 9987.
Place the decimal before the last digit: 998.7 hPa.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR
questions.w: Place the decimal before the last digit: 998.7 hPa.

questions.q: A wind barb has one long barb and one short barb. What is the wind speed in knots? (long = 10, short = 5)
sol: Add the barbs: 10 + 5.
The wind is 15 knots.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR
questions.w: The wind is 15 knots.

questions.q: A wind barb has one flag (pennant, 50 knots) and two long barbs (10 knots each). What is the wind speed in knots?
sol: The flag counts 50.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A METAR reports wind 29008KT. From what direction, in degrees, is the wind blowing?
sol: The first three digits are the direction wind comes from.
290° is a wind from the west-northwest.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR
questions.w: 290° is a wind from the west-northwest.

questions.q: In a METAR, the group 18/09 gives temperature and dew point in °C. Which number is the dew point?
sol: Temperature comes first, then dew point.
The dew point is 09 °C, so the air is 9 °C from saturation.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR
questions.w: The dew point is 09 °C, so the air is 9 °C from saturation.

questions.q: A station model has its wind staff pointing toward the northwest. The wind is blowing FROM the northwest. Drag the pointer to that direction.
sol: The staff points toward where the wind comes from.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: The wind is blowing FROM the southeast. Drag the pointer to the direction the wind comes from.
sol: Southeast lies halfway between east (90°) and south (180°).
That is 135°.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR
questions.w: That is 135°.

questions.q: On a weather map, two stations are 2.5 cm apart and 1 cm equals 120 km. How far apart are the stations?
sol: Multiply the map distance by the scale: 2.5 × 120.
Distance = 300 km.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR
questions.w: Distance = 300 km.

questions.q: A stationary front is drawn with alternating red half-circles and blue triangles on opposite sides. What does the front do?
sol: Neither air mass is winning.
The boundary stays nearly in place.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR
questions.w: The boundary stays nearly in place.

questions.q: Near the ground, temperature usually gets warmer or cooler as you climb higher in the atmosphere?
sol: Higher up, the air is thinner and farther from the warm ground.
In the troposphere the temperature falls with height.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: In the troposphere the temperature falls with height.

questions.q: What is the lowest layer of the atmosphere, where almost all weather happens?
sol: Tropo means to turn or mix.
The troposphere is the layer we live in.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: The troposphere is the layer we live in.

questions.q: A rising bubble of air is called an air…
sol: Forecasters imagine a small bubble of air.
They call it a parcel and follow it as it rises.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: They call it a parcel and follow it as it rises.

questions.q: Air pressure gets higher or lower as you climb up a mountain?
sol: There is less air above you pressing down.
Pressure falls with height.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: Pressure falls with height.

questions.q: When rising air cools enough, water vapor turns into tiny droplets. This change is called…
sol: Gas to liquid is condensation.
This is how clouds begin.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: This is how clouds begin.

questions.q: A graph of temperature and moisture at different heights, made from a weather balloon, is called a…
sol: The balloon measures as it climbs.
The record of those measurements is called a sounding.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: The record of those measurements is called a sounding.

questions.q: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is about 10 °C per kilometer. A dry parcel at 25 °C rises 2 km. What is its new temperature?
sol: Cooling = 10 °C/km × 2 km = 20 °C.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A saturated parcel cools about 6 °C per km as it rises. How many degrees does it cool in 3 km?
sol: Multiply: 6 × 3.
The parcel cools 18 °C.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: The parcel cools 18 °C.

questions.q: Estimate the lifting condensation level (cloud base) with 125 m × (T − Td). The surface temperature is 30 °C and the dew point is 18 °C. How high is the cloud base?
sol: T − Td = 12 °C.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: What does CAPE stand for?
sol: CAPE measures the energy stored for rising air.
Convective Available Potential Energy.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: Convective Available Potential Energy.

questions.q: CAPE is measured in joules per what?
sol: It is energy per mass of air.
The unit is J/kg.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: The unit is J/kg.

questions.q: Larger CAPE means a stronger or weaker possible updraft?
sol: CAPE is the energy that can lift a parcel.
More energy means stronger updrafts.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: More energy means stronger updrafts.

questions.q: On a sounding, the temperature is 20 °C at the surface and 4 °C at 2 km. What is the average lapse rate in °C per km?
sol: Temperature drop: 20 − 4 = 16 °C.
16 °C over 2 km is 8 °C per km.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE
questions.w: 16 °C over 2 km is 8 °C per km.

questions.q: The boundary between two different air masses is called a…
sol: Air masses have different temperature and moisture.
Where they meet is a front.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: Where they meet is a front.

questions.q: A large body of air with about the same temperature and moisture everywhere is an air…
sol: It forms over one kind of region for days.
This is called an air mass.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: This is called an air mass.

questions.q: Which is denser, warm air or cold air?
sol: Cold air has molecules packed closer.
Cold air is denser, so it sinks under warm air.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: Cold air is denser, so it sinks under warm air.

questions.q: Across the United States the jet stream mostly flows from which direction to which?
sol: Most of the winds above the middle latitudes blow from the west.
So the jet stream flows west to east.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: So the jet stream flows west to east.

questions.q: A cold front arrives and cool air replaces warm air. What usually happens to the temperature?
sol: Cold air is replacing warm air.
The temperature falls.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: The temperature falls.

questions.q: Wind shear means the wind changes with…
sol: Shear is a change in wind speed or direction.
It is usually measured between two heights.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: It is usually measured between two heights.

questions.q: The wind is 15 knots from the south at the surface and 55 knots from the south at 6 km. What is the wind speed shear in knots?
sol: Subtract: 55 − 15.
The speed shear is 40 knots.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: The speed shear is 40 knots.

questions.q: A dryline separates moist air from what kind of air?
sol: The dryline marks a sharp drop in dew point.
Moist Gulf air is on one side and dry desert air on the other.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: Moist Gulf air is on one side and dry desert air on the other.

questions.q: A low-level jet is strongest at what time of day?
sol: After sunset the surface layer decouples from the winds above.
Winds a few hundred meters up speed up, especially at night.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: Winds a few hundred meters up speed up, especially at night.

questions.q: Does strong wind shear tend to organize thunderstorms (such as supercells) or tear them apart?
sol: Moderate to strong shear tilts the updraft.
Rain falls away from the updraft, so the storm lasts longer.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: Rain falls away from the updraft, so the storm lasts longer.

questions.q: A warm front moves in. What does warm air do as it overruns the cooler air ahead?
sol: Warm air is less dense.
It rides up over the cold air, making broad cloud layers.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: It rides up over the cold air, making broad cloud layers.

questions.q: The jet stream at 300 hPa is blowing FROM the west-southwest. Drag the pointer to that direction.
sol: West is 270° and southwest is 225°.
West-southwest is halfway between them: 247.5°.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather
questions.w: West-southwest is halfway between them: 247.5°.

questions.q: What is the name for puffy, cotton-like clouds with flat bottoms?
sol: Cumulus means heap or pile.
These are puffy clouds.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds
questions.w: These are puffy clouds.

questions.q: What is the name for thin, wispy clouds high in the sky made of ice crystals?
sol: Cirrus means a curl of hair.
These are the highest wispy clouds.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds
questions.w: These are the highest wispy clouds.

questions.q: What is the name for a flat, gray layer of cloud that covers the sky like a blanket?
sol: Stratus means layer.
Stratus often brings drizzle.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds
questions.w: Stratus often brings drizzle.

questions.q: The word nimbus on a cloud name means the cloud brings…
sol: Nimbus is Latin for rain cloud.
Nimbostratus and cumulonimbus bring precipitation.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds
questions.w: Nimbostratus and cumulonimbus bring precipitation.

questions.q: What do we call a cloud that touches the ground?
sol: A cloud at ground level is fog.
It forms the same way as other clouds.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds
questions.w: It forms the same way as other clouds.

questions.q: The flat, spreading top of a thunderstorm is called an…
sol: Rising air hits a stable layer near the top of the troposphere.
It spreads sideways in the shape of an anvil.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds
questions.w: It spreads sideways in the shape of an anvil.

questions.q: A long, low roll of cloud along the leading edge of a thunderstorm's cool outflow is called a(n)…
sol: Cool air from the storm pushes warm air up.
A shelf cloud forms on the gust front.
From your notes · Winds from storms: Gust frontLeading edge of cool outflow
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds
questions.w: A shelf cloud forms on the gust front.

questions.q: A lowered, rotating cloud base beneath a supercell's updraft is called a…
sol: The wall cloud forms under the main updraft.
Tornadoes often form from it.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds
questions.w: Tornadoes often form from it.

questions.q: Put these cloud types in order from the lowest base height to the highest.
sol: Stratus clouds hug the ground.
Cumulus come next, altocumulus are mid-level, cirrus are highest.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds
questions.w: Stratus is low, altocumulus middle, cirrus high.

questions.q: Match each cloud feature to what it tells you.
pairs: Top of a thunderstorm spreading out
Rotating lowered base under a supercell
Gust front pushing warm air up
sol: Each feature has a typical position in a storm.
Learn them as a set when you read storm photos.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds
questions.w: Learn them as a set when you read storm photos.

questions.q: What should you drink more of during a heat wave?
sol: Your body loses water by sweating.
Drink water before you feel thirsty.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves
questions.w: Drink water before you feel thirsty.

questions.q: Should you ever leave a child or pet in a parked car on a hot day?
sol: A parked car heats up very fast, even with windows cracked.
Never leave a child or pet in a car.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves
questions.w: Never leave a child or pet in a car.

questions.q: The emergency condition when the body's cooling system fails, sweating stops and skin turns hot and dry is heat…
sol: In heat stroke the body's sweat cooling fails.
Core temperature climbs past 104 °F and the brain is affected.
Heat exhaustion is milder: heavy sweating and weakness.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves
questions.w: Heat stroke is an emergency: call 911.

questions.q: A town normally gets 40 mm of rain in a month but got only 10 mm. What percent of the normal rainfall fell?
sol: Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: The heat index makes 35 °C with high humidity feel hotter. If it feels like 41 °C, how many degrees hotter than the air temperature does it feel?
sol: Subtract: 41 − 35.
It feels 6 °C hotter.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves
questions.w: It feels 6 °C hotter.

questions.q: Why does high humidity make hot weather feel hotter?
sol: Sweat cools you only when it evaporates.
Humid air holds more water, so sweat evaporates slowly and cooling is weaker.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves
questions.w: Humid air holds more water, so sweat evaporates slowly and cooling is weaker.

questions.q: A heat dome is a strong area of what kind of pressure that traps hot air?
sol: Sinking air under a strong high heats up and clouds clear.
The air acts like a lid over the region.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves
questions.w: The air acts like a lid over the region.

questions.q: What is the main reason a drought raises wildfire risk?
sol: Dry vegetation burns easily.
A spark can start a fire that spreads quickly.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves
questions.w: Dry plants are easy fuel; a spark spreads fast.

questions.q: Overnight temperatures stay high during a heat wave. Why is this dangerous?
sol: The body needs a cool period to recover.
Warm nights add stress, especially for older adults.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves
questions.w: Warm nights add stress, especially for older adults.

questions.q: Rain falls at 5 mm per hour. Using light < 2.5, moderate 2.5 to 7.6, heavy > 7.6 mm/hr, how would you describe it?
sol: 5 is between 2.5 and 7.6.
That is moderate rain.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF
questions.w: That is moderate rain.

questions.q: A snowfall has a 10:1 snow-to-liquid ratio. How many cm of snow fall when the liquid equivalent is 5 cm?
sol: Multiply by 10.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A sudden, quick rise of water in a stream or on land after heavy rain is a…
sol: It can happen within minutes to hours.
This is a flash flood.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF
questions.w: This is a flash flood.

questions.q: If you see water covering a road, what should you do?
sol: Just 15 to 30 cm of moving water can carry a car away.
Turn around, don't drown.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF
questions.w: Turn around, don't drown.

questions.q: Which freezes into balls of ice during strong thunderstorms: rain or hail?
sol: Hail grows in strong updrafts.
Raindrops are lifted high and freeze in layers.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF
questions.w: Raindrops are lifted high and freeze in layers.

questions.q: A storm drops 12 mm of rain per hour for 4 hours. How many millimeters of rain is that in total?
sol: Rate × time = 12 × 4.
48 mm.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF
questions.w: 48 mm.

questions.q: Convert 2.54 cm of rain to inches. (1 in = 2.54 cm)
sol: Divide by 2.54.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A rain gauge records 3 inches of rain in 6 hours. What is the average rate in inches per hour?
sol: Divide total by time: 3 ÷ 6.
0.5 in/hr.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF
questions.w: 0.5 in/hr.

questions.q: A watch vs. a warning: which one means flooding is already happening or imminent?
sol: A watch means conditions are favorable.
A warning means it is happening or about to happen.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF
questions.w: A warning means it is happening or about to happen.

questions.q: Why do flash floods happen faster in cities?
sol: Pavement and roofs do not let water soak in.
Water runs off quickly into streets and streams.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF
questions.w: Water runs off quickly into streets and streams.

questions.q: Which travels faster, light or sound?
sol: Light is almost instant for our purposes.
So you see lightning before you hear thunder.
Notes|n-light|Lightning
questions.w: So you see lightning before you hear thunder.

questions.q: If you can hear thunder, are you close enough to be struck by lightning?
sol: Thunder can be heard about 10 miles away.
Lightning can strike that far from the storm: when thunder roars, go indoors.
Notes|n-light|Lightning
questions.w: Lightning can strike that far from the storm: when thunder roars, go indoors.

questions.q: Where is the safest place during a lightning storm?
sol: Fully enclosed buildings are safest.
A hard-topped car is the next best.
From your notes · Hazards and safety: Lightning = indoors or hard-topped car.
Notes|n-light|Lightning
questions.w: A hard-topped car is the next best.

questions.q: Should you stand under a lone tree during a thunderstorm?
sol: Tall isolated objects attract lightning.
Never shelter under a tree.
Notes|n-light|Lightning
questions.w: Never shelter under a tree.

questions.q: Sound travels about 340 m/s. You hear thunder 6 seconds after a flash. About how far away is the lightning in meters?
sol: Distance = speed × time.
Notes|n-light|Lightning

questions.q: A rough rule: divide the seconds between flash and thunder by 3 to get kilometers. The delay is 12 seconds. How many kilometers away?
sol: The strike is about 4 km away.
Notes|n-light|Lightning
questions.w: The strike is about 4 km away.

questions.q: The 30-30 rule says go indoors if flash-to-bang is 30 seconds or less. How long should you wait after the last thunder before going back out?
sol: Storms can still strike after they seem to pass.
Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
Notes|n-light|Lightning
questions.w: Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

questions.q: Heat lightning is just lightning from a storm that is too what?
sol: The storm is too far to hear thunder.
You see the flashes but thunder does not reach you.
Notes|n-light|Lightning
questions.w: You see the flashes but thunder does not reach you.

questions.q: Cloud-to-ground lightning that starts at the top of the storm and travels down starts as a stepped…
sol: A faint channel of charge moves down in steps.
When it meets an upward streamer, the return stroke flashes.
Notes|n-light|Lightning
questions.w: When it meets an upward streamer, the return stroke flashes.

questions.q: What three ingredients make a thunderstorm: moisture, lift and what else?
sol: Moisture gives fuel, lift gets air started, instability keeps it rising.
The three are moisture, lift and instability.
Notes|n-tstorm|Severe thunderstorms
questions.w: The three are moisture, lift and instability.

questions.q: A thunderstorm that makes strong rotating updrafts and lasts for hours is called a…
sol: Rotation helps the storm survive.
Supercells make most big tornadoes and large hail.
Notes|n-tstorm|Severe thunderstorms
questions.w: Supercells make most big tornadoes and large hail.

questions.q: The rotating updraft in a supercell is called a…
sol: Meso means middle scale.
A mesocyclone is the rotating updraft.
Notes|n-tstorm|Severe thunderstorms
questions.w: A mesocyclone is the rotating updraft.

questions.q: A strong rush of sinking air that spreads out at the ground and can cause straight-line wind damage is called a…
sol: Rain-cooled air sinks fast and fans out.
This sudden wind is a downburst.
Notes|n-tstorm|Severe thunderstorms
questions.w: This sudden wind is a downburst.

questions.q: Thunderstorms that form in a line are called a…
sol: Lines of storms move together.
A squall line often has damaging winds.
Notes|n-tstorm|Severe thunderstorms
questions.w: A squall line often has damaging winds.

questions.q: A multicell storm keeps renewing itself by forming new cells where?
sol: The cool outflow lifts warm air at its edge.
New updrafts form along the gust front.
Notes|n-tstorm|Severe thunderstorms
questions.w: New updrafts form along the gust front.

questions.q: To grow large hail you need a strong…
sol: Hail stones keep rising and freezing.
Stronger updrafts hold bigger stones aloft.
Notes|n-tstorm|Severe thunderstorms
questions.w: Stronger updrafts hold bigger stones aloft.

questions.q: The NWS defines a derecho as wind damage along a path of more than how many miles (with gusts of at least 58 mph along most of it)?
sol: A derecho is a long-lived, widespread windstorm from a fast-moving line of storms.
Its damage path is over 240 miles (about 400 km) with gusts 58 mph or more.
A single microburst is tiny by comparison: under 4 km wide.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
questions.w: NWS: damage swath of more than 240 miles with gusts of at least 58 mph.

questions.q: A wind gust measured at 40 knots. Convert to mph. (1 kt ≈ 1.15 mph)
sol: Multiply: 40 × 1.15.
46 mph.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
questions.w: 46 mph.

questions.q: A wind is reported as blowing FROM the northeast. Drag the pointer to that direction.
sol: Northeast lies halfway between north (0°) and east (90°).
That is 45°.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
questions.w: That is 45°.

questions.q: Where should you go in a house during a tornado warning?
sol: Get as low as you can and away from windows.
A basement or small interior room on the lowest floor.
From your notes · Hazards and safety: Actions: tornado = lowest floor, interior room, no windows.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
questions.w: A basement or small interior room on the lowest floor.

questions.q: A tornado watch means tornadoes are possible. A tornado warning means a tornado is…
sol: Warning means take action now.
It has been seen or radar shows rotation.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
questions.w: It has been seen or radar shows rotation.

questions.q: A radar image with a hook shape on the south side of a supercell is called a…
sol: The precipitation wraps around the rotation.
This is a hook echo.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
questions.w: This is a hook echo.

questions.q: On Doppler velocity radar, a tight pair of inbound and outbound winds next to each other shows…
sol: Green is toward the radar, red is away.
Side by side, they mean rotation.
From your notes · Tornadoes, scales, radar: TVSTight inbound-outbound velocity pair = intense rotation
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
questions.w: Side by side, they mean rotation.

questions.q: On radar, what is a debris ball (tornado debris signature) made of?
sol: Dust and objects lofted into the air.
Radar sees them as a signature.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
questions.w: Radar sees them as a signature.

questions.q: What do we call a huge spinning storm over warm ocean water with winds of 74 mph or more?
sol: Called typhoon or cyclone elsewhere.
74 mph is the threshold.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
questions.w: 74 mph is the threshold.

questions.q: In what season are most Atlantic hurricanes formed: summer-fall or winter?
sol: Ocean water is warmest then.
The Atlantic season is June 1 to November 30.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
questions.w: The Atlantic season is June 1 to November 30.

questions.q: A hurricane needs warm ocean water. About what temperature, in °C, is the minimum?
sol: Warm water supplies heat and moisture.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: The rising mound of ocean water pushed onto shore by a hurricane is the storm…
sol: It is the deadliest hurricane hazard.
Surge floods coastal areas.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
questions.w: Surge floods coastal areas.

questions.q: A tropical storm has winds of 65 mph. How many mph more are needed to be a hurricane (74 mph)?
sol: Subtract: 74 − 65.
9 mph.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
questions.w: 9 mph.

questions.q: What category is a hurricane with winds of 100 mph? (Cat 1: 74–95, Cat 2: 96–110, Cat 3: 111–129)
sol: 100 is between 96 and 110.
That is category 2.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
questions.w: That is category 2.

questions.q: Which side of a Northern Hemisphere hurricane moving north has the strongest winds: right or left?
sol: Storm motion adds to the wind speed on one side.
The right-front quadrant is strongest.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
questions.w: The right-front quadrant is strongest.

questions.q: How does a hurricane weaken when it moves over land: it loses its supply of…?
sol: Warm ocean water is the fuel.
Over land, friction also slows the wind.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
questions.w: Over land, friction also slows the wind.

questions.q: Which wintry precipitation builds up the heaviest ice on power lines: sleet or freezing rain?
sol: Sleet bounces like tiny pebbles.
Freezing rain sticks like glaze on a donut.
Glaze builds up on lines, so freezing rain is the line-breaker.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms
questions.w: Freezing rain freezes on contact and coats everything.

questions.q: Frozen raindrops that bounce off the ground as small ice pellets are…
sol: Rain freezes as it falls through a cold layer.
Sleet is ice pellets.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms
questions.w: Sleet is ice pellets.

questions.q: Rain that freezes when it touches the ground and coats everything with ice is…
sol: Drops are liquid until they touch cold surfaces.
Freezing rain makes roads very slippery.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms
questions.w: Freezing rain makes roads very slippery.

questions.q: A winter storm with strong winds and lots of blowing snow, with low visibility, is a…
sol: It needs winds of at least 35 mph for 3 hours.
Visibility is under 1/4 mile.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: BlizzardWind or gusts ≥ 35 mph + falling/blowing snow + visibility under ¼ mile, all for 3+ hours
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms
questions.w: Visibility is under 1/4 mile.

questions.q: What can make cold air feel even colder when the wind blows?
sol: Wind carries heat away from skin.
This is wind chill.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms
questions.w: This is wind chill.

questions.q: A snowfall is 24 cm. Assuming a 10:1 ratio, how many cm of liquid water does it contain?
sol: Divide by 10.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: For freezing rain, the temperature aloft is above 0 °C and at the ground is…
sol: A warm layer melts snow into rain.
Near the ground a thin cold layer refreezes the water on contact.
From your notes · Precipitation, flooding, IDF: SleetSnow melts, then refreezes as ice pellets in a cold layer near the ground
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms
questions.w: Near the ground a thin cold layer refreezes the water on contact.

questions.q: A lake-effect snow forms when cold air moves across what?
sol: Warm water adds heat and moisture.
Snow bands fall on the downwind shores.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: Lake effectCold air over warm open lake water, narrow heavy snow bands downwind
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms
questions.w: Snow bands fall on the downwind shores.

questions.q: A watch means be prepared. A warning means to…
sol: A warning means the hazard is happening or imminent.
Take action now.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety
questions.w: Take action now.

questions.q: What weather radio sounds a loud alarm to alert you of danger?
sol: It broadcasts alerts 24 hours a day.
A tone alert can wake you at night.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety
questions.w: A tone alert can wake you at night.

questions.q: A kit with water, food, flashlight and batteries for emergencies is an emergency…
sol: Keep it ready before a storm.
Enough for a few days.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety
questions.w: Enough for a few days.

questions.q: In a hurricane evacuation, you should follow orders from…
sol: They know the surge zones.
Follow their evacuation zones and routes.
From your notes · Hazards and safety: Hurricane = follow evacuation orders.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety
questions.w: Follow their evacuation zones and routes.

questions.q: A mobile home is safe in a tornado: true or false?
sol: Mobile homes are easily destroyed.
Go to a sturdy shelter.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety
questions.w: Go to a sturdy shelter.

questions.q: A family plans 4 liters of water per person per day for 3 days. There are 5 people. How many liters total?
sol: 4 L × 5 people × 3 days.
4 × 5 = 20 L per day.
20 × 3 = 60 L total.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: Why should you never run a generator indoors or in a garage?
sol: Engines make a deadly gas.
Carbon monoxide is odorless.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety
questions.w: Carbon monoxide is odorless.

questions.q: In what year did the Tri-State Tornado (the deadliest in U.S. history) occur?
sol: It crossed Missouri, Illinois and Indiana.
Notes|n-cases|Historic events and case analysis

questions.q: Hurricane Katrina (2005) caused major flooding in which U.S. city?
sol: Levees failed.
New Orleans.
Notes|n-cases|Historic events and case analysis
questions.w: New Orleans.

questions.q: The 1900 hurricane that killed thousands hit which Texas island city?
sol: It remains the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history.
Galveston.
Notes|n-cases|Historic events and case analysis
questions.w: Galveston.

questions.q: The 'Dust Bowl' of the 1930s was caused by drought and what kind of farming practices?
sol: Farmers plowed the prairie grass.
With drought, topsoil blew away.
Notes|n-cases|Historic events and case analysis
questions.w: With drought, topsoil blew away.

questions.q: The 2011 Joplin tornado hit which state?
sol: It was an EF5.
Missouri.
Notes|n-cases|Historic events and case analysis
questions.w: Missouri.

questions.q: The Tri-State Tornado track was about 219 miles long. At an average speed of 60 mph, how many hours did it take to travel that distance?
sol: Time = distance ÷ speed.
Notes|n-cases|Historic events and case analysis

questions.q: Hurricane Sandy (2012) was unusual because it merged with what kind of system before landfall?
sol: Sandy turned and merged with a cold front.
It became a large post-tropical storm.
Notes|n-cases|Historic events and case analysis
questions.w: It became a large post-tropical storm.

questions.q: The 1993 'Storm of the Century' brought snow to which part of the U.S.?
sol: It affected states from Alabama to Maine.
The East Coast.
Notes|n-cases|Historic events and case analysis
questions.w: The East Coast.

questions.q: After a historic case, weather scientists compile data to improve forecasts. This careful study is a…
sol: Look at what happened and why.
A case study.
Notes|n-cases|Historic events and case analysis
questions.w: A case study.

questions.q: A storm sits due north of a Doppler radar and the wind inside it blows straight from west to east. What does the radar's velocity product show for that wind?
o: Close to zero, because the wind moves across the beam, not along it
Strong outbound (red), because the wind is fast
Strong inbound (green), because the wind comes from the west
questions.w: Doppler radar only feels motion along its beam, toward or away.
sol: Picture the beam as a string from the radar to the storm. Doppler measures only how fast things slide along that string.
Wind crossing the string sideways adds nothing along it, so velocity reads near zero.
Common slip: thinking velocity shows true wind speed. It shows only the part of the wind along the beam.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: The beam points north. The wind blows at 40 kt from a direction that makes a 60° angle with the beam. What radial velocity does the radar measure (kt)?
questions.w: Radar sees only the part of the wind along the beam: speed × cos(angle).
sol: Radial speed = true speed × cos(angle between wind and beam).
At 90° the cosine is 0, which is why crosswind motion looks calm to radar. It is like feeling only the push straight at you when someone shoves you at an angle.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: On a velocity image you see a small, tight patch of bright green directly beside a bright red patch. Which description fits best?
o: Rotation: air moving toward and away from the radar at nearly the same spot
Heavy rain: green and red show rain rate
A cold front: green is cold and red is warm
Hail: green is small hail and red is large hail
questions.w: Inbound next to outbound in a small area means the air is spinning.
sol: Green means moving toward the radar. Red means moving away.
Side by side in a tiny area, the only way both can happen is spinning, like one side of a merry-go-round coming at you while the other side moves away.
This pattern is called a couplet. Color on velocity never shows rain, temperature or hail.
From your notes · Observation tools: Velocity: toward the radar is NEGATIVE (green).
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A radar pulse leaves, hits a storm, and its echo returns 1.2 milliseconds later. The pulse travels at 3.0×10⁸ m/s. How far away is the storm (km)?
questions.w: Distance = speed × time ÷ 2, because the pulse goes out and back.
sol: That is the round trip, so halve it: 180 km.
Like shouting at a far cliff: the echo time covers going and returning. Forgetting to halve is the common mistake.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A shallow storm 200 km from a radar produces only drizzle near the ground, yet the radar shows almost nothing. Why?
o: The beam passes above the low rain because it climbs as it travels
Drizzle drops are too large to reflect
Radar cannot detect any rain at night
The radar's wind profile is switched off
questions.w: Radar beams travel straight while Earth curves away, so far away they overshoot low weather.
sol: The beam starts about 0.5° above flat ground. Earth curves downward beneath it, so the beam gets higher above the ground with distance.
At 200 km it may be more than 3 km up, above shallow rain or snow.
Misconception: radar sees everything near the surface. Far from the site, it sees only the upper part of storms.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: On a clear calm morning a radar shows weak echoes in a ring around the site and no clouds are overhead. What are they most likely?
o: Insects, birds or ground clutter, not rain
Hail falling from a clear sky
questions.w: Radar returns come from anything that scatters the beam, not only raindrops.
sol: Radar bounces off whatever is in the beam: insects, birds, buildings, hills.
Near the site, ground clutter shows up as a ring or blobs even when it is dry.
Clue: weak echoes, clear sky, no motion pattern. Real rain would have a cloud overhead and a satellite view to match.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A radar shows an intense patch of 'heavy rain' on a clear, calm night after a cool night followed by a warm layer aloft (an inversion). Satellite shows no clouds. What is likely?
o: The inversion bent the beam down to the ground, giving false echoes
A tornado is hiding in clear air
Visible satellite is broken at night
questions.w: A temperature inversion can bend the radar beam toward the ground.
sol: Beams bend slightly depending on air density. Strong inversions bend them down more than usual.
The beam then strikes hills and buildings and looks like rain. This is called anomalous propagation.
Check other tools: no clouds on IR satellite and no reports of rain means the echo is false.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A fast outbound wind far above the radar's maximum measurable speed is displayed in the opposite color, as if it were inbound. What is this error called?
questions.w: Doppler can only unambiguously measure speeds up to a limit.
sol: Each radar has a Nyquist limit on measurable speed, like a clock face: a hand that goes past 12 starts over.
Speeds beyond the limit wrap around and appear with the wrong sign.
Misconception: the color is always right. Forecasters check for sudden sign flips next to very strong winds.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: In a tornadic storm, a hook echo on reflectivity sits with a velocity couplet. Dual-polarization correlation coefficient (CC) drops sharply inside the hook while reflectivity stays high. What does this combination suggest?
o: Debris lofted by a tornado, a strong sign it is on the ground
questions.w: High reflectivity plus low CC means a mix of target shapes and sizes, not uniform rain.
sol: CC measures how alike the targets are. Raindrops are similar, so rain gives CC near 1.
Leaves, dirt and pieces of buildings differ in size and shape, so CC falls (below about 0.8).
Together with rotation this is a tornado debris signature. A drop in CC alone is not enough; it can also be hail mixed with rain.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Select ALL targets that can produce a LOW correlation coefficient.
o: Flocks of birds or swarms of insects
questions.w: Low CC means the targets look different from each other.
sol: Rain is uniform, so CC stays near 1 and is not low.
Debris, hail mixed with rain, birds and insects all vary in size, shape and tumbling.
Think of a bag of identical marbles versus a bag of random junk: the junk gives scattered radar signals.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A radar reflectivity of 60 dBZ or more inside a storm usually points to…
o: Very heavy rain and possibly hail
questions.w: Reflectivity measures returned power. Bigger, more plentiful targets send back more.
sol: dBZ is a scale of echo strength. About 20 is light rain, 40 to 50 heavy rain.
Values of 60 or more mean very large or many targets, often large hail.
Misconception: high dBZ means high wind. It describes targets, not wind.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: An IR satellite shows a thunderstorm top at −45 °C. The ground is 25 °C. Temperature drops about 6.5 °C per km. About how high is the top (km)?
questions.w: Colder tops are higher, and the temperature drop tells you how far up.
sol: Total drop = 25 − (−45) = 70 °C.
IR sees only heat from the top. Cold equals high, like frost on the highest mountain peaks.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: On a night IR image, a low fog bank in a valley is almost invisible. Why?
o: Its top is nearly as warm as the ground, so it looks similar
Fog is too small for satellites to see anywhere
questions.w: IR images show temperature. Fog tops are low and warm.
sol: IR brightness depends on how cold the surface is. High cold tops stand out.
Fog tops are close to ground temperature, so they blend in, like a grey blanket on grey ground.
This is why forecasters use special channels or surface reports to find fog.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: On an enhanced water vapor image, a dark, dry-looking stripe curls into a storm system. What does the dark area usually show?
o: Dry air in the middle or upper levels
Land with no clouds at night
questions.w: Water vapor imagery reads moisture, not clouds on the ground.
sol: Water vapor channels show how much moisture is in the middle and upper air.
Dark areas mean dry air (less moisture to see). Bright areas mean moisture or high cloud.
Dry stripes wrapping into a storm often show where dry air is flowing in, so they help track the storm's circulation.
From your notes · Observation tools: Water vapor shows moisture in the middle and upper air.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the two main kinds of weather satellite?
o: Geostationary stays over one spot and shows the same region all the time; polar-orbiting circles pole to pole with more detail but passes only twice a day
Polar-orbiting satellites stay over one spot; geostationary ones circle the poles
Geostationary satellites orbit low and see the poles best; polar ones see the whole hemisphere
The two differ only in picture color
questions.w: A satellite 35,786 km up above the equator matches Earth's spin; a low one sweeps past.
sol: Geostationary orbit is high and matches Earth's rotation. It looks like a security camera, always on the same area.
Polar-orbiting satellites are lower, so they get sharper pictures and cover the poles, but each place gets a view only a couple of times a day. They are like a patrol car passing by.
Pick geostationary for tracking storms minute by minute.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A polar-orbiting weather satellite makes about 14 orbits in one 24-hour day. About how many minutes is one orbit?
questions.w: One orbit lasts a day divided by the orbits per day.
sol: 24 hours = 1440 minutes.
Low orbits are quick, like a runner on an inner track. A high geostationary orbit takes a full day.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A radiosonde balloon climbs at 5 m/s. About how many minutes to reach 25 km (25,000 m)?
questions.w: Time = distance ÷ speed, then change seconds to minutes.
sol: This is why a sounding takes well over an hour, and the instrument drifts far downwind while rising.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Why does a radiosonde balloon burst high in the atmosphere?
o: Outside pressure drops, so the balloon stretches until it pops
It runs out of helium and sinks
questions.w: The air gets thinner with height, so the gas inside expands.
sol: Air pressure falls steadily with height.
Gas inside pushes out harder than air outside, so the balloon grows, like a marshmallow in a vacuum.
At about 30 km it bursts. A parachute slows the instrument down. Misconception: heat pops it; actually it is expansion.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Why do radiosondes around the world launch at the same times (00Z and 12Z)?
o: So forecast models get a worldwide snapshot of the same moment
Because balloons rise only at those hours
So that each country uses its own local time
questions.w: Models need data that match in time to start forecasts.
sol: Computer models need a starting picture of the whole atmosphere.
Like a class photo, everyone must be in the picture at once.
Z is UTC. 12Z is early morning in California and 00Z is late afternoon.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: How are winds at each height found from a radiosonde flight?
o: By tracking how the balloon drifts, using GPS
By a cup anemometer on the balloon
By measuring how fast it rises
questions.w: The balloon moves with the wind like a leaf on a stream.
sol: The sonde measures temperature, pressure and humidity directly.
Winds come from tracking its position over time with GPS: how far it drifts in each minute.
A cup anemometer can't work on a drifting balloon, since it moves with the wind and feels almost no airflow.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Match each instrument to what it measures.
questions.w: Each name tells its job.
sol: Thermo = heat, baro = weight (pressure).
Anemo = wind.
Hygro = moisture.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Why is an official thermometer put in a shaded, ventilated shelter?
o: Sunlight on the sensor would read too warm; air flow keeps it at air temperature
So it stays dry in rain
To cool the air around it
Shade makes it more accurate at night only
questions.w: We want the temperature of the air, not of the thermometer.
sol: A thermometer in the sun heats like a dark car seat and reads above the real air temperature.
Shade stops sunlight; ventilation lets fresh air flow past so the reading matches the air.
This is why your car's temperature display is wrong when parked in the sun.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: On a sling psychrometer, the wet bulb thermometer reads lower than the dry bulb. When would they read the SAME?
o: When the air is saturated (100% humidity)
When the air is very dry
questions.w: Evaporation cools the wet bulb, and only works if the air can take more water.
sol: The wet bulb is wrapped in wet cloth. Evaporation cools it, like feeling cold after leaving a pool.
In dry air, evaporation is fast and the wet bulb reads much lower.
In saturated air there is no evaporation, so both match. Larger difference means drier air.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A narrow outflow boundary passes between two airports 80 km apart, and neither ASOS reports anything unusual. Which tool would best capture it?
o: A mesonet with stations every few km
A radiosonde from one of the airports
A polar-orbiting satellite pass the next day
questions.w: Dense networks fill gaps that spread-out stations miss.
sol: Features smaller than the station spacing slip through, like a fish through a wide net.
Mesonets place stations a few to tens of km apart and report often.
Radiosondes see height, not narrow ground features.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A rain gauge at a school reports 18 mm. Radar estimated 30 mm over the same spot. Which statement is best?
o: The gauge is a direct measure at one point; radar covers a wide area but is an estimate, so use both
Radar is always right, the gauge is broken
The gauge is always right, radar is useless
They must be averaged for every storm
questions.w: Direct measurement and wide coverage have different strengths.
sol: The gauge catches real water, but only where it sits.
Radar infers rain from echo strength over a whole region, so errors are possible (hail, beam height, drop size).
Forecasters use gauges to correct radar estimates, like checking a map against a few GPS points.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Put the steps of a radiosonde sounding in order.
items: Sensors measure temperature, pressure, humidity and radio the data down
Balloon expands and bursts high up
Instrument parachutes back to the ground
questions.w: The data come during the climb, not after.
sol: Launch and climb come first.
The sensors send data all the way up.
Burst happens at the top, then a parachute slows the fall.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A wind speed is 15 m/s. Convert to knots (1 m/s ≈ 1.944 kt).
questions.w: Multiply by the conversion factor.
sol: Round to about 29.2 kt.
A knot is smaller than a meter per second, so the number of knots must be larger.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: What is the name of the network of National Weather Service Doppler radars? (Give the short name.)
questions.w: It is the national radar network.
sol: NEXRAD stands for Next Generation Radar.
Its radars are called WSR-88D.
Each one is a Doppler radar, so it measures motion.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Why does the Doppler effect let radar measure wind motion?
o: The echo's frequency shifts up for approaching targets and down for receding ones
questions.w: Same idea as an ambulance siren that changes pitch when passing.
sol: An approaching siren sounds higher; as it passes and leaves, it drops lower.
Radar waves do the same: a higher return frequency means moving toward the radar, lower means away.
The size of the shift gives the speed along the beam.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A tornado-producing storm passes directly over a radar. Why might the radar fail to show the storm's top?
o: Its beam cannot point steeply enough, leaving a 'cone of silence' overhead
The radar only works for storms far away
Radar needs the storm to be rotating
questions.w: A radar's highest tilt is not straight up.
sol: The radar scans in tilted sweeps. The highest tilt is about 20° up.
Directly above, there is a cone-shaped gap that no tilt covers.
Like a flashlight tilted at an angle: you can't light the area right above your head.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Beam height ≈ r²/(2×(4/3)×6371) + r×sin(elevation), with r in km. For r = 120 km and elevation 0.5°, how high is the beam center (km)?
questions.w: Earth's curve and the beam's tilt both raise the beam above the ground.
sol: Sum ≈ 1.9 km. Like a ball moving across a curved globe: the farther you go, the higher the beam is above the surface.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A rain gauge catches rain in a narrow tube whose area is one-fifth of the funnel. The tube shows 2.0 cm. How much rain fell?
questions.w: The funnel collects over a larger area than the tube, so the depth is stretched in the tube.
sol: The funnel is 5 times wider in area, so water is 5 times deeper in the tube.
Divide: 2.0 ÷ 5 = 0.4 cm.
Like pouring a wide pond into a thin glass: the glass level looks much higher than the pond.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A storm moves toward the radar at 30 kt. Its own rotation has 20 kt winds. On base velocity both sides look inbound (green). What does storm relative motion do?
o: It removes the 30 kt, so one side turns outbound (red) and rotation becomes clear
It shows the rain rate instead
questions.w: Subtracting the storm's own motion reveals the spin.
sol: Base velocity: one side −50 kt (30 + 20), the other −10 kt. Both negative, so both green.
Subtract the storm's −30: one side becomes −20 (inbound), the other +20 (outbound).
Like watching a spinning wheel on a moving train: look at the wheel relative to the train to see the spin.
From your notes · Tornadoes, scales, radar: TVSTight inbound-outbound velocity pair = intense rotation
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Why are wind sensors usually placed about 10 m up in an open area?
o: So buildings and trees don't block or slow the wind, giving comparable readings
Because wind is always stronger on the ground
So they are hidden from birds
questions.w: Stations all need to measure under the same conditions to compare.
sol: Wind near the ground is slowed by friction from trees, buildings and fences.
A standard 10 m height in open ground makes stations comparable.
Like measuring a runner's speed: you must do it on a clear track, not in a crowd.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: Which choice is the best tool to see whether a thunderstorm complex is growing taller over the ocean at night?
questions.w: It must work at night and over water with no stations.
sol: Visible imagery needs sunlight.
IR works day or night and senses cloud-top temperature. Colder tops mean higher, stronger storms.
Surface stations don't exist over open ocean, so satellite is the choice.
Notes|n-obs|Observation tools

questions.q: A station model's pressure code is 500. What pressure is that?
questions.w: 500 or more gets a 9 in front.
sol: Codes of 500 or higher: put 9 in front, decimal before the last digit: 950.0.
Codes under 500 get a 10 in front. So 500 is the first code of the 9xx range.
Common slip: thinking 500 means 1050. Real surface pressures are between about 950 and 1050 mb, so only one choice is possible.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A station model's pressure code is 245. What is the pressure in mb?
questions.w: Under 500, put 10 in front.
sol: 245 is under 500, so add 10 in front: 10245.
Put the decimal before the last digit: 1024.5 mb.
Real pressures are near 1000, so 1024.5 is sensible; 924.5 would be unusually low.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A station model's pressure code is 603. What is the pressure in mb?
questions.w: 500 or more, put 9 in front.
sol: 603 is 500 or more, so add 9: 9603.
Decimal before the last digit: 960.3 mb.
960 mb is low pressure, a strong storm, which matches the guess that codes above 500 are low.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Two stations plot pressure codes 499 and 501. Which has the HIGHER pressure?
o: 501, because it is the bigger number
questions.w: The leading digit changes at 500, so the bigger code may be the lower pressure.
sol: 499 is under 500: add 10, giving 1049.9 mb.
501 is over 500: add 9, giving 950.1 mb.
The code is not a number line. It resets at 500, like a clock going from 12 to 1.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Three hours ago a station's pressure was 1010.5 mb. Now its code is 982. How much did the pressure change in mb (negative if it fell)?
questions.w: Decode the code first, then subtract.
sol: 982 is 500 or more: 998.2 mb.
A fall of more than 10 mb in 3 hours is dramatic, like a barometer dropping before a hurricane.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A wind barb has two pennants (triangles) and one half barb. What is the wind speed in knots?
questions.w: Pennant 50, full barb 10, half barb 5.
sol: Half barb: +5.
Total 105 kt, extremely strong, typical of jet-stream altitudes.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A wind barb has one pennant, three full barbs and one half barb. What is the wind speed in knots?
questions.w: Add each symbol's value.
sol: Pennant = 50.
Three full barbs = 30.
Half barb = 5. Total = 85 kt. Skipping the half barb gives 80, the usual slip.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Standing with your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere, where is low pressure?
questions.w: This is called Buys-Ballot's law.
sol: Wind circles counterclockwise around lows.
Imagine walking around a roundabout counterclockwise: the center is on your left.
With the wind at your back, you face the same direction the air is moving, so low pressure is to your left.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Near the surface, winds cross the isobars slightly toward lower pressure instead of blowing parallel. Why?
o: Friction slows the wind, so the pressure push wins over the sideways turn
Hot air rises in the center
questions.w: Two forces compete: pressure and Coriolis. Friction weakens one.
sol: Pressure pushes from high to low. Rotation (Coriolis) bends the wind sideways.
Aloft they balance and the wind blows parallel to isobars.
Near the ground friction slows the wind and weakens the bending, so air slides a little toward low pressure, like water going downhill but slowed by rough ground.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Isobars on a surface map are drawn every 4 mb starting from 1000 mb. Which of these values has an isobar?
questions.w: Multiples of 4 above 1000.
sol: 1016 fits; the others are not multiples of 4 steps.
Real maps use this fixed spacing so lines are easy to compare.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Isobars 4 mb apart are 100 km apart near city A and 250 km apart near city B. Where is the wind stronger, and why?
o: City A, since the pressure changes faster over distance
City B, since the isobars are far apart
Same, since both have the same 4 mb
questions.w: Wind depends on the pressure gradient.
sol: Pressure gradient is change in pressure per distance.
At A, 4 mb in 100 km is steeper than 4 mb in 250 km.
Like a steep hill: a ball rolls faster. Close isobars = steep hill = strong wind.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Isobars are 80 km apart and the wind is 30 kt. Assuming wind is proportional to the pressure gradient, what is the wind (kt) where the same isobars are 120 km apart?
questions.w: Larger spacing means a weaker gradient.
sol: Gradient ∝ 1 ÷ spacing.
Spacing grew by half, so the wind drops by one third. Like a gentler slope giving a slower roll.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A station's wind shifts from 200° to 320°, temperature falls 14 °F, dew point falls, and pressure bottoms out then rises. What passed?
questions.w: Wind veers clockwise and temperature drops behind a cold front.
sol: Behind a cold front, wind shifts from south-southwest to northwest, a clockwise turn.
Cooler, drier air arrives so temperature and dew point fall.
Pressure falls ahead of the front and rises as cold dense air arrives, like a heavy blanket settling on the ground.
From your notes · Station models and METAR: A station model packs temperature, dew point, pressure, wind and sky cover into one symbol.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A station's wind shifts from 120° to 210°, temperature rises from 55 °F to 68 °F and dew point rises. What passed?
questions.w: Warm moist air replaces cooler air.
sol: Behind a warm front the wind turns from southeast to south or southwest.
Temperature and dew point both rise as warm, humid air takes over.
Misconception: a wind shift always means cold air; the temperature change tells which.
From your notes · Station models and METAR: A station model packs temperature, dew point, pressure, wind and sky cover into one symbol.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A cold front is drawn with blue triangles pointing southeast. Which way is the front moving?
questions.w: Symbols point in the direction of motion.
sol: Triangles (cold) or half-circles (warm) point the way the front advances.
Triangles point southeast, so the front moves southeast.
A stationary front alternates sides, because it isn't going anywhere.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Station A (west) reports T 90 °F, dew point 35 °F. Station B, 80 km east, reports T 82 °F, dew point 68 °F. What boundary lies between them?
questions.w: A sharp dew point change with little temperature change marks dry and moist air masses.
sol: Dew point drops 33 °F in 80 km. That is a huge moisture contrast.
Temperature differs only 8 °F, so it is not mainly a cold front.
A dryline separates hot dry air from humid air. Storms can form along it, like where two different weather neighborhoods meet.
From your notes · Setup for severe weather: DrylineMoisture boundary (moist east, dry west on the Plains).
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: On a map, a purple line with alternating triangles and half-circles on the same side shows what?
questions.w: Occluded fronts form when a faster cold front catches a warm front.
sol: Occluded means the cold front overtook the warm front, lifting the warm air up.
Both symbols appear on the same side of the line.
Stationary fronts have them on opposite sides.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Altimeter setting A2992 means 29.92 inHg. Convert to mb (1 inHg = 33.86 mb), to the nearest 0.1.
questions.w: Multiply inches by 33.86.
sol: 29.92 × 33.86 ≈ 1013.1 (about 1013.2 with the more precise 33.864).
So 29.92 inHg is standard sea-level pressure, 1013.2 mb.
Memorize it: 29.92 inHg = 1013.2 mb.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Convert 1004 mb to inches of mercury (1 inHg = 33.86 mb), to the nearest 0.01.
questions.w: Divide mb by 33.86.
sol: Round: 29.65 inHg.
In a METAR it is written A2965, with no decimal point.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A METAR remark reads SLP045. What sea-level pressure is that?
questions.w: Same coding as station model pressure.
sol: SLP is sea-level pressure in the remarks, using the same code as station models.
045 is under 500: put 10 in front, add decimal: 1004.5.
Misreading it as 1045 forgets the decimal.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A METAR shows visibility 2 SM and BKN008. By flight categories (IFR ceiling 500 to under 1,000 ft, visibility 1 to under 3 mi), what is it?
questions.w: Use whichever of ceiling or visibility is worse.
sol: Ceiling is lowest BKN/OVC: 800 ft, which is IFR.
Visibility 2 miles is also IFR.
Both agree: IFR. If they disagreed, take the worse one, like a team limited by its weakest player.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A METAR reports FEW020 SCT040 BKN070 OVC120. What is the ceiling?
questions.w: Ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer.
sol: FEW and SCT layers don't count as a ceiling.
BKN070 is the lowest BKN or OVC, so ceiling = 7,000 ft.
Heights are in hundreds of feet.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A METAR gives visibility 6 SM and BKN030. Using VFR = ceiling above 3,000 ft and visibility above 5 mi, and MVFR = ceiling 1,000 to 3,000 ft or visibility 3 to 5 mi, what category is it?
o: MVFR, because a 3,000 ft ceiling is not above 3,000
questions.w: VFR needs the ceiling ABOVE 3,000 ft, so 3,000 exactly fails.
sol: Visibility 6 SM passes VFR.
Ceiling BKN030 = 3,000 ft. VFR needs more than 3,000, so it fails. MVFR covers 1,000 to 3,000 ft inclusive.
The worse factor wins: MVFR. Boundaries matter, like needing a score above 90 for an A, not equal to it.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A METAR temperature group reads 02/M01. What are the temperature and dew point?
questions.w: M means minus and it applies to the number right after it.
sol: Temperature first, dew point second.
02 has no M, so it is +2 °C.
M01 is −1 °C. Dew point below temperature, as it must be.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Which METAR temperature/dew point group cannot be right for a normal observation?
questions.w: Air cannot hold more than 100% humidity in normal conditions.
sol: Dew point is the temperature where the air is saturated. It can equal but not exceed the air temperature.
15/15 is saturated (fog or cloud). M02/M05 and 22/09 are allowed.
15/17 would mean over 100% humidity, which is an error.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: The surface temperature is 30 °C and the dew point is 18 °C. Cloud base ≈ 125 m for each °C of spread. About how high is the cloud base (m)?
questions.w: Spread = temperature − dew point.
sol: Smaller spread means lower base. Think of a rising bubble cooling until it hits its dew point, like a cold glass fogging.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Rule of thumb: relative humidity (%) ≈ 100 − 5 × (T − Td in °C). Find RH when T = 25 °C and Td = 15 °C.
questions.w: Compute the spread first.
sol: The exact answer is about 54%, so this is a quick estimate. Bigger spread = drier air.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A METAR was issued at 2053Z on December 5. What local time is that in California (PST = UTC − 8)?
questions.w: Subtract 8 hours from UTC.
sol: So it is 12:53 pm PST.
In summer (PDT = UTC − 7) it would be 1:53 pm.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A METAR is issued at 0215Z on December 6. What are the local date and time in California (PST = UTC − 8)?
questions.w: Subtracting past midnight changes the date.
sol: 02:15 − 8:00 is negative, so go back to the previous day.
The Z date is a day ahead of local time in the evening. Check the date first.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: In a METAR, wind reads 00000KT. What does it mean?
o: Wind from the north at 0 kt
questions.w: All zeros means no wind.
sol: Direction and speed are both zero.
The wind is calm, so there's no direction to report.
Variable winds are written VRB, such as VRB03KT.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Decode: KSJC 051953Z 31008KT 10SM FEW040 18/06 A3004. Which statement is correct?
o: Wind from the northwest at 8 kt, fairly dry air
Wind toward 310° at 8 kt, humid air
Wind from the northwest at 80 kt, storm
questions.w: Read it group by group.
sol: 310° is northwest, and the wind is FROM that direction. 08KT is 8 knots.
18/06 gives a spread of 12 °C: dry air, with a high cloud base. 10SM is excellent visibility.
FEW040 means just a few clouds at 4,000 ft. No storm.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, a station is directly north of a surface low-pressure center. In general, from which direction does its wind blow?
o: From the east (a bit northeast with friction)
questions.w: Winds circle counterclockwise around lows.
sol: Counterclockwise: picture the top of a clock moving left, that is toward the west.
The wind moving toward the west is a wind FROM the east.
Friction turns it slightly inward, giving northeast to east. People often give the direction the wind goes instead of where it comes from.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: Nor'easterStrong East Coast storm; northeast winds; snow, coastal flooding, wind
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A station lies directly east of a surface high in the Northern Hemisphere. Wind blows from which direction?
questions.w: Winds circle clockwise around highs.
sol: Clockwise: the east side of the circle (3 o'clock) moves downward, toward the south.
Moving toward the south is a wind FROM the north.
Check by opposite: east of a low would be a south wind.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A sky that is 6/8 covered by cloud is reported in METAR as…
questions.w: Broken = 5 to 7 eighths.
sol: FEW 1 to 2, SCT 3 to 4, BKN 5 to 7, OVC 8.
6 is in 5 to 7: broken.
Remember the order: Few, Scattered, Broken, Overcast, clouds filling the sky.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: In a METAR wind such as 27012KT, what does KT stand for?
questions.w: It is the unit.
sol: KT = knots, a nautical mile per hour.
1 knot is about 1.15 mph.
The first three digits are direction, next two (or three) the speed.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: Which evening set-up makes radiation fog most likely?
