o: Clear sky, calm wind, temperature 12 °C and dew point 10 °C
Cloudy sky, strong wind, temperature 20 °C and dew point 5 °C
Clear sky, calm wind, temperature 25 °C and dew point 2 °C
Overcast, wind 25 kt, temperature 10 °C and dew point 9 °C
questions.w: You need the air to cool to the dew point and little mixing.
sol: Clear skies let heat escape at night so the ground cools quickly.
A small spread (2 °C) means only a little more cooling reaches saturation. Calm wind keeps the fog layer from mixing away.
Strong winds stir the air, and clouds keep heat in, like a blanket.
From your notes · Station models and METAR: A station model packs temperature, dew point, pressure, wind and sky cover into one symbol.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A wind barb's staff points toward the southwest with 20 kt. Where is the wind going?
questions.w: Staff points to where wind comes from.
sol: Staff toward the southwest means the wind comes from the southwest.
It travels the opposite direction: toward the northeast.
A weather vane points the same way.
From your notes · Station models and METAR: Barb staffPoints toward where wind COMES FROM
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: A station reports pressure falling 7 mb in 3 hours, wind shifting from south to southwest, temperature 88 °F and dew point 70 °F. What does a forecaster most likely expect next?
o: A cold front arriving soon, with storms possible in the warm humid air
Clear and cool weather within the hour
A warm front with steady drizzle
questions.w: Combine all clues instead of one.
sol: Falling pressure means a low or front is approaching.
A wind shift toward the southwest ahead of a front, with warm moist air (dew point 70 °F), supplies fuel for storms.
Any single clue is weak. Together they are a classic warm-sector setup before a cold front.
Notes|n-maps|Station models and METAR

questions.q: About how high above sea level is the 500 mb level?
questions.w: Half the air's weight is below 500 mb, so it sits around 5.5 km up.
sol: Pressure is the weight of the air stack above you. Climb until half the stack is below you and you are near 500 mb.
Half the atmosphere's mass lies below about 5.5 km, so 500 mb (half of ~1000 mb) is there.
Memory ladder: 850 mb ≈ 1.5 km, 700 mb ≈ 3 km, 500 mb ≈ 5.5 km, 300 mb ≈ 9 km.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Order these upper-air levels from lowest altitude to highest.
questions.w: Lower pressure means higher up.
sol: Think of a stack of blankets: the more blankets on top of you, the higher the pressure. Fewer blankets means you are higher.
So pressure number goes down as height goes up: 850, 700, 500, 300.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A wind barb has one flag (pennant), two long barbs and one short barb. Using 50 kt per flag, 10 kt per long barb and 5 kt per short barb, what is the wind speed in knots?
questions.w: Add the pieces: 50 + 10 + 10 + 5 = 75 kt.
sol: A barb is like Roman numerals for wind: each mark has a fixed value you add up.
Flag = 50, long barb = 10, short barb = 5.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: On a wind barb, the long staff (the line the feathers attach to) points toward the direction the wind…
questions.w: The staff points into the wind, like a weather vane pointing at the source.
sol: A barb is like an arrow that has been flipped: the staff points to where the wind starts.
A staff pointing west with barbs means a west wind, blowing toward the east.
Common mix-up: students read it as where the air is going.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: On a 500 mb map, which feature is a trough?
o: A dip in the height lines, bending toward lower heights
A bulge in the height lines toward the north
A closed ring of the highest temperatures
questions.w: Troughs are valleys in the wave pattern at 500 mb.
sol: Picture a rope wiggling in the wind. The low dip is a trough and the high bump is a ridge.
Troughs bring rising air and unsettled weather ahead of them. Ridges bring sinking, warmer, drier air.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A 500 mb trough is moving east across Kansas. Where is the large-scale lift strongest?
o: Ahead of (east of) the trough axis
questions.w: Air spreading apart aloft downstream of a trough pulls air upward.
sol: Think of a crowd leaving a stadium: if the exit spreads out ahead, people from behind are pulled forward. Air aloft ahead of a trough spreads out and pulls air up from below.
That rising air cools and makes clouds and storms, so the weather turns stormy before the trough arrives.
Behind the trough, air sinks and skies clear.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: The surface air is 30 °C and the dew point is 18 °C. Use LCL ≈ 125 m × (T − Td). A dry parcel cools 10 °C per km up to the LCL. What is the parcel's temperature at the cloud base, in °C?
questions.w: LCL = 1.5 km, and the parcel cools 15 °C on the way up.
sol: First find the cloud base: 125 × 12 = 1500 m = 1.5 km.
A rising parcel cools 10 °C per km while it is dry: 1.5 × 10 = 15 °C of cooling.
30 − 15 = 15 °C. Notice the dew point fell to about the same value: that is why the cloud forms.
From your notes · Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE: LCL (m) ≈ 125 × (T − Td in °C)Dry parcel cools 10 °C per km.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Surface T = 30 °C, Td = 18 °C. A parcel rises to the cloud base (LCL = 125 m × spread, cooling 10 °C/km) and then keeps rising, cooling 6 °C per km inside cloud. What is its temperature at 4 km above the ground, in °C?
questions.w: Two stages: 15 °C at 1.5 km, then 2.5 km × 6 °C = 15 °C more of cooling.
sol: Stage 1 (dry): LCL = 125 × 12 = 1500 m. Parcel cools 1.5 × 10 = 15 °C, so it is 15 °C at 1.5 km.
Stage 2 (cloudy): condensation releases heat like a tiny heater, so the parcel cools slower: 6 °C per km. From 1.5 to 4 km is 2.5 km, so 2.5 × 6 = 15 °C.
15 − 15 = 0 °C. Common error: using 10 °C per km all the way gives −10 °C.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A surface temperature is 35 °C and the dew point is 20 °C. Estimate the cloud base (LCL) height in meters using 125 m per °C of spread.
questions.w: Spread = 15 °C and 15 × 125 = 1875 m.
sol: The LCL grows with the gap between T and Td. A big gap means dry air, so the parcel must rise far before it saturates.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A storm chaser sees a cloud base at 2,000 m. The surface temperature is 33 °C. Using LCL = 125 m × (T − Td), what is the surface dew point in °C?
questions.w: Work backward: 2000 ÷ 125 = 16 °C of spread.
sol: The formula can run backward. Spread = LCL ÷ 125 = 2000 ÷ 125 = 16 °C.
Td = T − spread = 33 − 16 = 17 °C.
A cloud base this high means fairly dry surface air, a hint of hail or wind more than tornadoes.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A lifted parcel is 8 °C at 3 km. The surrounding air at 3 km is 3 °C. What happens next?
o: The parcel is warmer, so it keeps rising
The parcel is colder, so it sinks
The parcel stops because it is saturated
questions.w: A parcel warmer than its surroundings is lighter and keeps accelerating upward.
sol: Think of a hot-air balloon: it rises because the air inside is warmer, hence lighter, than the air outside.
Compare the parcel to the environment at the same height. 8 °C is warmer than 3 °C, so it is buoyant.
CAPE adds up this warmth advantage over the whole climb.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: The air around you cools 4 °C per km with height. A dry parcel you push upward cools 10 °C per km. What happens if you lift it and let go?
o: It becomes colder than its surroundings and sinks back (stable)
It becomes warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising
It stays at the same temperature
It turns into a cloud immediately
questions.w: A parcel that cools faster than the surroundings ends up heavier than them.
sol: Race two cars down a hill: the environment cools slowly (4 °C/km), the parcel cools fast (10 °C/km), so the parcel falls behind in temperature.
After 1 km: parcel −10 °C, environment −4 °C, so the parcel is 6 °C colder and denser.
Colder, denser air sinks. That is stable air, like a ball in a bowl.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: The air around you cools 8 °C per km. A dry parcel cools 10 °C per km, but a saturated (cloudy) parcel only cools 6 °C per km. This layer is called…
o: Conditionally unstable: stable when dry, unstable once saturated
questions.w: The environment lapse rate lies between the dry and saturated rates.
sol: Dry parcel: cools faster (10) than the air (8), so it ends up colder and sinks. Stable.
Saturated parcel: cools slower (6) than the air (8), so it ends up warmer and rises. Unstable.
So the answer depends on a condition: whether the parcel is saturated. That is why this is the most common severe-weather setup.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A hot summer afternoon: the air right above a parking lot cools 11 °C per km with height. Compared with the 10 °C/km dry parcel rate, this is…
o: Absolutely unstable: a lifted dry parcel stays warmer than its surroundings
questions.w: Environment cooling faster than 10 °C/km makes any lifted parcel buoyant.
sol: After 1 km a dry parcel is 10 °C cooler but the air is 11 °C cooler, so the parcel is 1 °C warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising.
This only happens near very hot ground and is the reason dust devils form.
Think of a hot stovetop under a pot of water: the bottom layer is too hot to stay put.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A sounding shows 16 °C at 1.5 km (850 mb) and −12 °C at 5.5 km (500 mb). What is the average lapse rate in °C per km?
questions.w: Cooling of 28 °C over a 4 km climb is 7 °C per km.
sol: Lapse rate = temperature drop ÷ height climbed.
Drop = 16 − (−12) = 28 °C. Careful with the negative sign.
Height = 5.5 − 1.5 = 4 km, so 28 ÷ 4 = 7 °C/km, a little steeper than the 6.5 average.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: The temperatures at the surface, 1 km, and 2 km are 24 °C, 27 °C, and 20 °C. Which layer is an inversion?
o: Surface to 2 km as a whole
questions.w: An inversion is any layer where temperature goes UP with height.
sol: Look at each layer separately, not the total: 24 → 27 °C is a rise, so that layer is an inversion.
1 → 2 km: 27 → 20 is a normal drop.
A thin inversion like this acts like a lid (a cap) on rising parcels.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: What does CIN (convective inhibition) measure on a sounding?
o: The energy barrier a parcel must overcome to rise freely
questions.w: CIN is the 'speed bump' energy: how strong the cap is.
sol: Picture a ball that must be pushed over a hill before it rolls down the other side. CIN is the height of that hill, CAPE is the drop after it.
Large CIN (a strong cap) means storms need a strong trigger, like a front or dryline.
CIN is measured in J/kg, just like CAPE.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A morning sounding shows large CAPE and a strong cap. By afternoon the sun heats the ground 8 °C. How can this lead to explosive storms?
o: Heated surface parcels can break through the cap, releasing the stored CAPE all at once
Heating makes the wind shear zero
questions.w: A strong cap stores energy until a warmer parcel finally pushes through.
sol: Think of a shaken soda with a lid: pressure builds, and when the lid pops it all comes out at once.
Warmer surface parcels need less lift to reach the temperature of the air above the cap.
This 'loaded gun' setup gives few storms, but the ones that do form can be violent.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Forecasters call a sounding with a lot of CAPE under a strong cap a 'loaded gun.' Why?
o: Few storms form, but any that break the cap can be violent
questions.w: A cap delays storms but lets energy pile up.
sol: A cap keeps storms from starting early and using up the fuel.
When one finally breaks through at a boundary, it has loads of stored energy.
Misconception: a cap means a quiet day. It can mean a dangerous one if a trigger arrives.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: The surface wind is 30 kt from the south (blowing toward the north) and the wind at 6 km is 40 kt from the west (blowing toward the east). What is the size of the wind shear vector in knots?
questions.w: Shear is the vector difference, and here it forms a 3-4-5 right triangle.
sol: Shear is the change in wind, so you subtract the vectors, not the speeds. Speeds alone (40 − 30 = 10) would hide the turning.
North 30 and east 40 are at right angles, so the difference is the hypotenuse of a right triangle: √(30² + 40²).
√(900 + 1600) = √2500 = 50 kt. Strong turning plus speed makes 50 kt of shear, supportive of supercells.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: The surface wind is 20 kt blowing toward the west (an east wind). The wind at 6 km is 15 kt blowing toward the south (a north wind). What is the size of the wind shear vector in knots?
questions.w: Subtract the vectors: the two arrows are at right angles, so use √(20² + 15²).
sol: Draw the surface arrow pointing west and the 6 km arrow pointing south. The shear is the arrow from the tip of the lower one to the tip of the upper one.
Because west and south are at right angles, shear = √(20² + 15²).
√(400 + 225) = √625 = 25 kt. Adding speeds (35) is wrong: the arrows are not in line.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: The wind is from the southeast at the surface, south-southwest at 850 mb, and west at 500 mb. This turning with height is called…
questions.w: Southeast → southwest → west is a clockwise turn on a compass.
sol: Picture the compass: SE (135°), SSW (200°), W (270°). Numbers increase, so you turn clockwise.
Clockwise turning with height is veering, which in the Northern Hemisphere favors right-moving supercells.
Backing is the opposite, and is a warning sign that the setup is less favorable.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: On a hodograph, the curve bends clockwise with height. What type of storm motion does this favor in the Northern Hemisphere?
o: A right-moving supercell that deviates to the right of the mean wind
A storm that rotates clockwise only at the ground
questions.w: Clockwise turning favors storms that track right of the average wind.
sol: The hodograph curve is the 'turning staircase' of the wind. A clockwise staircase pushes updraft rotation in a way that favors the right flank.
Right-movers are the long-lived tornadic supercells most chasers watch.
Misconception: the hodograph shows storm movement. It shows the wind profile that causes it.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Tornado forecasters care about wind shear in the lowest 1 km in particular. Why?
o: Spin in the lowest layer is closest to the ground, where tornadoes form
The lowest 1 km has no air
Shear above 6 km is always zero
questions.w: Low-level turning gives spin that can be stretched into a tornado near the ground.
sol: Think of rolling a pencil between your hands near a table: the spinning air close to the ground is what gets pulled up into the storm's base.
Deep-layer shear (0–6 km) tells if a storm will be organized. Low-level shear tells if the rotation can reach the ground.
Combine with a low LCL for the best tornado setup.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Dry air at 700 mb on a sounding, above a moist low level, mainly raises the risk of…
o: Strong downdrafts and damaging winds as rain evaporates
questions.w: Rain falling into dry air evaporates, cools, and sinks fast.
sol: Evaporation takes heat from the air, like sweat cooling your skin. The cooled air gets denser and plunges.
A deep dry layer above moist low levels is the classic downburst setup.
Dry air aloft can also help large hail.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Which sounding feature most directly helps large hail grow?
o: A strong, long updraft (large CAPE) with a low freezing level
Saturated air near the ground only
questions.w: Hail grows in strong updrafts that hold ice aloft where it is cold.
sol: Think of a hailstone as an onion growing layer by layer; it needs to ride a strong updraft many minutes.
A lower freezing level means the stone spends less time melting on the way down.
Large CAPE means a strong updraft, enough to support heavy stones.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: The surface temperature is 26 °C and temperature falls 6.5 °C per km. At about what height (in km) is the freezing level?
sol: The freezing level is where temperature reaches 0 °C.
Divide the drop needed by the rate: 26 ÷ 6.5 = 4.0 km.
Hail forms and falls from near this level up, so a lower freezing level helps stones reach the ground.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Air with a temperature of −5 °C sinks 3 km in a dry downdraft, warming 10 °C per km (no evaporation). What is its temperature, in °C, at the ground?
questions.w: Sinking air warms by compression: 3 × 10 = 30 °C of warming.
sol: Compression warms air, like a bicycle pump heating up.
Warming = 10 °C/km × 3 km = 30 °C.
−5 + 30 = 25 °C. Chinook and Santa Ana winds work this way.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: The theoretical maximum updraft speed is w = √(2 × CAPE). For a CAPE of 1,250 J/kg, what is w in m/s?
sol: CAPE is energy per kilogram, like the energy a car has before braking. Turn all of it into motion: ½w² = CAPE.
Real updrafts are usually about half of this because of drag and mixing.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A CAPE of 4,200 J/kg is best described as…
questions.w: Over 4,000 J/kg is extreme in this scale.
sol: Use the ladder: under 1,000 marginal, 1,000–2,500 moderate, 2,500–4,000 strong, over 4,000 extreme.
4,200 is above the top step.
Big CAPE alone does not mean tornadoes: shear and a trigger matter too.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: On a sounding, the temperature and dew point lines are 15 °C apart from 800 to 600 mb. What does this say about that layer?
questions.w: A big gap between T and Td means low humidity.
sol: Dew point is the temperature the air would need to cool to for cloud. A wide gap means a long way to go.
Lines touching mean cloud, lines far apart mean dry air.
Dry mid-levels can strengthen downdrafts.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A 300 mb jet is far stronger than usual over the Plains, above a developing surface low. How does the jet help the surface low strengthen?
o: Air spreading apart (diverging) aloft pulls air up from below, lowering surface pressure
It pushes cold air straight down to the ground
questions.w: Divergence aloft lowers pressure below.
sol: Picture a vacuum cleaner on the top of the column: air leaving the top draws air up from the bottom.
Less air in the column means lower surface pressure, so the low deepens.
This is why strong jets, deep lows and severe outbreaks go together.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Why is the jet stream usually strongest in winter?
o: The temperature contrast between cold polar air and warm tropical air is greatest
The sun is closest to the poles
questions.w: Jet winds are driven by how sharply temperature changes from north to south.
sol: A bigger temperature gap is like a steeper hill: the air flows faster down it.
In winter the pole is very cold while the tropics stay warm.
In spring the jet moves north and weakens, but it can still overlap warm Gulf air to make severe storms.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A forecaster has a sounding with CAPE of 3,000 J/kg, deep moisture, a weak cap, and 10 kt of 0–6 km shear. What is the likely storm mode?
o: Disorganized pulse storms that collapse quickly
questions.w: Fuel without shear makes short-lived storms.
sol: Without shear, rain falls straight down through the updraft and chokes it, like a person cutting off their own air supply.
Pulse storms can still produce hail and microbursts for a short time.
Supercells need shear around 40 kt or more.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: At what height is the equilibrium level (EL) of a thunderstorm parcel found?
o: Where the rising parcel is no longer warmer than its surroundings, near the storm top
Where the dew point is highest
questions.w: The EL marks where buoyancy ends, close to the anvil level.
sol: A parcel rises while it is warmer than its surroundings. At the EL the temperatures match, so buoyancy ends.
Momentum carries it a bit higher: that is the overshooting top.
Spread at the tropopause makes the anvil.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Select ALL features you can read directly from a skew-T sounding.
o: Temperature and dew point at each pressure
How far T and Td are apart (dryness)
questions.w: A sounding shows how T and Td change with height, not radar or past rain.
sol: A sounding is a weather balloon's vertical profile of T, Td, and wind.
Inversions show as T rising with height, and dryness as a wide T–Td gap.
Radar and rainfall totals come from other tools.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Why does a long path on a hodograph mean strong shear?
o: Each point is the wind at a height, so a long path means the wind changes a lot with height
questions.w: The farther apart the points, the bigger the wind change.
sol: Each dot is one height's wind. Connect the dots like a path between two cities.
A short path means the winds are almost the same at all heights, little shear.
A long, curved path means lots of change in both speed and direction.
From your notes · Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE: A long, curving path means strong shear.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Which pair of 850 mb and 500 mb conditions makes the best recipe for steep mid-level cooling that supports big CAPE?
o: Warm, moist air at 850 mb with cold air at 500 mb
Cold air at 850 mb and warm air at 500 mb
questions.w: Warm and moist below with cold above makes a steep lapse rate.
sol: A steep temperature drop with height makes lifted parcels stay warmer than their surroundings.
Warm and moist at 850 supplies fuel, cold at 500 gives the buoyancy push.
Warm at 500 mb would cap the atmosphere.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Rising dry air cools by about how many °C per kilometer?
questions.w: Dry air cools about 10 °C for each kilometer it rises.
sol: As a parcel rises, pressure falls and it expands. Expanding takes energy, so it cools, like spray from a can feeling cold.
Dry rate: 10 °C/km. After condensation starts, the rate slows to roughly 6 °C/km.
Average real air: 6.5 °C/km.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A sounding has a surface cap at 900 mb, then a very deep dry layer, then cold air aloft. A storm forms along a dryline and rises through the cap. Which hazard is most likely from the dry layer?
o: Strong downdrafts and damaging outflow winds
questions.w: Rain falling through dry air evaporates and cools, speeding the downdraft.
sol: Step 1: the cap breaks and the storm forms.
Step 2: precipitation falls into dry air and evaporates.
Step 3: evaporation cools the air, so it sinks fast and spreads out as damaging wind.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: A student reads: 'LCL is low and shear is strong, so a tornado WILL happen.' What is wrong?
o: Favorable ingredients raise the odds but do not guarantee a tornado
Tornadoes only occur with a high LCL
questions.w: A forecast is about probability, not certainty.
sol: Ingredients are like the ingredients for a cake: you can have them all and still make a mess.
A trigger, storm interactions and details near the ground still decide.
A good forecast says 'the risk is higher', not 'it will happen'.
Notes|n-upper|Upper air, soundings, LCL, CAPE

questions.q: Match each front to its main feature.
pairs: Cold air pushes warm air up fast, sharp storms
Warm air slides over cold air, wide steady rain
Cold front has caught up to a warm front
questions.w: Each front is named for which air mass is winning.
sol: Cold front: cold air advances like a snowplow under warm air.
Warm front: warm air climbs a gentle ramp over cold air.
Stationary: neither side wins. Occluded: the faster cold front catches the slower warm front.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Which wind shift usually happens when a cold front passes in the Northern Hemisphere?
questions.w: Wind turns clockwise to the northwest behind the front.
sol: Ahead of the front, warm air flows from the south or southwest.
Behind it, cold air flows from the northwest.
Pressure also rises and dew points fall.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: As a warm front approaches, the sequence of clouds is usually…
o: Cirrus, then thicker layers, then steady rain clouds
questions.w: Warm air slides up a gentle slope, so clouds lower and thicken over many hours.
sol: Picture a long ramp: you see the highest wisps first and then lower layers.
That's why light signs hours ahead, like halos, signal a warm front.
Cold fronts are steep, so storms come with little warning.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Why do cold fronts usually bring a narrow band of intense storms but warm fronts bring wide, steady rain?
o: Cold fronts are steeper and faster, so lift is stronger and short
questions.w: Steeper slope means stronger lift in a smaller area.
sol: A cold front acts like a steep bulldozer scoop, forcing air up quickly.
A warm front is a long gentle ramp, so lift is gentle but widespread.
Quick lift makes cumulonimbus, gentle lift makes layered clouds.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: A cold front is 240 km away and moves toward you at 40 km/h. About how many hours until it arrives?
sol: Time = distance ÷ speed.
Fronts can speed up or slow down, so treat it as an estimate.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: A cold front passes. Which pairing of changes is typical?
o: Temperature falls, pressure rises, dew point drops
questions.w: Cold, dry, dense air replaces warm, moist air.
sol: Dense cold air presses down harder, so pressure goes up.
Cold air from Canada is also drier, so the dew point falls.
Ahead of the front, pressure was falling.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: A storm chaser wants to find lift on the Plains. Which boundary is mainly a MOISTURE boundary, not a temperature boundary?
questions.w: The dryline separates moist Gulf air from dry desert air.
sol: Fronts are named for temperature. The dryline is named for dryness.
Dew points can fall from 65 °F to 35 °F across just a few miles.
Often the dry side is hotter, which surprises people.
From your notes · Setup for severe weather: DrylineMoisture boundary (moist east, dry west on the Plains).
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Two stations: A reports T 72 °F, Td 66 °F. B reports T 78 °F, Td 40 °F. A dryline lies between them. Which side is east?
questions.w: On the Plains the moist Gulf air is to the east of the dryline.
sol: Compare dew points, not temperatures. A has a high dew point (moist), B has a low one (dry).
Moist Gulf air lies east of the dryline.
So A is east. Misconception: a dryline is a temperature boundary; here the dry side is actually warmer.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Why do storms often start along a dryline in the afternoon?
o: Air converges there and is forced upward, and daytime heating helps
Cold air pushes in from Canada
questions.w: Converging air must rise, and afternoon heat adds fuel.
sol: Two streams of air running into each other have nowhere to go but up, like cars merging into one lane.
Afternoon heating weakens the cap and lifts parcels.
Storms often pop up in a line along the boundary.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: On the Plains, the dryline usually moves…
o: East during the day and back west at night
West during the day and east at night
questions.w: Daytime mixing pulls dry air eastward, and night allows moisture to return.
sol: Sunshine stirs the air, bringing dry air from aloft down to the surface and pushing the dryline east.
After sunset, mixing stops and moist air flows back west on the low-level jet.
So chasers watch its position hour by hour.
From your notes · Setup for severe weather: DrylineMoisture boundary (moist east, dry west on the Plains).
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a way to lift air into a storm?
o: Sinking air in a high-pressure center
questions.w: Sinking air warms and dries, which suppresses storms.
sol: Lift mechanisms push or pull air upward.
Fronts, mountains, outflow boundaries and sea breezes all do.
High pressure is the opposite: air sinks, skies stay clear.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Select ALL that can trigger thunderstorms by lifting air.
o: Outflow boundary from an earlier storm
Center of a strong high pressure
questions.w: Lift comes from converging air or terrain. Highs mean sinking air.
sol: Fronts, drylines, outflow boundaries and sea-breeze fronts all force air to converge and rise.
An outflow boundary is a mini cold front made by a storm's cool downdraft.
A high's sinking air suppresses storms.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: An old thunderstorm sent out a boundary of cool air. Why can it trigger new storms?
o: It acts like a small cold front lifting the warm air
questions.w: The cool pool shoves warm air up where it meets warmer air.
sol: The cool air is denser, so it spreads out under the warm air like a tiny cold front.
Warm moist air riding up over it can fire storms hours later.
Forecasters watch radar for thin lines called outflow boundaries.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: What is a low-level jet?
o: A ribbon of fast wind a few hundred to a thousand meters up
questions.w: It carries moisture north on the Plains.
sol: It is much lower than the high jet stream, near 850 mb.
It often blows from the south, bringing Gulf moisture.
It is strongest after midnight.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Why does the low-level jet often speed up after sunset?
o: The ground cools, so the surface layer is cut off from friction and the air above speeds up
questions.w: At night, friction no longer slows the air just above the surface layer.
sol: By day, mixing connects the wind to the slow-moving ground, like a ball of dough sticking to a table.
At night a cool layer forms at the ground and the winds above slide freely.
This speeds up moisture transport and adds low-level shear for night tornadoes.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Strong vertical wind shear HELPS thunderstorms organize into supercells but HURTS most hurricanes. Why?
o: Shear tilts a hurricane's warm core and blows its tops away, but tilts a supercell's updraft away from its rain
Shear has the same effect on both
questions.w: A hurricane needs a tall, stacked column; a supercell needs a tilted one.
sol: Hurricane: stacked like a smokestack. Shear leans it over and mixes dry air in.
Supercell: tilting separates the updraft from the cold rain downdraft so the storm can keep going.
Contrast the two cases rather than memorizing 'shear is good/bad'.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Which setup is best for supercells?
o: Gulf moisture, steep lapse rates, and strong turning shear
Cold dry air and light wind
A stable cap over weak winds
questions.w: You need fuel (moisture, instability) and organization (shear).
sol: Moisture and instability give fuel.
Strong, turning shear provides rotation and storm longevity.
Missing any one of these usually reduces the severe threat.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Which factor lets wave heights grow bigger: a longer fetch or a shorter fetch (same wind)?
questions.w: Wind has more distance to pass energy to the water.
sol: Fetch is the stretch of open water the wind blows across, like how long you push a swing.
More distance and time means more energy transferred to the waves.
Wave height depends on wind speed, duration and fetch.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Select ALL that make bigger wind waves.
questions.w: Three factors build waves: wind speed, duration, and fetch.
sol: More wind, more time, more distance means more energy.
Less open water limits fetch.
Calm air adds no energy.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Hurricanes need ocean water at least about…
questions.w: Warm ocean water is the fuel.
sol: Warm water evaporates heat and moisture into the storm like a stove under a pot.
The warmth must be deep (50 m or more), or mixing brings up cool water.
Cool wakes weaken storms that follow.
From your notes · Setup for severe weather: Ocean heat contentWarm deep water fuels hurricanes.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: A hurricane moves over a deep warm eddy of Gulf water. What will probably happen?
questions.w: Deep warm water means more fuel and little cooling from mixing.
sol: Ocean heat content measures how deep the warmth goes.
A hurricane stirs up water from below. If that water is still warm, no cooling happens.
Over thin warm layers, stirring brings up cold water and weakens the storm.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Moist air flows up the windward slope of a mountain and rains there. What is the dry area on the lee side called?
questions.w: Air loses its moisture on the way up and arrives dry on the other side.
sol: Lifting cools air so rain falls on the windward side.
The air sinks on the lee side and warms, becoming drier.
Deserts often sit in a rain shadow.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: An atmospheric river hits the California coast and rises over the coastal mountains. Why does this raise flood risk?
o: Lifting wrings out the heavy water vapor as intense rain
questions.w: Mountains force the vapor up, where it cools and condenses.
sol: Think of squeezing a wet sponge: lift squeezes out the water.
An atmospheric river is a narrow stream of very moist air, like a firehose in the sky.
Steady supply plus lift for hours means flooding and landslides.
From your notes · Setup for severe weather: Atmospheric riverNarrow stream of heavy water vapor.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Which statement about an atmospheric river is right?
o: It is a long, narrow band of strong water vapor transport
It is a type of tornado
questions.w: It is a stream of water vapor in the sky.
sol: It transports vapor, not liquid water.
Some reach California from near Hawaii (the 'Pineapple Express').
Landfall with mountain lift is when the heaviest rain falls.
From your notes · Setup for severe weather: Atmospheric riverNarrow stream of heavy water vapor.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: A stationary front sits over one area for days with warm, moist air flowing along it. What is the main danger?
o: Flooding from repeated storms over the same area
questions.w: Storms keep forming and moving over the same spot.
sol: Like train cars on a track, storms pass the same place again and again.
Totals pile up even if each storm is only moderate.
This 'training' is a flash flood setup.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: A warm sector is the area…
o: Between the cold front and the warm front where warm moist air sits
questions.w: It lies between the two fronts around a low.
sol: In a mid-latitude cyclone the warm front is on the east, cold front on the west or southwest.
In between is the warm, moist air that fuels storms.
Severe weather is often found in the warm sector ahead of the cold front.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Air flows around a low pressure in the Northern Hemisphere…
questions.w: Counterclockwise spin with inflow toward the center.
sol: Pressure pulls air inward, and Earth's rotation turns it to the right.
The result is counterclockwise spin around lows and clockwise around highs.
Southerly winds in the east of the low bring Gulf moisture north.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Match the air mass to its source and type.
pairs: Warm and moist, from the Gulf
Cool and moist, from the north oceans
questions.w: Letter 1: c or m for land or sea. Letter 2: P or T for cold or warm.
sol: c means continental (land, so dry), m means maritime (ocean, so moist).
P means polar (cold), T means tropical (warm).
So cP is cold and dry, mT is warm and moist.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: A forecaster sees Gulf moisture, strong jet stream, steep lapse rates, a strong cap, and no front or dryline anywhere nearby. Which ingredient is most likely missing?
o: Lift, so storms might not start
questions.w: A cap stays closed without a trigger.
sol: The list covers moisture, instability and shear.
Lift has no source, and a cap needs lift to break.
Result: possibly a quiet day despite scary numbers.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Warm air flows over cold ground ahead of a warm front. Why does it make low clouds and fog?
o: The air is cooled from below to its dew point
questions.w: Cooling to the dew point makes cloud.
sol: Cooling from below reduces the gap between T and Td until the air saturates.
The same idea explains why a cold drink glass 'sweats'.
Steady drizzle is common with warm fronts.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Before a cold front, pressure usually…
o: Falls, then rises after the front passes
questions.w: Pressure bottoms out at the front.
sol: Warm air ahead is light, so pressure falls.
Cold dense air arrives and pressure climbs.
A pressure trace shaped like a V marks the front.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: A line of storms (a squall line) often forms…
o: Along or ahead of a fast cold front
questions.w: The front gives strong lift in a line.
sol: A cold front lifts air along its whole length, so a line of storms results.
Shear and a strong cold pool keep the line organized.
Squall lines often bring straight-line wind damage.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: Which is the best explanation of why strong shear keeps a supercell alive?
o: It tilts the updraft away from the rain-cooled downdraft
questions.w: A separate updraft and downdraft don't cut each other off.
sol: In a no-shear storm, rain falls through the updraft and kills it.
With shear, the updraft leans and the rain falls beside it.
That lets the storm last for hours.
Notes|n-setup|Setup for severe weather

questions.q: A spotter sees a lowered, rotating cloud base. Where is it usually found relative to the heavy rain?
o: In the rain-free part of the base, next to the heavy rain
In the middle of the rain core
questions.w: A wall cloud sits where air is flowing into the updraft, not under falling rain.
sol: Inflow air rushes toward the updraft in a rain-free area, like a straw sucking air in beside a glass of water.
Rain pours down on the other side where the downdraft is.
If the tornado gets wrapped in rain, it is hard to see.
From your notes · Severe-weather clouds: Wall cloudLowered, often rotating base under the updraft.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A funnel does not reach the ground, but dust and debris swirl on the ground beneath it. What should it be reported as?
questions.w: A tornado is rotating air in contact with the ground, even without the full funnel visible.
sol: Funnel clouds are condensation only. Look at the ground: if debris is swirling, the circulation is touching it.
The visible funnel is just where air cooled enough to make cloud.
Misconception: tornado needs a funnel to touch the ground.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts a shelf cloud and a wall cloud?
o: A shelf cloud is on the cool outflow edge and is not rotating, a wall cloud is under the updraft and can rotate
A wall cloud is on the gust front
A shelf cloud is a tornado
questions.w: Shelf: outflow side. Wall: inflow side.
sol: Shelf clouds look like a long wedge at the storm's front edge and bring a cool, gusty wind.
Wall clouds are a smaller lowering beneath the updraft and may rotate.
Rotation is the key difference.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Ragged low clouds are quickly rising toward the base of a storm. What does this tell you?
o: Strong inflow is feeding the updraft
questions.w: Rising scud shows air flowing up into the storm.
sol: Scud is small cloud fragments below the main base.
Watching them climb is like watching leaves sucked into a vacuum.
Fast rise plus rotation makes for a more serious sign.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A tail cloud is…
o: A low band of cloud extending from the wall cloud toward the rain
questions.w: It shows inflow streaming into the wall cloud.
sol: Think of a stream flowing into a river.
It is low and connected to the wall cloud.
It is a sign of inflow, not a tornado.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Why does a thunderstorm top flatten into an anvil?
o: The rising air hits the stable layer at the tropopause and spreads sideways
The cloud runs out of water
questions.w: Above the tropopause the air stays warmer than a lifted parcel, so it can't rise further.
sol: Rising air stops when it is no longer warmer than its surroundings.
It spreads like water hitting a ceiling.
Winds aloft stretch it downwind.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: An overshooting top is a dome that pokes above the anvil. What does it show?
questions.w: Fast updraft momentum carries air past its equilibrium level.
sol: A rocket coasting past the point where thrust ends.
The more it pokes up, the stronger the updraft.
Sustained overshooting tops hint at severe hail.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: What most clearly separates a towering cumulus from a cumulonimbus?
o: The cumulonimbus top has turned to ice and looks fuzzy or fibrous
questions.w: Glaciation of the top marks a cumulonimbus.
sol: A growing cauliflower with sharp edges is liquid droplets: towering cumulus.
Once the top turns to ice, the edges blur and an anvil can form.
Lightning is only produced once ice is present.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Put the thunderstorm life cycle in order.
items: Mature stage: updraft and downdraft, heavy rain
questions.w: Storms grow, peak, and then die as downdrafts take over.
sol: Growth stage: warm air rises and builds towering cumulus.
Mature stage: rain starts and cool downdrafts form beside the updraft, with hail and lightning.
Dissipating stage: the downdraft cuts off the warm inflow and the cell fades.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Put the clouds seen as a warm front approaches in order, first to last.
questions.w: Clouds thicken and lower as the front nears.
sol: The front's gentle ramp shows its top first, so you see the highest wisps first.
Then a thin high veil (maybe a halo), then a gray midlevel sheet.
Finally dark, low rain clouds.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Match each cloud word part to its meaning.
questions.w: Cloud names are built from simple word pieces.
sol: Combine them: cumulo + nimbus = rain heap.
Alto means middle level.
Learning the pieces lets you decode any cloud name.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Surface temperature is 22 °F warmer than the dew point. Using about 1,000 ft of cloud base height per 4.4 °F of spread, what is the cloud base in feet?
sol: The °F rule is 1,000 ft for each 4.4 °F of spread.
22 ÷ 4.4 = 5 thousand ft.
The same rule in °C is 125 m per °C; a big spread means high cloud bases and drier air.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: The temperature is 32 °C and the dew point is 20 °C. Using 125 m per °C of spread, how high (m) is the cloud base?
sol: Find the spread: 32 − 20 = 12 °C.
Cloud base = 12 × 125 = 1,500 m.
The smaller the spread, the lower the base.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A thunderstorm has a high cloud base (about 3 km) and virga hanging underneath, with a dry surface. Which hazard is the best guess?
questions.w: Rain evaporating below a high base cools air that crashes down.
sol: Virga is rain that evaporates before it hits the ground.
Evaporation cools the air, making it dense, so it plunges and spreads out.
Dry microbursts can cause damaging winds with little rain.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A microburst is a downburst with damaging winds spread over a distance of at most…
questions.w: Microbursts are small; larger ones are macrobursts.
sol: Microburst: ≤ 4 km. Macroburst: > 4 km.
Pilots fear microbursts because of sudden wind shifts near the ground.
Damage is straight-line, not swirling like a tornado.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Which cloud would you see before damaging straight-line winds arrive in a squall line?
o: A shelf cloud on the leading edge
questions.w: The gust front's lifting makes a shelf.
sol: The cool outflow pushes underneath warm air and lifts it into a low wedge.
Winds hit just before the rain.
Seeking shelter before it arrives matters: damaging winds come first.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Are mammatus clouds a sign that a tornado is about to form?
o: No: they are pouches in sinking air under an anvil, and can appear with severe storms
Yes: they always come before tornadoes
Yes: they are the same as wall clouds
No: they only form in winter
questions.w: Mammatus alone do not tell about tornadoes.
sol: Mammatus are pouches formed by sinking, cooled air under the anvil.
They can show up near severe storms, but they are not rotation signs.
Look for a rotating wall cloud and funnel instead.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A short-lived swirl of dust appears along a storm's gust front with no rotation overhead. This is most likely…
o: A funnel from a wall cloud
questions.w: A gustnado forms from outflow shear, not the updraft's rotation.
sol: The gust front has strong horizontal shear, like water swirling at the edge of a fast stream.
It's usually weak and short-lived, not tied to the updraft.
Misconception: all ground swirls near a storm are tornadoes from a wall cloud.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A cloud that is lens-shaped and stands still near a mountain is a…
questions.w: Lenticulars are made by air waves over mountains.
sol: Air rises and falls over the peaks in standing waves, like ripples behind a rock in a stream.
Cloud forms at the crest, so the shape stays still while wind blows through.
They are not storm clouds, but warn of turbulence.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A thin cloud cap appears above a growing cumulus tower. What is it?
o: A pileus, showing a strong updraft pushing moist air upward
questions.w: Pileus forms as the tower lifts a layer above it.
sol: Think of a pot lid sitting on top of a bubbling tower.
The rising cloud shoves the moist layer above and cools it to make a thin cap.
It signals a quick-growing tower, which may be about to turn into Cb.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Why does a funnel cloud become visible?
o: Low pressure inside the vortex cools the air until water vapor condenses
questions.w: Air is cooled by expansion where pressure is lowest.
sol: Inside the whirl, pressure is lower, and expanding air cools like spray from a can.
Cooled below the dew point, vapor condenses to droplets and you see a funnel.
So a tornado can exist even if the funnel part is thin or missing.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Select ALL that are signs of possible rotation near the base of a storm.
o: A wall cloud that appears to rotate
Debris swirling on the ground under the base
A smooth shelf cloud moving ahead of the storm
questions.w: Rotation clues are at the base, not the anvil or outflow front.
sol: Wall clouds, funnel clouds and swirling debris all show spinning air.
Mammatus are anvil-pouches and shelf clouds mark outflow.
Treat any rotation as dangerous and report it.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A gust front with a shelf cloud is moving toward you at 45 mph. The leading edge is 9 miles away. How many minutes until it arrives?
sol: Time = distance ÷ speed = 9 ÷ 45 = 0.2 hours.
Convert to minutes: 0.2 × 60 = 12.
Common error: leaving the answer in hours.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A spotter reports: sharp low wedge, no rotation, sudden cool wind at the ground before rain. Which cloud and hazard?
o: Shelf cloud with a gust front
questions.w: Cool outflow arriving first, with no rotation, points to a gust front.
sol: Gust fronts reach you first, with cool, gusty wind.
Wall clouds sit in the inflow area and tend to rotate.
Straight-line wind is the hazard.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A waterspout is…
o: A shelf cloud on a lake
questions.w: A rotating column of air over water.
sol: Like a tornado but over a lake or ocean.
Some are weak fair-weather types, some from storms.
Treat them as hazards to boats.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Which cloud height group do altocumulus and altostratus belong to?
questions.w: Alto- means middle.
sol: Alto is the middle floor of the sky.
High clouds start with cirro-.
Low ones are strato- and cumulus.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A cumulonimbus is called a cloud that spans all heights. How does that fit the family of cloud levels?
o: It has a low base but its top reaches the high levels
questions.w: The base can be near 1 km while the top reaches around 12 km.
sol: Cb is a tall tower, like a skyscraper.
Its base sits low and its top can be at the tropopause.
That's why it is classed as a vertical-development cloud.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A halo around the Moon usually comes from…
questions.w: Ice crystals in high thin cloud bend light into a ring.
sol: The ring is made when light passes through tiny hexagonal ice crystals, like a prism.
Cirrostratus often leads a warm front.
Rain may follow within about a day.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: Which cloud type produces most thunderstorm hail, lightning and heavy rain?
questions.w: Cb has a deep updraft with ice and water.
sol: Strong updrafts lift water into the cold zone where it freezes.
Collisions of ice and water make charge and lightning.
Cirrus is just ice and does not produce storms.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A spotter says 'there's a tornado, but I can't see a funnel; it's wrapped in rain.' Why is a rain-wrapped tornado especially dangerous?
o: It is hidden from view, so people may not see it coming
It is only a gust front
It is not on the ground
questions.w: Rain curtains hide the vortex.
sol: Rain hides the tornado like fog hides a road sign.
Warnings and radar become more important than eyesight.
A low-hanging cloud base can add to the problem.
Notes|n-clouds|Severe-weather clouds

questions.q: A hiker is confused, has hot dry skin and a body temperature of 104 °F. What is the right first move?
o: Call 911 and start cooling the person right away
Give salty snacks and let them nap
Wait an hour to see if sweating starts
Give a hot drink to settle the stomach
questions.w: Hot, dry skin plus confusion is heat stroke, a medical emergency.
sol: Heat stroke means the body's cooling system (sweating) has failed, like a car engine with no coolant.
Call 911 first, then move the person to shade and cool them with cold water or ice packs.
Common slip: treating it like tiredness. Waiting lets organ damage build up fast.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Convert 40 °C to °F.
sol: Multiply by 9/5: 40 × 1.8 = 72.
Memory hook: 40 °C is also the heat-stroke body temperature, 104 °F.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Why do high-pressure ridges bring clear, hot, dry weather?
o: Air sinks, warms and dries, so clouds fade away
Air rises fast and builds big storm clouds
Cold air is pulled in from the north
Wind speeds are always very strong
questions.w: Sinking air warms and dries, so clouds dissolve.
sol: Picture air as a crowd being pushed down from above. Sinking air gets squeezed, so it warms and its clouds evaporate.
Rising air (low pressure) is the one that makes clouds and rain.
So a stuck ridge can give days of sun, heat and no rain.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: The air temperature is 32 °C and the heat index is 38 °C. Which number tells you how hot it feels to your body?
questions.w: The heat index adds humidity to temperature to show how it feels.
sol: A thermometer only measures air. The heat index also counts how hard it is for sweat to evaporate.
So your body acts as if it were 38 °C.
Plan activities using the heat index, not the thermometer alone.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Match each type of drought to what it means.
pairs: Rain and snow far below normal for a long time
Soil too dry for crops to grow
Low streams, lakes, reservoirs and groundwater
Water shortage that hurts people and businesses
questions.w: Drought is named by what is short: rain, soil moisture, water supply or people's needs.
sol: Think of a chain: first the rain stops (meteorological), then soil dries (agricultural), then rivers and reservoirs fall (hydrological).
Socioeconomic drought is when all of this hits towns, farms and businesses.
One dry spell can show up as all four types, at different times.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Order the US Drought Monitor categories from least to most severe.
questions.w: D0 is the mildest and D4 the worst.
sol: The scale runs D0 to D4. A higher number means worse drought.
D0 is not yet drought; it is a warning that things are getting dry.
D4, exceptional, means widespread crop and water losses.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Which sign points to heat exhaustion rather than heat stroke?
o: Heavy sweating, cool clammy skin and weakness, but thinking clearly
Confusion or fainting with no sweating
questions.w: Heat exhaustion: still sweating. Heat stroke: sweating stops and the brain is affected.
sol: Heat exhaustion is a car engine running hot but still cooled by its fan. Move to a cool place, loosen clothing and sip water.
Heat stroke is the fan failing: hot dry skin and confusion. That needs 911.
Misconception: both are the same. Exhaustion can turn into stroke if ignored.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Order heat illnesses from mildest to most dangerous.
questions.w: Muscle cramps come first, then exhaustion, then life-threatening stroke.
sol: Heat cramps are painful muscle spasms from losing water and salt.
Heat exhaustion adds heavy sweat, dizziness and weakness.
Heat stroke is the emergency: body temp 104 °F or more and the cooling system fails.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Why are city nights often hotter than nights in nearby countryside during a heat wave?
o: Pavement and buildings soak up heat by day and release it at night
Rural areas have thicker clouds at night
City air is always more humid
questions.w: Concrete and asphalt store heat like a brick left in the sun.
sol: A brick left in the sun stays warm long after sunset. Streets and walls do the same.
Grass and trees cool by evaporation, so rural areas lose heat faster.
This is the urban heat island, and warm nights stop people from recovering.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Why does dry soil make a heat wave hotter?
o: Sunlight heats the air instead of evaporating water from wet ground
questions.w: With no water to evaporate, the Sun's energy goes into heating the air.
sol: Compare a wet sponge with a dry one in the sun. Evaporating water uses energy and cools.
When the ground is dry, that energy heats the air instead.
This feedback is why drought and heat waves often come together.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: A town's normal rain over three months is 60, 70 and 80 mm. It received 30, 35 and 40 mm. What percent of normal fell?
questions.w: Percent of normal = actual ÷ normal × 100.
sol: Normal total: 60 + 70 + 80 = 210 mm. Actual: 30 + 35 + 40 = 105 mm.
Add totals first; do not average the three percents carelessly.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Select ALL good ways to avoid heat illness.
o: Drink water before you feel thirsty
Take breaks in shade or air conditioning
Never leave a child or pet in a parked car
Do your hardest exercise at 2 pm
Drink sugary or alcoholic drinks for hydration
questions.w: Fluids, cooling breaks and light clothing protect you; midday exertion and alcohol raise risk.
sol: Thirst shows up after you are already low on water, so drink early.
Cars heat far above the outside air within minutes.
Alcohol and sugary drinks pull water out of the body; hard exercise at the hottest hour adds heat.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: What is a drought called that builds fast, within a few weeks, as heat and dry weather quickly dry out the soil?
questions.w: Flash droughts intensify rapidly.
sol: Most droughts creep in over months, like a slow leak.
A flash drought is a burst pipe: heat plus no rain dries soil in weeks.
Crops can fail before anyone sees a drought declared.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: A ridge sits over a region and air sinks through it with no heat added or lost. What happens to the air's temperature as it sinks?
o: It warms, because the air is squeezed as pressure rises
It cools, because it is moving away from the Sun
It cools, because sinking air is always cold
questions.w: Sinking air is compressed, and compression warms it.
sol: Pump a bicycle tire fast and the pump gets hot. Compressing air heats it.
Air sinking in a ridge gets squeezed by the heavier air above, so it warms (about 10 °C per km).
That is why heat domes can bake a region even with little sunshine change.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Two cities both have air at 36 °C. City A has a dew point of 10 °C. City B has a dew point of 24 °C. Which is more dangerous and why?
o: B, because moist air slows sweat evaporation so the body cools less
A, because dry air burns skin
They are equal because air temperature is the same
A, because lower dew point means higher heat index
questions.w: Higher dew point means more moisture in the air, so cooling by sweat is weaker.
sol: Your body cools when sweat evaporates, like a wet towel drying.
In moist air the towel dries slowly, so cooling is weak.
Same temperature, but B has the higher heat index. Misconception: only temperature matters.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Heat index values assume shade. In full sunshine the heat index can be higher by up to how many °F?
questions.w: NWS notes direct sun can add up to 15 °F.
sol: The heat index is figured for shade and light wind.
Standing in full sun adds extra heat from sunlight, up to about 15 °F.
So a shade value of 98 °F could feel like 113 °F in the open.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Why is wet-bulb temperature a better heat-stress measure than ordinary air temperature?
o: It includes the cooling limit set by humidity and evaporation
It is always lower than dew point
questions.w: A wet-bulb thermometer shows how much evaporation can cool you.
sol: Wrap a wet cloth on a thermometer. In dry air it cools a lot; in humid air it cools little.
That cooling is exactly what your sweat can do.
So wet-bulb blends heat and humidity into one number about body cooling.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Rain returns to normal for two months, but reservoirs and groundwater are still low. Which drought type is likely continuing?
questions.w: Water storage recovers slowly after rain returns.
sol: Rain is like income; reservoirs and aquifers are savings.
After a long deficit you must refill the savings before the shortage ends.
So the rain deficit may end while the hydrological drought continues.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Phoenix has a typical July high near 104 °F. It hits 105 °F for a day. Is that a heat wave?
o: No: a heat wave needs unusual heat for the region, lasting several days
No, heat waves happen only in humid places
questions.w: A heat wave is defined relative to local normals and duration.
sol: A 105 °F day is normal for Phoenix but would be shocking in Seattle.
Heat wave means unusually hot for that place for a period of days.
Misconception: one fixed temperature defines a heat wave.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Which best describes why a heat wave ends?
o: A trough or front arrives and the ridge weakens or moves away
The ridge always lasts exactly 5 days
questions.w: Heat waves end when the steering pattern changes.
sol: A blocking ridge is a boulder in a stream. When the flow pushes it away, weather moves on.
A trough or cold front brings cooler air and storms.
Forecasters watch upper-air maps for that change.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: While waiting for an ambulance for a heat stroke victim, which action is best?
o: Move to shade and cool the body with cold water or ice packs on neck, armpits and groin
Give a large amount of hot tea
Wrap them in a blanket to sweat it out
Make them run to cool off
questions.w: Fast cooling is the treatment while help arrives.
sol: The body is overheating like a stuck engine; remove the heat as fast as possible.
Ice packs on neck, armpits and groin cool blood flowing near the surface.
Do not force drinks on someone who is confused.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: La Niña winters tend to make which part of the US drier than normal?
questions.w: La Niña shifts the winter storm track north, leaving the south dry.
sol: Picture the jet stream as a river of storms. In La Niña it flows farther north.
The southern states then miss many storms and run dry.
Misconception: La Niña is dry everywhere. It is wetter in parts of the north.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: The Palmer Drought Severity Index reads −3.8 in one county and +3.8 in another. What does that mean?
o: The first county is in severe drought and the second is unusually wet
The first is wet and the second is in drought
questions.w: Negative Palmer values mean dry, positive mean wet.
sol: Think of the index as a moisture bank balance: negative means in debt.
About −3 or lower is severe drought.
Positive values show soil moisture above normal.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: A heat wave has daily highs of 95, 98, 102 and 105 °F. What is the average high in °C (nearest degree)?
questions.w: Average first, then convert.
sol: Round to 38 °C.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: A storm drops 3 inches of rain on a county that is in drought, and creeks flash flood. What is the best explanation?
o: Baked, hard soil absorbs water slowly so most of it runs off
Dry soil is soft and absorbs everything
Rain in a drought is always colder
questions.w: Hard dry ground sheds water like a roof.
sol: Pour water on a dry, hard sponge or clay: it beads and runs off.
Runoff reaches creeks fast and floods them.
Drought and flood can happen in the same place.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Air starts at −5 °C at 3 km up in a ridge and sinks to the ground. Dry air warms about 10 °C per km when sinking and nothing else changes. What is its temperature at the surface in °C?
questions.w: Compression warming is 10 °C for each km of sinking.
sol: Distance sunk: 3 km.
Warming: 3 × 10 = 30 °C.
−5 + 30 = 25 °C. This is why sinking air in ridges bakes the surface.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Why do doctors worry when wet-bulb temperature reaches about 35 °C, even for a healthy person resting in shade?
o: Skin is near 35 °C, so heat cannot flow out and sweat cannot evaporate
Sweat glands run out of water at 35 °C
questions.w: Cooling needs a temperature gap or evaporation; at this point both fail.
sol: Heat flows from hot to cold. Skin at about 35 °C cannot dump heat into 35 °C air.
At 35 °C wet-bulb the air is nearly saturated, so sweat will not dry.
With both routes shut, the core temperature climbs like a locked car.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Which statement about a heat dome is true?
o: It is a strong ridge where sinking air warms, acting like a lid over the region
It is a bubble of cold air
questions.w: A heat dome is a persistent strong high-pressure ridge.
sol: The ridge pushes air down and traps heat like a pot lid.
Under the lid the air is warm, dry and stagnant.
Heat dome and blocking ridge are close cousins in the same pattern.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: Name the type of drought when streams, lakes and reservoirs run low.
questions.w: Water supply is what is short.
sol: Rain deficit is meteorological; dry soil is agricultural.
Low surface and groundwater supply is hydrological (hydro = water).
These can lag each other by months.
Notes|n-dh|Drought and heat waves

questions.q: How many inches of fast-moving flood water can knock an adult off their feet?
questions.w: Six inches can knock you down; about 12 can carry away a car.
sol: Moving water pushes harder than it looks, like a strong wave at the beach.
Six inches can sweep your feet away.
Twelve inches can float and carry a car. So turn around, don't drown.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Hail with a diameter of about 1 inch is the size of which coin?
questions.w: 1 inch is quarter size, the NWS severe hail threshold.
sol: Pea is ¼ in, penny ¾ in, quarter 1 in.
One inch or bigger counts as severe hail.
Learn the coin ladder: pea, penny, quarter, golf ball, baseball.
From your notes · Severe thunderstorms: NWS "severe": hail ≥ 1 inch, wind ≥ 58 mph, or a tornado.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Order hail sizes from smallest to largest.
questions.w: Pea ¼ in, penny ¾ in, quarter 1 in, golf ball 1¾ in, baseball 2¾ in.
sol: Use the numbers: ¼, ¾, 1, 1¾, 2¾ inches.
The quarter marks the severe threshold.
Bigger stones need stronger updrafts.
From your notes · Precipitation, flooding, IDF: Hail: pea ¼ in, penny ¾ in, quarter 1 in (severe), golf ball 1¾ in, baseball 2¾ in.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A flash flood WATCH means…
o: Conditions could lead to flash flooding; be ready
questions.w: Watch means be ready; warning means act now.
sol: A watch is like ingredients on the counter: a flood could be cooked up.
A warning means the flood is happening or about to.
Misconception: watch and warning are the same.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Match each precipitation type to how it forms.
pairs: Warm all the way down, or warm layers melt snow
Melted drops refreeze in a deep cold layer near the ground
Liquid drops freeze when they touch cold surfaces
questions.w: The temperature layers a drop falls through decide its type.
sol: Picture a drop riding an elevator through layers.
Sleet refreezes before landing; freezing rain stays liquid until it hits.
Both need a warm layer aloft.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Order the steps of sleet formation.
items: Snow melts in a warm layer aloft
Drops fall into a deep cold layer near the ground
questions.w: Sleet is snow that melts, then refreezes before reaching the ground.
sol: It is like a snowball dipped in water and then put in the freezer.
The cold layer near the ground is deep enough to refreeze drops.
If that cold layer is shallow, you get freezing rain instead.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A cloud at −15 °C holds both supercooled droplets and ice crystals. What happens?
o: Ice crystals grow while droplets shrink
questions.w: Water vapor prefers to deposit on ice, so ice grows at the droplets' expense.
sol: Ice crystals are bullies that steal moisture from nearby droplets.
Air saturated for water is extra saturated for ice, so vapor goes onto ice.
This is the Bergeron process.
From your notes · Precipitation, flooding, IDF: Bergeron processIce crystals grow while supercooled drops shrink (cold clouds)
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A tropical cloud top never gets below freezing. How does rain form?
o: Ice crystals grow by the Bergeron process
questions.w: Warm clouds make rain only by droplets colliding.
sol: Big droplets fall faster, run into small ones and swallow them, like a snowball rolling downhill.
No ice means no Bergeron process.
Misconception: all rain starts as snow.
From your notes · Precipitation, flooding, IDF: Collision-coalescenceDrops merge into bigger drops (warm clouds)
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Fluffy snow has a 15:1 ratio. If the liquid equivalent is 2 cm, how many cm of snow fall?
questions.w: Snow depth = liquid × ratio.
sol: Ratio 15:1 means 15 cm of snow for each 1 cm of liquid.
Warm wet snow has a lower ratio, around 5:1 to 8:1.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A rain gauge catches 0.75 inch in 15 minutes. What is the rate in inches per hour?
questions.w: Rate = amount ÷ time.
sol: 15 minutes is ¼ hour.
Always convert to the unit asked before dividing.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Compared with a forest, a paved parking lot makes the flood peak…
questions.w: Pavement sheds water quickly.
sol: Forest soil is a sponge; pavement is a slide.
Water slides to drains and creeks within minutes.
Result: shorter lag time and a bigger peak.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Select ALL conditions that raise flash flood risk.
questions.w: Fast runoff plus heavy rain over one place causes flash floods.
sol: Burned ground repels water and steep slopes speed it.
Saturated soil cannot take more, like a full sponge.
Drizzle on absorbent ground or leaf litter soaks in.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Why does a 100-year flood not mean it only happens once every 100 years?
o: It means a 1% chance each year, and it can happen in back-to-back years
It is guaranteed once per century
questions.w: Return period is an average, not a schedule.
sol: Each year is like a fresh roll of a 100-sided die.
Rolling a 1 this year does not lower next year's chance.
Misconception: after one, we are safe for 100 years.
From your notes · Precipitation, flooding, IDF: Chance in any year = 1 ÷ return period.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A hailstone cut open shows alternating clear and cloudy layers. What does that tell you?
o: It was carried through zones with different amounts of supercooled water, often lofted more than once
It fell from a cold cloud
questions.w: Layers record the stone's trips through the storm.
sol: Like tree rings, layers show growth history.
Clear ice forms when lots of supercooled water freezes slowly; cloudy ice when less.
The stone rose and fell in the updraft, gaining layers.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Which weather map clue means a shallow below-freezing layer at the surface with warm air above?
questions.w: Rain has no time to refreeze in a shallow cold layer, so it freezes on contact.
sol: Sleet needs a deep cold layer for refreezing in the air.
Shallow cold layer: drops stay liquid, then freeze when they hit cold roads and wires.
Surface at 28 °F and rain falling is the classic ice storm setup.
From your notes · Precipitation, flooding, IDF: Freezing rainRain falls on a surface below 0 °C and freezes on contact
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A forecast sounding shows a warm layer at 2 km and a 1.5 km deep subfreezing layer below it. Which precipitation is most likely?
questions.w: A deep cold layer lets melted drops refreeze before landing.
sol: Snow melts at 2 km, then falls through 1.5 km of cold air.
Long exposure refreezes drops into pellets.
Misconception: freezing rain is the worst case everywhere. Layer depth decides.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A 40% chance of rain in a forecast means…
o: A 40% chance that measurable rain (at least 0.01 in) falls at any given point in the forecast area
It will rain on 40% of the day
40% of the area will get rain for sure
It will rain for 40% of the day everywhere
questions.w: PoP is the chance of measurable rain at a point.
sol: Think of rolling a 10-sided die for your backyard: 4 out of 10 times you get wet.
It is a probability, not a share of time or area.
Forecasters combine confidence and area covered.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Why do the biggest, most delicate snow crystals often grow near −15 °C?
o: The gap between vapor pressure over water and over ice is largest there, so ice grows fastest
questions.w: Ice growth by vapor deposition peaks around −12 to −18 °C.
sol: At −15 °C the Bergeron effect is strongest; ice grabs moisture fastest.
Fast growth in humid air makes branching arms (dendrites).
Colder or warmer, crystals are plainer.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Storm A has updrafts of 15 m/s and Storm B has 35 m/s. Which can grow bigger hail?
o: Storm B, because strong updrafts hold heavier stones up longer
Storm A, because weak updrafts are gentler
Equal, because hail depends only on temperature
Storm A, because stones fall faster
questions.w: Stones keep growing only while the updraft holds them up.
sol: A heavier stone needs a stronger wind to float, like a bigger leaf needing a stronger gust.
Longer time in the cold supercooled zone means more riming.
Weak updrafts drop small stones early.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A storm drops 25 mm of rain evenly over 10 km². What volume of water fell, in cubic meters? (1 km² = 1,000,000 m²)
questions.w: Volume = area × depth, in meters.
sol: That is about 100 Olympic pools from a modest rain.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A dry desert wash floods during clear skies overhead. Why?
o: Rain fell upstream and the runoff arrived down the channel
questions.w: Flash floods can be far from the rain.
sol: Water flows downhill like cars on a highway, arriving long after rain starts.
Hard dry ground adds fast runoff.
Do not camp in washes when storms are nearby.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Which snow gives more depth for the same amount of liquid?
questions.w: Cold snow has more air in it.
sol: Powder is like a fluffy pillow; wet snow is packed like a snowball.
Powder ratios can reach 20:1 or more, wet snow 5:1 to 8:1.
Same liquid, more depth for powder.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Rain falls on deep snow during a warm spell. Why is flooding likely?
o: Rain adds water and speeds melting, so the snowpack releases a lot at once
questions.w: Rain-on-snow combines new water and melted water.
sol: Snowpack is a frozen reservoir. Warm rain opens the tap.
The pack can only hold so much liquid.
Add frozen ground that blocks soaking and rivers rise.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: What is the chance (nearest %) of at least one 25-year flood in 25 years? Use 1 − 0.96^25.
questions.w: Chance of at least one = 1 minus chance of none.
sol: Each year the flood misses with probability 0.96.
Missing 25 years in a row: 0.96^25 ≈ 0.36.
1 − 0.36 = 0.64, so 64%. Not 100%: a 25-year flood is not guaranteed in 25 years.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: A warmer climate changes a 100-year rainfall to a 50-year event. What is the chance (%) of at least one in 30 years now? Use 1 − 0.98^30.
questions.w: New yearly chance is 2%.
sol: Return period 50 years: 1 ÷ 50 = 2% per year.
Miss all 30 years: 0.98^30 ≈ 0.545.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: An IDF curve for a 100-year storm gives 0.7 in/hr over 6 hours. What total depth falls, in inches?
questions.w: Depth = intensity × duration.
sol: Rate 0.7 in/hr for 6 hours.
Shorter bursts have higher rates but less total depth, so longer storms add up to more water.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: Why does a 100-year storm plot higher than a 10-year storm on an IDF chart at the same duration?
o: Rarer storms are more intense for the same duration
Longer return periods mean longer duration
questions.w: Rare storms are heavier.
sol: Each curve is one return period.
A rarer storm needs a heavier rain rate at the same duration.
Read across at one duration to compare.
From your notes · Precipitation, flooding, IDF: Rarer storms (100-yr) plot higher.
Notes|n-precip|Precipitation, flooding, IDF

questions.q: What does the C in IDF curve stand for? Give the full word.
questions.w: Intensity-Duration-Frequency curve.
sol: I is intensity, D is duration, F is frequency.
The curve shows how heavy rain gets for each length of storm.

50 × 1.15 = 57.5 mph, which the NWS rounds to 58.

questions.q: Sinking air inside a storm is called a…

sol: Storms have two big air streams: rising air (updraft) and sinking air (downdraft).

questions.q: Why does air in a thunderstorm downdraft speed toward the ground?
questions.w: Cool, rain-loaded air is heavy, so it sinks.
sol: Evaporating rain takes heat from the air, like sweat cooling your skin, so the air gets cold and dense.
Falling raindrops also drag the air with them, like a crowd pulling you along in a stampede.
Dense air sinks quickly and then spreads out, which makes damaging winds. Misconception: warm air rises, it does not sink.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: Rain evaporating cools it and falling rain drags it, so it is denser than the air around it
The Sun heats the ground and pulls it down
Wind shear pushes it down from above

questions.q: Which describes a dry microburst?
questions.w: Dry microbursts often hit with little or no rain, so there is no warning from the rain.
sol: In dry places, such as the western US, cloud bases are high and the air below is dry.
Rain evaporates on the way down (virga), chilling the air a lot, and that air crashes down.
Danger: no rain at the surface does not mean no wind.
