o: A high-based storm whose rain evaporates before reaching the ground, yet its cooled air still rushes down
A downburst that only happens in winter snow
A microburst that carries a lot of heavy rain to the ground
A tornado with no funnel cloud

questions.q: Two storms have the same size. Storm A has rain falling into a thick layer of very dry air under the cloud. Storm B has humid air all the way down. Which likely has stronger downdraft winds?
questions.w: More evaporation means more cooling, and colder air sinks faster.
sol: Evaporation is the engine of a downburst: the drier the air under the cloud, the more rain evaporates.
Think of dropping an ice cube into a glass: the more it melts, the more it cools the water. Here the cooling is done by the evaporating rain.
So a big gap between temperature and dew point below the cloud signals strong downdrafts. Humid air stops the cooling.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: Storm A, because more rain evaporates and the air gets much colder and heavier
Storm B, because humid air is heavier
They are equal, since the storms are the same size
Storm B, because it keeps its rain longer

questions.q: A plane flies through a microburst on takeoff. Put what the pilot experiences in order.
questions.w: Wind blows outward from the burst, so the plane first meets a headwind, then sinking air, then a tailwind.
sol: A microburst is like water from a tap hitting a sink: it spreads out in all directions.
Flying in, you meet the outflow coming toward you (headwind), pass the middle where air goes straight down, then meet outflow going the same way you are flying (tailwind).
Lift depends on airspeed over the wings, so the tailwind leg is when the plane loses lift.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
items: Strong downdraft pushes the plane down
Wind turns to a tailwind (lift drops)

questions.q: Why is the tailwind part of a microburst the most dangerous for a plane near the runway?
questions.w: Less air flowing over the wings means less lift.
sol: Wings make lift from the air rushing past them, like a hand held flat out of a car window.
In a tailwind, the air moves with the plane, so the air speed over the wings drops fast.
Combined with the downdraft, the plane may not be able to climb. That is why airports have wind shear alerts.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: Airspeed over the wings drops suddenly, so lift falls while the plane is already sinking
Tailwinds make the engines stall from rain
The pilot cannot see because of the rotation
Tailwinds raise the air pressure under the wings

questions.q: A Doppler velocity image shows strong inbound winds right next to strong outbound winds along the same radar beam. The inbound side is closer to the radar. This pattern means…

sol: Radar only measures motion toward or away along its beam.
Air spreading out from a downburst moves toward the radar on the near side and away on the far side: that is divergence.
Rotation is different: inbound and outbound sit side by side across the beam, not one behind the other. Misconception: any inbound-outbound pair is a tornado.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: Divergence, such as a downburst spreading out
Air flowing in one direction only

questions.q: Surveyors find trees and corn lying in one direction over a wide area, with no twisting or crossing debris. Which fits this damage?

sol: Tornado debris is thrown in crossing, converging patterns, like water spinning down a drain.

The pattern on the ground tells you the type of wind that did it.
From your notes · Winds from storms: Straight-line winds = damage not from rotation.

questions.q: A gust front passes your weather station. What do you most likely see?
questions.w: The gust front is the edge of cold air, so it brings fast changes.
sol: The outflow is a dome of cold, dense air, like cold air spilling out of an open freezer.

A cold front is larger and changes things over hours, not minutes.

o: A sudden wind gust and shift, a temperature drop, and a quick pressure rise
A temperature rise and falling pressure
Wind stops and the sky clears
A slow steady wind change over many hours

questions.q: Select ALL changes you expect when a thunderstorm gust front passes.
questions.w: Cold, dense outflow cools the air, raises the pressure, and gusts.
sol: Cold outflow = cooler air.
Dense air piles up, so pressure goes up, and air is flowing outward, so winds gust.
A temperature jump and a pressure drop are the opposite and would happen ahead of the storm, not at the gust front.

questions.q: A low, wedge-shaped cloud on the front edge of a storm, over the gust front, is a…

questions.q: In desert areas such as Phoenix, a wall of dust pushed along by thunderstorm outflow is called a…
questions.w: A haboob is a dust wall lifted by a gust front.

questions.q: Santa Ana winds in Southern California are…
questions.w: They blow out of high desert and are heated by sinking.
sol: High pressure over the Great Basin pushes air toward the coast, down mountain slopes.

Moist winds from the ocean that bring rain
Cold winds from the Arctic Ocean

questions.q: Dry air at 0 °C starts at the top of a mountain and flows 2 km down a slope. It warms about 10 °C per km of descent. What is its temperature at the bottom, in °C?
sol: As air sinks to higher pressure it is squeezed and warms; no heat is added.
Warming = 10 °C per km × 2 km = 20 °C.
Start at 0 °C, so end at 20 °C. This is why chinook and Santa Ana winds feel warm and dry.

questions.q: Why does a line of storms often bow outward into a bow echo?

Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms

questions.q: A weather station reports a gust of 28 m/s. About how many mph is that? (1 m/s ≈ 2.24 mph)
questions.w: 28 × 2.24 = 62.7 mph, above the 58 mph severe limit.
sol: Each m/s is about 2.24 mph.
That is above 58 mph, so it counts as a severe thunderstorm wind.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms

questions.q: A line of storms produced wind damage along a path 300 miles long in 6 hours. What was its average speed, in mph?
questions.w: Speed = distance ÷ time = 300 ÷ 6 = 50 mph.
sol: Average speed is distance divided by time.
300 mi ÷ 6 h = 50 mph.
Long path (over 240 mi) with gusts over 58 mph is what makes a storm a derecho.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms

questions.q: A gust front is 25 miles away and moving toward you at 50 mph. In how many minutes does it arrive?
questions.w: 25 mi ÷ 50 mph = 0.5 h = 30 min.
sol: Time = distance ÷ speed = 25 ÷ 50 = 0.5 hour.
0.5 hour × 60 = 30 minutes.
The gust front can arrive before any rain, so there may be no warning.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms

questions.q: Why can a gust front race out ahead of the rain?
questions.w: Cold outflow flows out like a spilled liquid.
sol: Pour water on a table: it spreads out far past where you poured it.
Outflow is dense and spreads along the ground, even beyond the storm's rain.
So wind and dust may hit you minutes before the first drops.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: Cold, dense outflow spreads out along the ground faster than the storm itself moves
The rain is slower because it is cold
Wind is created only after rain stops
The gust front is warmer, so it moves faster

questions.q: A rear-inflow jet is…
questions.w: It helps push damaging winds to the surface at the bow.
sol: Air behind the storm line flows in at mid levels and descends.
Dry air evaporates rain and cools further, so it sinks more strongly.
Picture a fan blowing from behind to push the front forward. That is why bow echoes can produce widespread wind damage.
From your notes · Winds from storms: On radar: bow echo (derecho/damaging wind), fine line (gust front), bowing segment on a squall line.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: A stream of drier air entering the back of a squall line that sinks and speeds toward the front
A jet stream wind at 40,000 ft above a hurricane
A warm front that crosses the line

questions.q: How does a gust front differ from a cold front?
questions.w: The gust front is made by one storm, the cold front by a big weather system.
sol: Gust front: cold air spilled out by a storm, lasting an hour or two.
Cold front: the leading edge of a big cold air mass that can stretch over states.
Both bring wind shifts and drops in temperature, so people confuse them, but their size and cause differ.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: A gust front is a small, short-lived edge of storm outflow; a cold front is a large air-mass boundary lasting days
A gust front is warmer than the air around it
A cold front only forms over the ocean

questions.q: A downburst hits the ground. Which way does the wind blow at the surface near the impact?
questions.w: Think of a stream of water hitting a plate.
sol: Sinking air cannot go through the ground, so it spreads sideways.
The result is a diverging pattern, like water from a tap hitting a flat sink.
A tornado, in contrast, has winds that spin around a center.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: Outward in all directions from the point it hits

questions.q: As a severe storm approaches, what often arrives first?
questions.w: Gust fronts run ahead of the storm.
sol: Cool outflow spreads ahead of the main storm.
That is why a dust cloud or sudden wind may hit before any rain.
Take the first gust as a signal to go inside.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: Gusty outflow winds from the gust front

questions.q: On successive radar scans, a small, very high reflectivity core (heavy rain and hail) is falling from mid levels toward the ground. What might happen next?
questions.w: A descending core often means a strong downdraft is about to hit the ground.
sol: The heavy rain and hail core is the weight pulling the downdraft down.
When it sinks quickly it may reach the ground as a microburst.
Forecasters watch for this sign as a warning for damaging wind, but it does not mean a tornado.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: A downburst may reach the ground and cause a burst of damaging wind
The storm is dying and harmless

questions.q: A storm sits northwest of you. A gust front reaches you. The outflow wind most likely blows from the…
questions.w: Outflow spreads away from the storm toward you.
sol: Cold air spreads outward from the storm in all directions.
The storm is northwest of you, so the air travels from the northwest to you.
Wind direction is the direction it comes FROM, so it is a northwest wind.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms

questions.q: After a storm, a town has 90 mph winds for about 20 minutes across a swath 10 miles wide, with trees falling in one direction. Which term fits best?
questions.w: 10 miles is over 4 km wide, and 20 minutes is long.
sol: 10 miles is about 16 km, which is more than 4 km, so it is a macroburst.
Microbursts are under 4 km and brief.
A gustnado is a small whirl and a waterspout is over water.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms

questions.q: A gustnado is…
questions.w: It is a brief vortex on the ground made by the outflow, not by a mesocyclone.
sol: Along a sharp gust front, wind differences can make little swirls near the ground, like eddies where fast water meets slow water.
They are usually weak, brief, and show up as dusty swirls.
A true tornado is linked with the base of a rotating storm cloud.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: A short-lived whirl along a gust front that is not connected to the storm's rotating updraft
The same as a supercell tornado
A cloud shaped like a funnel high in the sky

questions.q: A station reports: 3:00 pm, 87 °F, wind SW 10 kt, 1010 mb. At 3:10 pm: 71 °F, wind NW 45 kt, 1014 mb. What happened?
questions.w: Sudden cool-down, strong wind shift, and a pressure rise within minutes.
sol: A 16 °F drop and strong wind change in 10 minutes means very cold outflow arrived.
The pressure rise comes from the dense, cold dome of air.
A warm front would make it warmer and change slowly.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: A gust front or outflow boundary passed

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.w: Each term describes a part of the straight-line wind story.
sol: Downburst is the cause.
Gust front is the leading edge.
Shelf cloud is what you see.
Derecho is the big event with hundreds of miles of damage.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
pairs: Sinking air that hits the ground and spreads out
Low wedge-shaped cloud on the gust front

questions.q: A uniform 50 kt wind blows toward the east. A radar sits directly south of a point where the radar sees a velocity of 0 kt. Why?
questions.w: Doppler sees toward or away, not sideways.
sol: A radar beam pointing north measures motion toward or away, like a speed gun along a road.
A car driving across in front of the speed gun reads about zero.
So the east wind, crossing the beam, shows ~0 even though it is 50 kt.
Notes|n-winds|Winds from storms
o: Radar measures only the part of the motion along its beam, and this wind is across the beam
The wind stopped at that point
Radar cannot see wind from the east
The wind is too strong to measure

questions.q: An EF5 tornado has winds estimated above what speed, in mph?
questions.w: EF5 is over 200 mph.
sol: The EF scale goes EF0 to EF5.
Each step is roughly 25 to 35 mph higher.
EF4 tops out at 200 mph, so EF5 is above 200.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: Which wind range matches EF3?
questions.w: EF3 is 136–165 mph.
sol: Remember: EF3 starts at 136.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: Radar-based estimates put a tornado's wind at 120 knots. Convert to mph (1 kt ≈ 1.15 mph) and give the EF range it matches.
questions.w: 120 × 1.15 = 138.0 mph, which is EF3.
sol: Step 2: look up the EF range (EF3 is 136–165, EF4 is 166–200).
138.0 mph falls in EF3. Remember that real ratings come from damage, not from radar.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: Radar-based estimates put a tornado's wind at 150 knots. Convert to mph (1 kt ≈ 1.15 mph) and give the EF range it matches.
questions.w: 150 × 1.15 = 172.5 mph, which is EF4.
sol: Step 2: look up the EF range (EF3 is 136–165, EF4 is 166–200).
172.5 mph falls in EF4. Remember that real ratings come from damage, not from radar.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: A tornado causes mostly EF1 damage, but one well-built house is swept off its foundation (EF4 damage). The tornado is rated…
questions.w: The rating uses the worst damage found.
sol: Surveyors walk the whole path and note the strongest damage.
That strongest damage sets the rating for the whole tornado.
Like a test where your top score counts, one strong sign counts.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: EF4, the highest damage found along the path
EF5, because it hit a house

questions.q: A strong tornado crosses only open farmland, with no buildings or trees. Why might it get a low rating?
questions.w: Ratings are based on damage, not on how strong it really was.
sol: Surveyors use damage indicators: houses, barns, trees, and so on.
With nothing to damage, a strong tornado can leave a low or even unrated (EFU) mark.
It is like grading a test by the answers: no answers means no grade.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: The EF scale rates damage to structures and trees, so little damage means a low rating
Tornadoes over farmland are always weak
The EF scale ignores wind speed

questions.q: The old F scale has F3 as 158–206 mph, while EF3 is 136–165 mph. Why were the EF winds lowered?
questions.w: The EF scale matched wind to damage better.
sol: The EF scale kept the same idea (damage rates tornadoes) but corrected the wind estimates.
Same damage, lower wind needed.
That is why ratings before and after 2007 are not exactly equal.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: Engineering studies showed the old scale overestimated the wind needed to cause the damage
The EF scale measures wind with new radars
The F scale used knots instead of mph

questions.q: What is a funnel cloud?
questions.w: If it touches the ground, it is a tornado.
sol: A funnel cloud is condensation in a rotating air column hanging from the cloud.
When the circulation reaches the ground, we call it a tornado.
Like a cone that has not yet touched the table.
From your notes · Tornadoes, scales, radar: Tornado = violently rotating column touching the ground and a cloud base.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: A rotating cone of cloud that does not reach the ground
A cloud over the ocean only

questions.q: A rain-wrapped tornado is hard to see. Why does it matter for safety?
questions.w: Rain can hide the tornado.
sol: In heavy rain or darkness, there may be no visible funnel.
So the only reliable way to know is a warning or radar data.
Misconception: a tornado needs a visible funnel.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: You cannot rely on seeing a funnel, so warnings and radar matter

questions.q: Which way do most tornadoes in the Northern Hemisphere spin?
questions.w: Nearly all spin counterclockwise, like the mesocyclone that makes them.
sol: Most tornadoes come from a counterclockwise-rotating storm.
A few weak ones spin the other way.
Cyclonic means the same spin as a low-pressure system.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: In a standard Doppler velocity image, red colors show winds moving…
questions.w: Green is toward and red is away.
sol: Radar only sees motion along its beam.
Green is toward the radar and red is away.
Think: red = runs away, green = comes toward you (go).
From your notes · Observation tools: Velocity: toward the radar is NEGATIVE (green).
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: A tornado is due north of a radar. It spins counterclockwise as seen from above. On the velocity image, which side shows outbound (red) winds?
questions.w: Counterclockwise rotation sends the east side northward, away from the radar.
sol: Picture a counterclockwise spinning wheel above you: its east edge moves north.
The radar is south, so north is away from radar: outbound.
The west edge moves south, toward the radar: inbound.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: A tornado is due east of a radar, spinning counterclockwise as seen from above. Which part shows inbound winds (toward the radar)?
questions.w: On the north side, counterclockwise flow goes west toward the radar.
sol: Counterclockwise rotation: on the north edge the air moves west.
The radar is to the west, so west is toward the radar: inbound.
The south edge moves east, away: outbound.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: A velocity couplet shows inbound winds of 40 kt and outbound winds of 60 kt next to each other. Rotational velocity is the average of these two speeds. What is it, in kt?
questions.w: Average of 40 and 60 is 50 kt.
sol: Add the two speeds: 40 + 60 = 100.
Divide by 2: 50 kt.
Forecasters use the rotational velocity to tell how strong the rotation is, like measuring how fast a merry-go-round turns.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: A velocity couplet shows inbound winds of 35 kt and outbound winds of 55 kt next to each other. Rotational velocity is the average of these two speeds. What is it, in kt?
questions.w: Average of 35 and 55 is 45 kt.
sol: Add the two speeds: 35 + 55 = 90.
Divide by 2: 45 kt.
Forecasters use the rotational velocity to tell how strong the rotation is, like measuring how fast a merry-go-round turns.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: A west-to-east wind of 60 kt is blowing. A radar beam points 60° away from the wind direction. The radar measures only the part along the beam: 60 × cos 60°. What speed does it show, in kt?
sol: Doppler radar sees only the part of the wind along the beam.
So the radar reads 30 kt even though the wind is 60 kt. If the beam were at 90°, it would read 0.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: A tornado is 120 miles from the radar. Why might the radar miss its low-level rotation?
questions.w: The farther away, the higher the beam is above the ground.
sol: Think of a flashlight tilted slightly upward across a flat field.
Far away its spot is high above the ground.
So storms far from a radar may show only what is high up, missing tornadoes near the ground.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: The beam rises with distance and the Earth curves away, so it passes above the low rotation
Radar cannot see anything beyond 100 miles
Tornadoes cannot be seen on radar
The beam bends toward the ground

questions.q: Inside a hook echo, radar shows a velocity couplet and, at the same spot, the correlation coefficient (CC) drops from 0.98 to 0.6 with high reflectivity. What does this indicate?
questions.w: Low CC means the targets differ in shape and size, like debris.
sol: CC compares how similar the radar targets are. Raindrops are all alike, so CC is near 1.
Mixed debris (leaves, boards, insulation) is not alike, so CC falls.
Rotation + debris = tornado confirmed by radar.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: Debris is being lofted, so a tornado is likely on the ground (tornado debris signature)

questions.q: Why does correlation coefficient (CC) drop inside a debris ball?
questions.w: CC is high for similar targets and low for mixed ones.
sol: Compare a bag of identical marbles with a bag of random junk.
Radar signals bounce back similarly from the marbles but differently from the junk.
Mixed scatterers give low CC.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: Debris has many different shapes and sizes, unlike nearly identical raindrops
Debris is bigger, so it reflects less

questions.q: Put the stages of a supercell tornado in order.
questions.w: A supercell's spin organizes, lowers, touches down, then fades.
sol: First the updraft rotates (mesocyclone).
Then a wall cloud lowers, a funnel grows, and the funnel reaches the ground.
At the end, the tornado often thins into a rope shape and dies.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
items: Tornado narrows into a rope and dissipates

questions.q: Who issues a tornado warning for your county?
questions.w: Local offices warn; the SPC issues watches.
sol: The SPC issues the larger tornado watches.
Your local NWS office watches radar and issues warnings for specific areas.
Watch = prepare; warning = take cover now.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: The local National Weather Service forecast office
Only the Storm Prediction Center in Oklahoma

questions.q: During a tornado warning, a highway overpass is…
questions.w: Overpasses can channel wind and debris.
sol: Wind squeezes under the bridge, like water speeding through a narrow pipe.
There is no protection from flying debris.
Better choices: a sturdy building or a ditch only as a last resort.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: Not safe, because the wind can speed up under it and debris flies
Safe if you climb up to the girders

questions.q: Should you open windows during a tornado warning to even out the pressure?
questions.w: Damage comes from wind and debris, not from pressure.
sol: Houses are damaged mainly by strong winds and flying debris.
Opening windows wastes precious time.
Go to a safe place right away.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: No, it wastes time and does not protect the house
Yes, to stop the roof from exploding
Yes, on the side facing the storm
Yes, but only on the second floor

questions.q: During a tornado warning, what should people in a mobile home do?
questions.w: Mobile homes are not safe in a tornado.
sol: Winds that are only moderate can flip or destroy a mobile home.
Get to a strong building or storm shelter before the storm arrives.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: Leave and go to a sturdy building

questions.q: A tornado is 15 miles away and moving toward you at 30 mph. In how many minutes does it arrive?
questions.w: 15 mi ÷ 30 mph = 0.5 hour = 30 min.
sol: Time = distance ÷ speed.
0.5 hour × 60 = 30 minutes. Not much time, so move to shelter at once.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: On radar, a hook echo moves 12 miles in 24 minutes. What is its speed, in mph?
sol: Convert minutes to hours: 24 ÷ 60 = 0.4 h.
Speed = distance ÷ time = 12 ÷ 0.4 = 30 mph.
Forecasters use this speed to figure out when a tornado reaches a town.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: A landspout is…
questions.w: Landspouts spin from the ground up, with no mesocyclone.
sol: Along boundaries, air spins near the ground and a growing updraft stretches it, like an ice skater pulling in arms.
They are usually weaker than supercell tornadoes and have no mesocyclone.
They show weak or no hook echo on radar.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: A weak tornado that forms from spin near the ground under a growing cloud, without a supercell
A supercell tornado with a hook

questions.q: Why are nighttime tornadoes especially dangerous?
questions.w: Visibility and sleep, not stronger winds.
sol: At night it's hard to see the storm and people may not hear a warning.
Keep a weather radio or phone alert on.
Misconception: tornadoes are not stronger at night, just harder to see.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: People may be asleep or cannot see the storm, so warnings are missed
Radar does not work at night

questions.q: A radar shows a hook echo and a strong velocity couplet (55 kt) but the CC stays 0.98 everywhere. Best interpretation?
questions.w: Rotation is the warning sign even without debris.
sol: Debris signature appears only after the tornado is on the ground and lofting debris.
Strong rotation alone is enough to issue a warning.
Missing signs do not mean safe, just less certain.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: Strong rotation is present; a tornado may be forming or hidden, but no debris signature is seen yet
No threat, since there is no debris
A confirmed large tornado is on the ground
The couplet is a radar error

questions.q: Why is it hard for radar to tell a mesocyclone from a tornado at long range?
questions.w: The beam widens with distance.
sol: Radar beams spread out; at long range one beam may be miles wide.
A tornado can be a few hundred yards wide, so it blends into the bigger circulation.
Think of trying to photograph a pencil from a mile away.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: A tornado is far narrower than the radar beam, so radar sees only the broader parent rotation

questions.q: A tornado is one mile wide. Is it automatically EF5?
questions.w: A wide tornado can be weak and a narrow one violent.
sol: EF ratings come from damage to buildings and trees.
Width, path length and duration do not set the rating.
A big weak funnel and a small violent one both exist.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: No, rating depends on the damage, not the width
Yes, but only if it lasts an hour

questions.q: A mesocyclone is…
questions.w: Mesocyclones are the parent rotation that can spawn tornadoes.
sol: A mesocyclone is the storm-sized rotating updraft.
A tornado is the much smaller, violent vortex on the ground.
Not every mesocyclone makes a tornado.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: A rotating updraft a few miles wide inside a supercell
A fast jet of air high above

questions.q: Match each radar signature with its meaning.
questions.w: Each shape or color shows one thing.
sol: Reflectivity shows precipitation shapes.
Velocity shows rotation.
CC shows how similar the targets are.
Bow echoes show a line of wind damage.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
pairs: Rain and debris wrapped around a mesocyclone

questions.q: Select ALL signs that suggest a tornado is likely on radar.
questions.w: Rotation, hook shape, and debris signals point to tornadoes.
sol: Couplet = rotation.
Hook = rain wrapping the mesocyclone.
Low CC = debris.
A thin line ahead is a gust front; uniform inbound wind has no rotation.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar
o: A thin line of weak echo far ahead of the storm
Uniform inbound winds across the storm

questions.q: A tornado's damage suggests a 3-second gust of 135 mph. What is its EF rating?
questions.w: 111–135 mph is EF2.
sol: EF2 range is 111 to 135 mph.
135 is the top of EF2.
One mph more (136) would be EF3.
Notes|n-torn|Tornadoes, scales, radar

questions.q: A hurricane warning means hurricane conditions are expected within about how many hours?
questions.w: Warning: within 36 hours.
sol: A hurricane watch means conditions are possible within 48 hours.
A warning means they are expected within 36 hours.
Watch = get ready; warning = finish preparations.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: A hurricane watch means hurricane conditions are possible within about how many hours?
questions.w: Watch: within 48 hours.
sol: The watch comes first, with more time.
48 hours for a watch, 36 for a warning.
Use the time to get supplies and leave if told to.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: A hurricane's sustained winds are 100 mph. About how many knots is that? (1 kt ≈ 1.15 mph)
sol: To go from mph to knots, divide by 1.15.
The NHC reports in knots and mph.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: In the US, a hurricane's sustained wind is the average over…
questions.w: Sustained = 1-minute average; gust = a few seconds.
sol: A gust is a brief burst, usually a few seconds.
Sustained winds smooth these out over one minute.
Category is based on sustained winds, so gusts are higher.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: A hurricane has sustained winds of 156 mph. What Saffir-Simpson category is it? (Cat 4 is 130–156, Cat 5 is 157+)
questions.w: 156 mph is the top of Cat 4.
sol: Cat 4 goes up to 156.
Cat 5 starts at 157.
Boundaries matter in competition: one mph can change the category.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: A hurricane has sustained winds of 70 kt. Convert to mph (1 kt ≈ 1.15 mph) and give the Saffir–Simpson category (1: 74–95, 2: 96–110, 3: 111–129, 4: 130–156, 5: 157+).
questions.w: 70 × 1.15 = 80.5 mph, so category 1.
sol: Step 1: kt × 1.15 = 80.5 mph.
Step 2: match to the mph ranges.
80.5 mph is in category 1.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: A hurricane has sustained winds of 100 kt. Convert to mph (1 kt ≈ 1.15 mph) and give the Saffir–Simpson category (1: 74–95, 2: 96–110, 3: 111–129, 4: 130–156, 5: 157+).
questions.w: 100 × 1.15 = 115.0 mph, so category 3.
sol: Step 2: match to the mph ranges.
115.0 mph is in category 3.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: A hurricane has sustained winds of 120 kt. Convert to mph (1 kt ≈ 1.15 mph) and give the Saffir–Simpson category (1: 74–95, 2: 96–110, 3: 111–129, 4: 130–156, 5: 157+).
questions.w: 120 × 1.15 = 138.0 mph, so category 4.
sol: Step 2: match to the mph ranges.
138.0 mph is in category 4.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: Why can a Category 1 hurricane still cause a deadly disaster?
questions.w: The scale rates wind only.
sol: Saffir–Simpson ranks only the sustained wind.
Surge and rainfall flooding depend on size, speed and coast shape.
A slow, wet, weak storm can be deadlier than a fast, strong one.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: The category only rates wind; storm surge and heavy rain flooding can be huge
Category 1 storms are really Category 3 storms

questions.q: What is the main energy source of a hurricane?
questions.w: Condensation releases latent heat.
sol: Warm ocean water evaporates into vapor.
When vapor condenses into cloud, it releases heat, which makes air rise faster and drops pressure.
Think of it as an engine fueled by the warm ocean.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: Heat released when water vapor from warm ocean condenses

questions.q: A hurricane stalls over the same water for two days and weakens. Which process helps explain this?
questions.w: Mixing brings cold water up.
sol: Winds churn the ocean like a spoon stirring a mug of hot cocoa with cold milk at the bottom.
Cooler water means less heat and moisture for the storm.
Fast-moving storms leave less time for this.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: Its winds stir up cold water from below, cooling the surface
The ocean gets warmer from the storm

questions.q: Why do tropical storms rarely form within about 5° latitude of the equator?
questions.w: No Coriolis, no rotation.
sol: Earth's rotation bends moving air, and this effect nearly vanishes at the equator.
Without it, air flows straight into a low and fills it.
Hurricanes need that bending to spin up.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: The Coriolis effect is too weak to start the spin

questions.q: A Northern Hemisphere hurricane has sustained winds of 100 mph and moves forward at 15 mph. Roughly, how strong are the winds on its right side? (Add the forward speed.)
sol: On the right side, the storm's forward motion adds to its spin.
On the left side it subtracts: 100 − 15 = 85.
So the right-front side usually has the strongest winds and surge.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: A Northern Hemisphere hurricane has sustained winds of 120 mph and moves forward at 20 mph. Roughly, how strong are the winds on its right side? (Add the forward speed.)
sol: On the right side, the storm's forward motion adds to its spin.
On the left side it subtracts: 120 − 20 = 100.
So the right-front side usually has the strongest winds and surge.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: A hurricane moves north and makes landfall on a Gulf coast that faces south. Which place likely gets the biggest surge?
questions.w: East is the right side, where winds blow water onshore.
sol: Counterclockwise winds on the east side blow from the south, pushing water onto the coast.
Add the storm's forward speed, and winds on the right side are stronger.
The west side has winds blowing offshore.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: A town 30 miles east of the center (right side)
A town 30 miles west of the center

questions.q: Storm surge is 12 ft and it arrives at a time when the astronomical tide is 3 ft above normal. What is the storm tide, in ft?
sol: Storm tide = storm surge + normal tide.
That is why landfall at high tide is worse.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: What is the difference between storm surge and storm tide?
questions.w: Total water level = surge + tide.
sol: Storm surge is the extra water the storm pushes up.
The tide is the normal rise and fall of the sea.
Storm tide is the total water level you see, so timing with the tide matters.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: Storm tide is surge plus the normal tide
Surge is rain; tide is wind

questions.q: The cone of uncertainty on a hurricane forecast map shows…
questions.w: The cone is about the track of the center.
sol: The cone covers the area where the center is expected to pass about two-thirds of the time.
Dangerous winds and surge can extend far outside the cone.
Misconception: being outside the cone does not mean you are safe.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: The probable path of the storm's center, not the size of the storm or its impacts
The area of the hurricane's winds

questions.q: Why are hurricane intensity forecasts usually less accurate than track forecasts?
questions.w: Track is set by big flow patterns; intensity depends on small details.
sol: Steering winds are large and easier to forecast.
Internal changes like eyewall replacement are small.
Like predicting where a leaf goes in a river versus how fast it spins.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: Small-scale changes inside the storm, such as eyewall changes and shear, are hard to predict
Forecast models cannot see the ocean

questions.q: During an eyewall replacement cycle, a hurricane…
questions.w: An outer ring replaces the inner ring.
sol: A new ring of storms forms outside the original eyewall.
It chokes off the inner one, so the wind drops for a while.
Then the new eyewall contracts and the storm may strengthen again, with a larger eye.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: Builds an outer eyewall; the inner one weakens, so winds dip and then the larger eye re-strengthens

questions.q: The NHC defines rapid intensification as an increase in sustained winds of at least…
questions.w: 30 kt (35 mph) in 24 h.
sol: It is a fast jump in one day.
30 kt is about 35 mph.
These storms are hard to forecast and dangerous.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: Many Atlantic hurricanes begin as…
questions.w: Waves in the winds seed the storms.
sol: These are ripples in the wind pattern over Africa.
They cross the warm Atlantic, where they can grow into tropical storms.
They are one of the seeds for the Cape Verde storms.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: African easterly waves moving off the coast of Africa

questions.q: The Saharan Air Layer is…
questions.w: Dry air weakens storms.
sol: Dry air makes clouds evaporate and downdrafts chill the storm.
Dusty air is also stable, which prevents rising air.
It is like throwing a dry towel on a campfire.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: A dry, dusty air mass from Africa that can weaken Atlantic tropical storms
A warm, humid air mass that helps storms grow

questions.q: Why do hurricanes rarely reach California?
questions.w: Cold water cuts off the heat source.
sol: The California Current brings cool water from the north.
Hurricanes need about 26.5 °C or warmer.
So storms that approach fade away.
From your notes · Hurricanes: Land cuts off the heat source, so storms weaken.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: The ocean off California is too cold and storms turn away
California is too far north from the equator, so there is no rain

questions.q: Northern Hemisphere hurricanes spin…
questions.w: In the north they spin counterclockwise; in the south, clockwise.
sol: The Coriolis effect turns inflowing air.
North of the equator that turn is to the right, so storms spin counterclockwise.
Southern Hemisphere storms spin clockwise.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: Match each region to the name used for its tropical cyclones.
questions.w: Same storm, different names.
sol: Hurricane: Atlantic and eastern Pacific.
Typhoon: northwestern Pacific.
Cyclone: Indian Ocean and South Pacific.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: After moving north, a hurricane gets fronts and gains energy from temperature contrasts. It is now…
questions.w: Its fuel is no longer ocean heat.
sol: A hurricane has a warm core and no fronts.
Moving north, it meets cold air and fronts.
It becomes a cold-core storm, still dangerous with wind and rain.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: When does a tropical cyclone get a name?
questions.w: Names begin at 39 mph.
sol: A depression has a number.
At 39 mph it gets a name from the list.
Names of very deadly storms are retired.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: When it reaches tropical storm strength
When it forms as a disturbance

questions.q: Order these from the weakest to the strongest.
questions.w: Strengthening ladder.
sol: Depression: under 39 mph.
Tropical storm: 39–73 mph.
Hurricane: 74+ mph; Cat 3 starts at 111 and Cat 5 at 157.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: A hurricane is 320 miles away moving toward you at 10 mph. In how many hours does it arrive?
sol: Time = distance ÷ speed.
That is less than 36 hours, so you would already be in the warning window.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes

questions.q: Why does a slow-moving hurricane often cause more flooding rain?
questions.w: More time over the same place means more rain.
sol: Picture a hose: if you hold it still, the spot gets soaked; if you walk, each spot gets less.
Speed matters as much as strength for rain totals.
Example: Harvey (2017) stalled over Texas.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: It sits over one place longer and drops more rain there

questions.q: In a hurricane, tornadoes most often form in the…
questions.w: Right-front quadrant is the favorite spot.
sol: Extra wind shear is greatest there.
Spiral bands over land spin up small rotations.
Tornadoes in hurricanes are usually weak.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: Outer rain bands in the right-front quadrant

questions.q: A dropsonde, dropped from a hurricane hunter aircraft, measures…
questions.w: It is a weather instrument on a parachute.
sol: Hurricane hunters fly into the storm.
They drop instruments that radio data back.
This helps forecasters know the true strength.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: Pressure, temperature, humidity, and wind as it falls

questions.q: Why does a lower central pressure usually mean stronger winds?
questions.w: Wind blows from high to low pressure; steeper difference means faster wind.
sol: Picture a ball rolling down a hill: steeper hill, faster ball.
Pressure difference is the hill for air.
So a very low center pressure with high pressure outside means a steep drop and strong wind.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: A bigger pressure difference over a short distance drives faster winds
Low pressure makes the ocean colder

questions.q: Forecasters expect La Niña this summer. The Atlantic hurricane season is more likely to be…
questions.w: La Niña reduces shear in the Atlantic.
sol: El Niño raises shear over the Atlantic and suppresses storms.
La Niña does the reverse.
Low shear lets storms grow tall and organized.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: More active, because wind shear is lower
Less active, because wind shear is higher

questions.q: Why is the eye of a hurricane clear?
questions.w: Sinking air dries out.
sol: Air in the eye sinks, like air pressed by a pump.
Sinking air warms and its clouds evaporate.
The eyewall has the rising air and the storm.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: Air sinks in the eye, warming and drying it so clouds evaporate
It is above the cloud layer

questions.q: Atlantic hurricanes usually move west, then curve north and east. What mostly causes the curve?
questions.w: Large wind patterns steer.
sol: Winds flow clockwise around the Bermuda high, west in the tropics and north at its edge.
Farther north, westerlies carry storms east.
Like a leaf in a river bend.
Notes|n-hurr|Hurricanes
o: Steering winds around the subtropical high, then westerlies

questions.q: A forecast says air temperature 10°F and wind chill −5°F. What does the wind chill describe?
o: How cold the wind makes exposed skin feel
The new air temperature once the wind arrives
How cold a parked car's engine will get
The temperature at which snow forms
questions.w: Wind chill is a feels-like number for skin, not a new air temperature.
sol: Wind sweeps away the thin warm layer of air next to your skin, like blowing on hot soup to cool it faster.
So skin loses heat faster and feels colder than 10°F.
A thermometer still reads 10°F. Cars and water bottles cannot cool below the air temperature.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: A blizzard needs sustained winds or frequent gusts of at least how many mph?
questions.w: Blizzard wind is 35 mph or more.
sol: Blizzard needs three things: wind of 35 mph or more, falling or blowing snow that cuts visibility under ¼ mile, and all of it for 3+ hours.
Think of 35 as the 'speed limit' for blizzard wind.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Blizzard conditions must last at least how many hours?
questions.w: A blizzard must last 3 hours or longer.
sol: Blizzard conditions have to hold for 3 hours or more.
A one-hour whiteout is a snow squall, not a blizzard: the storm has to 'stay on' like a long movie, not a short clip.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Cold wind blows across a big lake. Which shore gets the lake-effect snow?
o: The downwind shore, where the wind leaves the lake
The upwind shore, where the wind arrives
questions.w: Lake-effect snow falls downwind of the lake.
sol: The air picks up heat and moisture while crossing the water, like a sponge soaking up water.
When it reaches land it is squeezed out as snow, so the sponge 'drips' on the downwind side.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Match each winter hazard to its description.
pairs: Loose snow lifted by the wind
questions.w: Know the four winter precipitation and wind terms.
sol: Sleet is frozen before it lands, like tiny pebbles.
Freezing rain is liquid until it touches something, then it glazes it like icing on a donut.
Blowing snow is old snow moved by wind, so a blizzard does not need new snow.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: A watch means conditions are favorable. Which alert means winter weather is happening or about to happen, so act now?
questions.w: Warning means happening or about to happen.
sol: Watch = ingredients are in the kitchen. Warning = the meal is being served.
Act on a warning: stay off the roads.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Why do bridges and overpasses ice up before ordinary roads?
o: Cold air touches them from above and below, and no ground under them stores warmth
Bridges are made of steel, which creates ice
Bridges get more freezing rain than roads
Salt cannot be used on bridges
questions.w: Bridges lose heat from both sides.
sol: A road sits on warm-ish ground, like a cup sitting on a heated table.
A bridge is like a cup held in the air: cold air wraps it from every side.
So the bridge surface cools to freezing first, and wet pavement becomes ice.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: A snow squall warning is issued for your town. What is coming?
o: A brief, intense burst of snow with gusty wind and sudden whiteouts
A two-day snowstorm with two feet of snow
Ice building on power lines overnight
questions.w: Snow squalls are short but can make roads treacherous fast.
sol: A squall is like a sudden shower in a sunny day, but made of snow and wind.
Visibility can drop from clear to near zero in seconds, and roads may flash-freeze.
Danger comes from the speed of the change, not the total snow.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: An Alberta clipper is usually…
o: A fast-moving low from Canada with light snow, gusty wind and colder air behind it
A slow Gulf storm that drops two feet of snow
questions.w: Clippers move quickly, so snow totals stay modest.
sol: Think of a speedboat: it moves quickly and makes a big wake of wind and cold air, but does not stay long in one spot.
Little time over each town means light snow, usually a few inches.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: A storm drops 1.5 inches of liquid-equivalent precipitation as snow with a 12:1 snow-to-liquid ratio. How many inches of snow fall?
questions.w: Snow depth = liquid × ratio.
sol: Ratio 12:1 means 12 inches of snow melt down to 1 inch of water.
Fluffy snow is like popcorn: lots of volume, little 'corn'.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Put the freezing rain steps in order, from cloud to ground.
items: Snow forms high in the cloud
Snow falls into a warm layer and melts to rain
Rain falls into a shallow below-freezing layer at the ground
Drops freeze on contact with cold surfaces
questions.w: Freezing rain needs a warm layer aloft and a thin cold layer below.
sol: Snow starts the trip, melts in the warm 'middle floor', then reaches the cold 'basement' too fast to refreeze in the air.
The drops stay liquid (supercooled) and freeze the moment they touch a branch or wire.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Lake-effect snow often fades in late winter after the lake freezes over. Why?
o: Ice cuts off the heat and moisture that the open water supplies
questions.w: Open water is the engine of lake-effect snow.
sol: The lake is the stove and the water is the pot of steam. Freeze the lake and the pot has a lid on it.
No heat and moisture transfer means no unstable air and no heavy bands.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: Lake effectCold air over warm open lake water, narrow heavy snow bands downwind
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Cold wind blows from the west across a long lake that runs north to south. Which shore gets lake-effect snow?
questions.w: Snow falls downwind, so for a west wind, east.
sol: Follow the wind: it enters on the west shore and leaves on the east.
Moisture is picked up on the way across, so snow falls where the air leaves the lake.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Hypothermia begins when core body temperature falls below about how many °F?
questions.w: Hypothermia starts below about 95°F (35°C).
sol: Normal core temperature is about 98.6°F.
Below 95°F the body cannot make heat as fast as it loses it, like a car running out of fuel on a cold day.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: After a snowball fight in strong wind, a student's fingertips are numb, white and waxy. This is most likely…
o: Hypothermia, a low core body temperature
questions.w: Frostbite is local freezing, hypothermia is the whole body cooling.
sol: Frostbite hits the parts farthest from the 'furnace': fingers, toes, ears, nose.
Hypothermia shows as shivering, slurred speech, confusion.
Warm slowly and get medical help for frostbite.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Why can a nor'easter cause coastal flooding that lasts through several high tides?
o: Winds from the northeast push ocean water onto the coast for many hours
Rain from the storm is always saltwater
Nor'easters rotate clockwise and suck water up
questions.w: Long-lasting onshore wind piles water up.
sol: Imagine blowing across a bathtub: water piles up at the far end.
The storm stays offshore for a day or more, so the 'blowing' goes on through multiple tides.
Each high tide rides on top of the extra water.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: Nor'easterStrong East Coast storm; northeast winds; snow, coastal flooding, wind
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Which has the LOWEST wind chill? Choose the (air temperature, wind speed) pair.
questions.w: Wind chill depends on both temperature and wind, and temperature matters more here.
sol: Misconception: more wind always wins. Wind helps, but a much colder start beats it, like a deep freezer with a small fan.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: The NWS wind chill formula is only valid when…
o: The air is at or below 50°F and wind is above 3 mph
questions.w: No cold or no breeze means no wind chill.
sol: Wind chill is about heat loss from skin, so you need cold air and moving air.
On a calm 70°F day there is nothing to 'chill'.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Which snow adds more weight to a roof per inch of depth?
questions.w: Wet snow holds much more water per inch.
sol: Powder is mostly air, like a sponge cake. Wet snow is packed and full of water, like a soaked sponge.
More liquid per inch means heavier roof load.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Soundings: cloud top −10°C, a 2-km layer at +4°C (1 to 3 km up), then a thin layer from the ground to 200 m at −2°C. What reaches the ground?
questions.w: A deep warm layer plus a shallow cold layer gives supercooled liquid drops.
sol: Snow melts completely in the warm layer, becoming rain.
The cold layer at the ground is too thin to refreeze the drops in the air.
They stay liquid until they hit something below 0°C, then freeze: freezing rain.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Soundings: cloud top −10°C, a layer at +3°C from 1.5 to 3 km, then a deep layer at −5°C from the ground to 1.5 km. What reaches the ground?
questions.w: A deep cold layer refreezes melted drops into pellets.
sol: Snow melts in the warm layer.
The cold layer below is deep (1.5 km), giving drops time to refreeze, like water drops dropped into a deep freezer.
They land as ice pellets: sleet.
From your notes · Precipitation, flooding, IDF: SleetSnow melts, then refreezes as ice pellets in a cold layer near the ground
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: A flat roof of 1,000 ft² carries 8 inches of snow at a 10:1 snow-to-liquid ratio. Water weighs 62.4 lb per cubic foot. About how many pounds of snow are on the roof?
questions.w: Convert snow depth to water depth, then weigh the water.
sol: Water depth = 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8 inch = 0.067 ft.
Volume = 1,000 ft² × 0.067 ft = 66.7 ft³.
Weight = 66.7 × 62.4 ≈ 4,160 lb, about two small cars. Light fluffy flakes add up.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: A foot (18 inches) of snow falls from 0.9 inch of liquid-equivalent precipitation. What is the snow-to-liquid ratio? Give the first number of the ratio, ___:1.
questions.w: Ratio = snow depth ÷ liquid depth.
sol: 18 ÷ 0.9 = 20, so the ratio is 20:1.
That is very fluffy snow, typical of cold dry air, like a pillow full of feathers.
Typical snow is about 10:1 and wet snow is lower.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: 'Bomb cyclone' means a storm deepens a lot in 24 hours. The threshold is 24 mb at 60°N and smaller at lower latitudes (about 18 mb at 40°N). A storm at 40°N drops 20 mb in 24 hours. Is it a bomb?
o: Yes, 20 mb is above the 18 mb needed at 40°N
No, it must be at least 24 mb everywhere
No, bombs need winds of 74 mph
Only if it is a hurricane
questions.w: The threshold scales with latitude.
sol: Same pressure drop means stronger storm at lower latitudes, because the Coriolis effect is weaker there.
So the bar is lower at 40°N.
20 mb is greater than 18 mb, so yes. Misconception: a fixed 24 mb everywhere.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Rule of thumb for lake effect: the lake surface should be at least 13°C warmer than the air at 850 mb (about 1.5 km up). The lake is 6°C, and the 850 mb air is −12°C. Is lake-effect snow likely?
o: No, the lake must be above 15°C
Only if the lake is frozen
questions.w: Difference = lake − 850 mb air.
sol: The bigger the gap, the more unstable the air, like a pot on a hot burner versus a warm one.
Unstable air rises fast and builds snow bands.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Lake water is 8°C. Using the 13°C rule, what is the warmest 850 mb air temperature (°C) that still supports lake-effect snow?
questions.w: 850 mb air must be at most lake temperature − 13.
sol: Need lake − air ≥ 13, so air ≤ 8 − 13 = −5°C.
Any warmer, and the gap shrinks, so the air stays too stable. Like a hot bath: if the room is almost as warm, nothing 'steams'.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: The sky is clear. Wind gusts 42 mph on loose old snow, visibility is under ⅛ mile, and this lasts 4 hours. Is this a blizzard?
o: No, a blizzard needs 12 inches of new snow
Only if the temperature is below 0°F
questions.w: Blizzard needs wind, low visibility, and 3+ hours, not new snow.
sol: A ground blizzard happens when wind lifts old snow like dust off a dry field.
Wind of 35+ mph, visibility under ¼ mile, 3+ hours: all met.
Common mistake: thinking a blizzard needs new snow.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: BlizzardWind or gusts ≥ 35 mph + falling/blowing snow + visibility under ¼ mile, all for 3+ hours
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Air temperature is 20°F and the wind chill is 5°F. A bowl of water sits outside all night. How cold can the water get?
o: Below 5°F because wind keeps pulling heat
questions.w: Wind speeds up cooling but cannot beat the air temperature.
sol: A fan can cool a hot bowl faster, but never below room temperature.
Water freezes at 32°F and keeps cooling toward 20°F, the air temperature.
Wind chill applies to warm, living skin, not to objects.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: A strong low moves north along the coast. Town X is inland, 60 miles northwest of the track. Town Y is 60 miles southeast, on the ocean side. Which usually gets heavy snow?
o: Town X, on the cold northwest side
Town Y, near the ocean moisture
Neither; the center always misses snow
questions.w: Heavy snow usually falls northwest of the track; the east side gets warm ocean air.
sol: Winds spin counterclockwise around a low.
Northwest of the track, winds bring cold air from the north: snow.
Southeast of the track, winds bring mild ocean air: rain or mix. Track matters more than strength.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Select ALL conditions that favor lake-effect snow.
o: Lake water much warmer than the air
Wind crossing many miles of open water
Cold air mass moving over the lake
Lake mostly covered with thick ice
Warm air arriving from the south over land
questions.w: Warm water, long fetch, and cold air together build lake bands.
sol: Fetch is the length of water the wind travels, like the distance a sponge drags across a wet table.
Cold air over warm water becomes unstable and rises.
Ice and warm southerly air shut the process off.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: Lake effectCold air over warm open lake water, narrow heavy snow bands downwind
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Sleet and freezing rain can both fall with the same liquid amount. Why does freezing rain usually do more damage to trees and power lines?
o: It freezes on contact and builds a heavy ice coat
It is heavier, because raindrops are bigger
questions.w: Sleet is already frozen and bounces; freezing rain sticks and builds up.
sol: Sleet is like pebbles hitting a wire: they bounce and pile on the ground.
Freezing rain is like paint: it coats every side of a branch and wire.
¼ inch of ice can bring down lines.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: Ice stormFreezing rain builds up ice. ¼ inch can bring down lines
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Hourly obs (gust mph / visibility mi), snow falling all hours: 1 pm 30/0.5, 2 pm 37/0.2, 3 pm 40/0.1, 4 pm 36/0.2, 5 pm 34/0.2, 6 pm 38/0.15, 7 pm 41/0.1. When were blizzard conditions first met for 3 straight hours?
questions.w: Check each hour for 35+ mph and under ¼ mile, then count a streak of 3.
sol: 1 pm fails (30 mph, 0.5 mi). 2, 3, and 4 pm pass: that is 3 in a row.
5 pm fails (34 mph), which breaks the streak. 6 and 7 pm pass but only 2 hours.
Like a basketball streak, one miss resets the count.
From your notes · Severe winter storms: BlizzardWind or gusts ≥ 35 mph + falling/blowing snow + visibility under ¼ mile, all for 3+ hours
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: A storm drops 1.8 inches of liquid-equivalent precipitation. The first 0.6 inch falls as wet snow (8:1), the remaining 1.2 inches as fluffy snow (15:1). How many inches of snow in total?
questions.w: Convert each part with its own ratio, then add.
sol: Wet part: 0.6 × 8 = 4.8 in.
Fluffy part: 1.2 × 15 = 18 in.
Total: 4.8 + 18 = 22.8 in. Do not use one average ratio: each period gets its own.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: A roof is rated for 12 lb per ft². It holds 15 inches of wet snow (8:1), then rain adds 0.7 inch of liquid that the snow absorbs. One inch of water over 1 ft² weighs 5.2 lb. What is the load in lb/ft²?
questions.w: Add the snow's water equivalent and the rain, then convert to weight.
sol: Snow water = 15 ÷ 8 = 1.875 in.
Add rain: 1.875 + 0.7 = 2.575 in of water.
2.575 × 5.2 ≈ 13.4 lb/ft², above 12. Rain-on-snow is like pouring water on a sponge already full: weight jumps, depth does not.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Put the lake-effect snow steps in order.
items: Cold air blows over warmer open water
The air gains heat and moisture
The air becomes unstable and rises into clouds
Snow bands fall on the downwind shore
questions.w: Heat and moisture make unstable air, which makes bands.
sol: The lake warms the bottom of the air like a pot warming the bottom of a soup.
Warm air at the bottom rises and forms clouds.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Rule of thumb: the 1000–500 mb thickness near 5,400 m separates rain from snow, and thinner means colder. A city has 5,250 m. Ignoring surface temperature, what is more likely?
o: Rain, because thinner air is warmer
questions.w: Thickness measures the average temperature of the air layer.
sol: Warm air expands like a balloon, making the layer thicker. Cold air shrinks, making it thinner.
5,250 m is below 5,400 m, so a cold layer favors snow.
It is only a guide; the surface layer can still be warm.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Winds 36 mph, visibility 0.2 mile, falling snow, for 3.5 hours. Is this a blizzard?
o: Yes, all three tests are met
No, it lasted too short a time
No, visibility must be under ⅛ mile
questions.w: 35+ mph, under ¼ mile, 3+ hours.
sol: Like a checklist: three ticks mean blizzard.
Notes|n-winter|Severe winter storms

questions.q: Match each hazard to the right action.
questions.w: Each hazard has a basic safe action.
sol: Tornado: put walls between you and the wind, like hiding behind a tall fence.
Flash flood: water flows downhill, so go up.
Lightning: a building or hard-topped car, not a tree.
Surge: get out of the water's path before it comes.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: You hear thunder but the sky overhead is blue. Are you safe outdoors?
o: No, lightning can strike miles from the storm
Yes, lightning only comes from overhead clouds
Yes, if you are not near water
questions.w: If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck.
sol: Lightning can travel sideways ten miles or more, like a long jump from the storm.
Blue sky above does not mean the storm is far enough.
Go inside at the first thunder.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: What is the National Weather Service slogan about flooded roads? Complete it: Turn Around, ___.
questions.w: Never drive through floodwater.
sol: Water on a road hides washed-out pavement, like a trap door.
Six inches of fast water can knock you down, and about a foot can float many cars.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: Select ALL items that belong in a basic emergency kit.
questions.w: Kits hold safe basics; flames and indoor generators are hazards.
sol: Water, light, and first aid keep you going for a few days.
Candles can start fires and generators make carbon monoxide: both are dangerous in a storm.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: Plan 1 gallon of water per person per day. A family of 4 prepares for 3 days. How many gallons?
questions.w: People × days × gallons.
sol: 4 people × 3 days × 1 gallon = 12 gallons.
This is drinking water; it is like packing a lunch for each day.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: You see lightning and hear thunder 15 seconds later. Sound travels about 1 mile in 5 seconds. How many miles away is the strike?
questions.w: Divide seconds by 5.
sol: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 miles.
Light arrives almost instantly, sound takes its time, like seeing a far-away hammer hit before hearing it.
3 miles is close enough to be struck: go inside.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: Thunder was last heard at 4:10 pm. When is the earliest safe time to resume outdoor practice?
o: 4:40 pm, 30 minutes after the last thunder
Right away if the rain stops
questions.w: Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
sol: The storm can leave and still strike behind it, like a bully who keeps swinging while backing off.
Restart the 30-minute clock with each new thunder.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: A flash flood warning is issued for your area and you are near a creek. What should you do?
o: Move to higher ground right away
Wait for the creek to rise
Drive through shallow water to get out
questions.w: Flash floods rise in minutes.
sol: Water behaves like a slide: low spots get it first.
Basements fill quickly.
Do not walk or drive through floodwater.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: A highway overpass is a safe place to shelter from a tornado.
o: False: wind speeds up under it and debris flies through
True if you climb up high
questions.w: Overpasses are a deadly myth.
sol: An overpass is like a wind tunnel: air squeezes through and speeds up.
You are also exposed to flying debris.
Instead: a sturdy building or a low ditch as a last resort.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: A tornado is coming. Should you open the windows to equalize the pressure?
o: No, it wastes time and does nothing to protect the house
Yes, it prevents the house from exploding
Yes, on the side facing the storm
questions.w: Winds and debris do the damage, not pressure.
sol: Damage comes from wind and flying objects.
Open windows just let debris in. Use the time to get to shelter.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: At school, a tornado warning is issued. Where should students shelter?
o: An interior hallway on the lowest floor, away from the gym or large rooms
The gym, which is the biggest room
questions.w: Wide-roof spans collapse easily.
sol: Wide flat roofs are like a tabletop without legs.
Small interior rooms on the lowest floor give walls on all sides.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: Which alert system sends a loud message to phones in a warned area, no app needed?
questions.w: WEA is from the official alert system.
sol: It uses cell towers to 'ring everyone in the room' at the same time.
Apps need to be installed, but WEA is built into the phone.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: A portable generator should be run at least how many feet from the house, doors and windows?
questions.w: Run it outdoors at least 20 feet away.
sol: Carbon monoxide has no smell or color and can drift in.
20 feet is about the length of a school bus's front half; farther is safer.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: A power outage begins. About how many hours does an unopened refrigerator keep food safe?
questions.w: Fridge: about 4 hours, if the door stays shut.
sol: Cold stays in like in a cooler; each time the door opens, the cold escapes.
After 4 hours, throw out meat, milk and leftovers.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: A severe thunderstorm warning is issued for a storm with hail at least ___ and wind gusts at least ___.
questions.w: These are the severe criteria used by the NWS.
sol: Quarter-size hail dents cars and 58 mph wind breaks branches.
A storm below this is not called severe, but can still be dangerous.

questions.q: A hurricane watch means hurricane conditions are possible within about how many hours?
questions.w: Watch is 48 hours; warning is 36 hours.
sol: Watch = 48 hours lead time, warning = 36 hours.
Use the watch time to get ready and leave if told.

questions.q: Put these tornado alerts in order, from earliest to most urgent.
questions.w: Alerts get more urgent as the threat gets closer.

questions.q: A swimmer is pulled away from the beach by a rip current. What should they do?
o: Swim parallel to shore until free, then angle back
questions.w: Do not fight the current.
sol: A rip current is like a treadmill going out: running against it tires you.
Step off the side of the treadmill (swim parallel), then walk back.

questions.q: At 90°F, which feels hotter?

sol: Sweat cools you only when it evaporates.
Humid air is like a wet towel that cannot dry.
Heat index is a feels-like number for this.

questions.q: The county is under a tornado watch at 2 pm. At 3 pm a tornado warning is issued for your town. What changed?
o: A tornado is occurring or imminent nearby, so act now
questions.w: A watch says 'be ready', a warning says 'act'.
sol: Watch = favorable conditions. Warning = tornado spotted or on radar.
Move to shelter without waiting for more information.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: Why is leaving a child in a parked car on a mild day dangerous?
o: The inside heats far above outdoor temperature within minutes
Cars cool faster than the outdoors

Children's bodies heat up faster than adults'.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: A wall of blowing dust appears ahead while you drive. What does the NWS advise?
o: Pull off the road, turn lights off, foot off the brake
Keep driving fast with lights on
Stop in the lane with brake lights on
questions.w: Pull aside, stay alive.
sol: Cars behind you may follow your lights and crash into you.
Off the road, lights off and foot off brake: nobody follows.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: Why is a hard-topped car safer in lightning?
o: Its metal body carries the current around you
questions.w: The metal frame protects, not the tires.
sol: The current flows around the outside of the metal shell, like water around a boat.

questions.q: The calm eye of a hurricane passes over your town. What comes next?
o: The eyewall returns with strong winds from the opposite direction
questions.w: The eye is a gap in the storm.
sol: Think of a donut: the hole is calm but the rest is stormy.

questions.q: A flood moves at twice the speed. The force on a person rises with the square of speed. By what factor does the force increase?
questions.w: Force ∝ speed².
sol: Double the speed: 2² = 4 times the force.
Like standing in a fast current: twice as fast pushes four times harder.

questions.q: A tornado warning is issued while you are driving and no shelter is close. What is the best option?
o: Park, buckle up, head below the windows and cover yourself
Outrun the tornado in a straight line
Stay in traffic with the windows open
questions.w: Use the best option when no shelter exists.
sol: Seat belts and covering protect against debris.
Do not shelter under an overpass.
A low ditch is a last resort.

questions.q: Which situation is most dangerous?

questions.w: Heat stroke is a medical emergency.
sol: Heat stroke is when the body's cooling system fails, like a radiator with no coolant.
Heat exhaustion is milder: heavy sweating, cool clammy skin.

questions.q: You are stuck in a car in a blizzard with the engine on. What should you do?

Run the engine with the tailpipe buried
Leave the engine on all the time

sol: Cars are shelter and easier for rescuers to find.

Run the engine briefly to save fuel.

questions.q: A 'tornado emergency' differs from a tornado warning because it means…
o: A confirmed, damaging tornado is threatening a populated area
questions.w: It is the highest tornado alert.
sol: A warning says 'take cover'. An emergency says 'a large tornado is on the ground in a populated area'.

questions.q: Storm surge of 9 ft arrives at high tide that is 3 ft above normal sea level. How tall is the storm tide (water above normal), in feet?

sol: Surge rides on the tide like a wave on a stepladder: timing matters.
A surge at low tide does less harm than at high tide.

questions.q: A dry desert wash floods under a clear sky. How?
o: Heavy rain fell miles upstream and rushed down
Flash floods only occur under rain
questions.w: Flash floods can arrive from far away.
sol: Water runs through a wash like water through a gutter after rain on the roof.
You may never see the rain.
Notes|n-safety|Hazards and safety

questions.q: Select ALL actions that are safe during a thunderstorm.
o: Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder
Stand under a tall lone tree
questions.w: Buildings are safe; trees and metal are not.
sol: Lightning can travel through pipes and wires.
A lone tree is a lightning rod, and so is a metal umbrella.

o: A small but extremely intense storm that crossed a populated area

questions.q: Ida's remnants flooded the Northeast with winds well below hurricane strength. What is the lesson?
o: Weak winds do not mean weak rain, remnants can flood

The eye pushes the water down
Surge only happens north of the eye

questions.q: Helene (2024) killed many people far inland in the Appalachians. What made the flooding so extreme?
o: Heavy tropical rain lifted by mountains onto already wet ground

o: Yes to both: +40 mph, and 115 mph is Category 3
Yes, but 115 mph is only Category 2
No, it needs a 60 mph rise
No, and Category 3 starts at 130 mph
questions.w: Category 3 is 111–129 mph, and the rise is above 35 mph.
sol: 115 − 75 = 40 mph, more than 35.
Major hurricanes are Category 3 or higher (111+ mph).

questions.q: The Great Flood of 1993 lasted for months. What best explains it?

obs: ASOS = automated airport stations. Mesonets = dense local stations. Buoys = water. Radiosondes = balloon packs that profile the air above.
Shows how much rain or hail and where. Stronger echoes look hotter or darker. Composite shows the strongest echo at any height.
Shows motion toward or away from the radar. Toward is green (negative). Away is red (positive).
Tells how alike the targets are. Rain is high. Debris is low. A low spot in a hook echo can mean a tornado is lofting debris.
Takes out the storm's own movement. Rotation is easier to see.
Visible needs daylight. Infrared and water vapor work at night. Cold tops show bright on IR, so tall storms stand out.
maps: Temperature upper left. Dew point lower left. Pressure upper right. Pressure change lower right. Sky cover is the circle. Wind barb is the staff.
The staff points to where wind comes FROM. Half flag 5 kt. Full flag 10. Triangle 50. Add them up.
Take the three digits. 500 or more? Put 9 in front. Less than 500? Put 10. Add a decimal before the last digit.
FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC get cloudier. The three digits are height in hundreds of feet. BKN040 = 4,000 ft.
27/22 means 27 °C and dew point 22 °C. An M means minus.
upper: 850 mb = low moisture. 700 mb = steering. 500 mb = troughs and ridges. 300 mb = jet stream.
A plot of wind at each height. A long curved path means strong shear. Clockwise turning with height helps supercells.
Temperature solid. Dew point dashed. Lines close = moist or cloudy. Far apart = dry.
A layer where temperature rises with height. Very stable. It can act as a cap that holds storms back.
Same skills as Stüve. The lines are just tilted to spread them out. (States/Nationals)
Height where a rising parcel makes cloud. Lower LCL means lower cloud base and higher tornado risk.
Storm fuel in J/kg. Under 1000 marginal. 1000–2500 moderate. 2500–4000 strong. Over 4000 extreme.
setup: Moisture, instability, lift, and shear. Miss one and storms struggle.
Fast river of air aloft. It steers storms and adds energy.
Cold front: fast and sharp storms. Warm front: wide steady rain. Occluded: cold catches warm. Stationary: stalled.
Boundary between moist and dry air. It is about moisture, not temperature. Common on the Plains.
Wind changing with height. It lets updraft and downdraft work apart. Direction change starts rotation.
A narrow stream of heavy water vapor. Can drop extreme rain at landfall.
Long fetch and warm water give storms energy. Storms leave a cooler wake. Mountains can trigger, weaken, or redirect storms.
clouds: The thunderstorm cloud. It can bring every type of severe weather.
A lowered, often rotating base under the main updraft. A key tornado warning sign.
A wedge along the leading edge. It marks the gust front.
Rotating cone from the storm base. Not on the ground yet.
Pouches under an anvil. Often seen as a storm weakens.
dh: A long period with far too little precipitation. Water runs short.
A long period of unusually high temperatures.
A blocking high-pressure ridge. It parks over a region and pushes storms away.
Crop loss, water limits, wildfire risk, and heat illness.
precip: Collision-coalescence: small drops bump and merge into raindrops.
Bergeron process: ice crystals grow while supercooled droplets shrink.
Riming: drops freeze onto ice, making graupel and hail. Aggregation: ice crystals stick to make snowflakes.
Snow: cold all the way. Sleet: refreezes in a cold layer near the ground. Freezing rain: falls as liquid, freezes on contact.
Pea ¼ in. Penny ¾. Quarter 1 in (severe). Golf ball 1¾. Baseball 2¾. Bigger means stronger updraft.
Flash: minutes to hours. River: days. Urban: drains overwhelmed. Heavy rain on burn scars makes debris flows.
Intensity versus duration. Short bursts are more intense. Rarer storms plot higher. Chance per year = 1 ÷ return period.
light: Ice and graupel collide. Light ice rises (positive). Heavy graupel falls (negative). The base ends up mostly negative.
Seconds from flash to thunder ÷ 5 = miles away.
Networks of sensors time the signal to find each strike.
tstorm: Hail 1 inch or bigger, wind 58 mph or more, or a tornado.
A cluster or line. New cells keep forming.
One long-lived storm with a rotating updraft called a mesocyclone. Makes the strongest tornadoes.
A big, round, long-lived cluster of storms.
Cumulus: updraft only. Mature: updraft and downdraft, worst weather. Dissipating: downdraft only.
winds: Any storm wind damage that is not from rotation. The most common wind report.
A downdraft that hits the ground and spreads out.
Microburst: under 4 km wide. Macroburst: 4 km or more.
The leading edge of cool outflow. It can show as a shelf cloud.
Squall line: organized line of storms. Derecho: long-lived windstorm with hundreds of miles of damage.
Air speeds up as it sinks down a mountain. No thunderstorm needed.
Bow echo = derecho or damaging wind. Fine line = gust front. Bowing segment = strongest wind on a squall line.
torn: A violently rotating column touching the ground and a cloud. A waterspout is the same thing over water.
Late afternoon, spring, Plains and Southeast. But it can happen any time.
Before 1 Feb 2007: Fujita (F). On or after: Enhanced Fujita (EF). Both rate damage.
A reflectivity hook wrapping around the mesocyclone.
Strong inbound and outbound velocity side by side. Intense rotation.
Low correlation coefficient inside the hook. Debris is in the air.
hurr: Hurricane, typhoon, and cyclone are one storm type named by ocean.
Invest, depression, tropical storm (39–73 mph), hurricane (74+), major hurricane (Cat 3+).
Warm water (26.5 °C+), moisture, low shear, away from the equator.
Eye: calm. Eyewall: worst wind and rain. Spiral bands: showers, tornadoes.
Water pushed onshore. Bigger with strong, large, slow storms and shallow coasts. Often the deadliest hazard.
Land, wind shear, dry air, and cooler water all weaken a storm.
winter: Wind or gusts of 35 mph or more, snow in the air, and visibility under ¼ mile. All for at least 3 hours.
Wind blowing old snow can meet the blizzard test.
Big East Coast storm. Northeast winds. Snow, wind, and coastal flooding.
Cold air over warm open lake water makes narrow heavy snow bands downwind.
Freezing rain coats everything. ¼ inch can break lines and branches.
safety: Happening or about to. Act now.
Lowest floor, interior room, away from windows.
Follow evacuation orders. Surge is often the deadliest part.
Flood: go high, never drive through water. Lightning: get indoors or into a hard-topped car.
weather.gov, spc.noaa.gov for storms, nhc.noaa.gov for tropics.
Use generators outside. Stay away from downed lines. Power loss can cause carbon monoxide danger.
cases: Galveston 1900, Andrew 1992, Katrina 2005, Sandy 2012, Ida 2021, Ian 2022, Hilary 2023, Helene 2024, Erin 2025, Melissa 2025.
Blizzard of March 1888. Dust Bowl 1930s. Xenia tornado 1974. April 2011 outbreaks. Great Flood 1993. Storm of the Century 1993.
The rules say you analyze data given. Know what type each event was.
1) Name the storm type. 2) List the clues. 3) Use the right scale or signature. 4) Check the date against cutoffs.
Long drought plus plowed soil gave huge dust storms on the Plains.
Months of heavy rain flooded the Mississippi and Missouri rivers.

A balloon instrument package that measures the air above.
Radar measure of how much is falling.
Radar measure of how alike targets are. Low means debris or mixed targets.
A plot of wind speed and direction at each height.
A layer where temperature rises with height.
Lifting condensation level: height where a rising parcel becomes cloud.
Convective available potential energy: storm fuel.
A boundary between moist and dry air.
A narrow stream of heavy water vapor.
The distance wind blows over open water.
A rotating updraft inside a supercell.
Ocean water pushed onshore by a storm.
Average time between storms of a given strength.
stuck: Write down what you KNOW and what the question wants.
Find the figure or number clue. Read the labels and units.

cards.t: ASOS = automated airport stations. Mesonets = dense local stations. Buoys = water. Radiosondes = balloon packs that profile the air above.

s.t: Thermometer: air temperature.
Barometer: air pressure. Falling pressure often means a storm is coming.
Anemometer: wind speed. Wind vane: wind direction.
Hygrometer: humidity. Rain gauge: rainfall.

dd.why: Different tools watch different places. ASOS stations are automated and sit mostly at airports. Mesonets are dense local networks that fill gaps. Buoys measure over water.
