Radiosondes are balloon instruments that rise and send back temperature, humidity, and wind at each height. Together they make a full picture of the air.
dd.pic: Draw a vertical column of air. Put a station at the bottom, a buoy on a wave, and a balloon rising with a small box.
dd.analogy: A school with security cameras: some at doors, some in halls, some on the roof. Each camera covers a spot. It stops working because cameras do not measure wind.
ways: ASOS airport, mesonet local, buoy water, balloon upper air.
Radiosondes launch twice a day at 00Z and 12Z.
Surface by ASOS, upper air by balloon.

ex.q: Which network of automated airport weather stations is the main surface observing system in the U.S.?

dd.trap: Mixing ASOS and mesonet. ASOS is airports, mesonet is dense local.

cards.t: Shows how much rain or hail and where. Stronger echoes look hotter or darker. Composite shows the strongest echo at any height.

dd.why: Radar sends a pulse, then listens for the echo. Bigger or more drops and hail send back more energy. Reflectivity measures that echo strength in dBZ. Higher dBZ means heavier rain or hail. Composite reflectivity shows the strongest echo at any height above a point.
dd.pic: Draw a radar dot with a beam going out to a storm and a returning arrow. Color the storm green to red from outside to the core.
dd.analogy: Like shouting at a cliff and hearing a louder echo from a bigger cliff. It stops working because radar uses radio waves.
ways: Brighter or hotter colors mean stronger echoes.
20 dBZ is light rain, 40 dBZ is moderate to heavy, 60 dBZ and up can be hail.
Red or purple means big drops or hail.

ex.q: Which radar product shows how much precipitation is in a storm and where?

dd.trap: Thinking reflectivity shows wind. It shows amount.

cards.t: Shows motion toward or away from the radar. Toward is green (negative). Away is red (positive).

dd.why: Doppler radar uses the shift in the returning wave. Targets moving toward the radar squeeze the wave, away stretches it. The radar shows this as motion. Toward is green, called negative. Away is red, called positive. It only sees the motion along the radar beam, not across it.
dd.pic: Draw a radar at the left. Draw an arrow pointing toward it labeled green and an arrow pointing away labeled red.
dd.analogy: Like an ambulance siren: higher as it comes, lower as it leaves. It stops working because radar sees only toward or away.
ways: -20 kt is toward the radar. +20 kt is away.
Red is away, green is toward.

ex.q: Which radar product shows motion toward or away from the radar?

dd.trap: Confusing red with hot weather. Red is away.

cards.t: Tells how alike the targets are. Rain is high. Debris is low. A low spot in a hook echo can mean a tornado is lofting debris.

dd.why: Correlation coefficient (CC) measures how alike the targets are in each radar pulse. Raindrops are similar in shape, so CC is high, near 1. Debris, hail mix, and birds are mixed shapes, so CC is low. A low spot inside a hook can mean a tornado is lofting debris.
dd.pic: Draw a hook echo. Inside it draw a small blue spot labeled low CC.
dd.analogy: A class of students in the same uniform (high CC) versus a crowd in costumes (low CC). It stops working because debris is not alive.
ways: Rain is alike, debris is not.
Rain CC about 0.97 to 1.0. Debris may drop below 0.8.
Low CC in a hook is a debris sign.

ex.q: What does a low correlation coefficient value inside a storm usually mean?
steps: So something non-rain is there, such as debris.
Answer: mixed or non-rain targets such as debris.

dd.trap: Thinking low CC means light rain. It means mixed targets.

cards.t: Takes out the storm's own movement. Rotation is easier to see.

dd.why: Storms move, and that motion hides the spin. Storm relative motion subtracts the storm's own movement. After that, wind toward and away from the radar shows the rotation more clearly. Without it, the signal looks mixed.
dd.pic: Draw a storm moving east. Draw wind arrows. Then draw them again with the storm's motion removed, showing a clear pair.
dd.analogy: Like walking on a moving train: you judge your motion relative to the train. It stops working because the radar frame is the ground.
ways: Remove the storm's travel to see the spin.
Storm moves 30 kt east. Wind of 50 kt east becomes 20 kt east relative to the storm.

ex.q: A wind of 50 kt east is measured while a storm moves 30 kt east. What is the storm-relative wind?
steps: Storm relative means subtract storm motion.

dd.trap: Adding instead of subtracting.
dd.tip: Subtract the storm to see the swirl.

cards.t: Visible needs daylight. Infrared and water vapor work at night. Cold tops show bright on IR, so tall storms stand out.

dd.why: Satellites see from above. Visible imagery uses reflected sunlight, so it works only in daylight. Infrared measures heat given off, so it works day and night. Colder cloud tops are higher and show bright, so tall storms stand out. Water vapor shows moisture in the upper air.
dd.pic: Draw a satellite above Earth with two arrows: sun to cloud to satellite (visible) and cloud to satellite (infrared).
dd.analogy: Visible is a camera with no flash, so it needs light. Infrared is a heat camera that works in dark. It stops working because satellites also use filters.
ways: Visible needs the sun. IR does not.
Tops at -60 C are much higher than tops at +10 C.

ex.q: Which satellite imagery works only in daylight?
steps: Infrared and water vapor use heat or moisture.

dd.trap: Thinking infrared needs light. It does not.

cards.t: Temperature upper left. Dew point lower left. Pressure upper right. Pressure change lower right. Sky cover is the circle. Wind barb is the staff.

dd.why: A station model packs a whole weather report into a small space. Every number has a fixed spot, so you read it like a form, not a picture. Temperature sits upper left, dew point lower left, pressure upper right, pressure change lower right. The circle in the middle shows how much sky is covered, and the staff shows the wind. Fixed spots let hundreds of stations fit on one map.
dd.pic: Draw a small circle. Write T at upper left, Td at lower left, P at upper right, change at lower right. Draw a line (staff) out of the circle for wind.
dd.analogy: Like a score box in a sports broadcast: the same spot always shows the same stat. Mapping: the circle is the game, each corner is one stat. It stops working because a score box has words, while a station model has only numbers.
ways: Left side is temperature and dew point. Right side is pressure and its change.
72 at upper left, 65 at lower left: temperature 72, dew point 65 (7 degrees apart, so fairly humid).
Top left is temperature, below it is dew point.

ex.q: On a station model, where is the dew point plotted?
steps: Picture the circle with four corners.
Dew point is always directly below it.
So dew point is lower left.
Answer: lower left of the circle.

dd.trap: Swapping temperature and dew point. Dew point is never larger than temperature, so the top number should be bigger.
dd.tip: Temperature on top, dew point drops below.

cards.t: The staff points to where wind comes FROM. Half flag 5 kt. Full flag 10. Triangle 50. Add them up.

s.t: The staff points from the direction the wind comes FROM.
A short line (half barb) = 5 knots. A long line = 10 knots. A flag (triangle) = 50 knots.
Add them up. One long + one short = 15 knots.

dd.why: A wind barb tells you wind direction and speed. The staff points toward where the wind comes FROM, like a weather vane. Flags on the end tell speed. A half flag is 5 knots, a full flag is 10, a triangle is 50. You add them. More flags mean stronger wind because each mark is a fixed chunk of speed.
dd.pic: Draw a staff pointing to the northwest. At the far end draw one triangle, two full lines, and one short line. Label 50, 10, 10, 5.
dd.analogy: Like coins: a triangle is a 50-cent coin, a full flag a dime, a half flag a nickel. You add them for the total. It stops working because wind is not money, and direction matters too.
ways: Staff points to the source. Add the flags.

ex.q: A wind barb staff points toward the north. Where is the wind coming from, and what is the speed with 1 full flag and 1 half flag?
steps: Staff points to where wind comes FROM.
Staff is north, so wind is from the north.
Add: 10 + 5 = 15 knots. Answer: from the north at 15 knots.

dd.trap: Reading the staff as where the wind is going. It is from the staff side.
dd.tip: Staff is the source, flags are the force.

cards.t: Take the three digits. 500 or more? Put 9 in front. Less than 500? Put 10. Add a decimal before the last digit.

dd.why: Pressure is printed as three digits to save space. The leading 9 or 10 and the decimal point are left out because pressure on Earth is almost always 950 to 1050 mb. So you rebuild it. If the three digits are 500 or more, the real value starts with 9. If less than 500, it starts with 10. Then put a decimal before the last digit.
dd.pic: Draw a number line from 950 to 1050 with a mark at 1000. Above numbers under 500 draw an arrow to the right of the 1000 mark. Above numbers 500 or more draw an arrow to the left.
dd.analogy: Like a cashier writing 199 for $1.99. The dollar sign and dot are understood. It stops working because the pressure code rule changes at 500.
ways: Three digits, then add 9 or 10, then a decimal.
132 is under 500, so 10 in front, decimal: 1013.2. 998 is 500 or more, so 9 in front: 999.8.

ex.q: A station model shows pressure code 998. What is the pressure?
steps: Look at 998: that is 500 or more.
Put a decimal before the last digit: 999.8.
Check range: 999.8 mb is a normal low.

dd.trap: Always adding 10. Use 10 only for codes under 500.
dd.tip: Big code, nine in front, small code, ten at the front.

cards.t: 18018G28KT means from 180°, 18 knots, gusting 28.

dd.why: A METAR is a short code pilots use. The wind group is easy to read as pieces: three digits for direction, two digits for speed, optional G and two digits for gust, then KT for knots. Direction is where wind comes FROM. A gust is a short burst above the steady speed.
dd.pic: Write 18018G28KT. Draw boxes under each piece: 180, 18, G28, KT. Add a compass with an arrow pointing in from the south.
dd.analogy: Like a license plate where each part means something. It stops working because plates are random.
ways: From direction, speed, gust, in knots.
18018G28KT = from 180 degrees (south), 18 kt steady, gusting to 28 kt.

ex.q: METAR 18015G25KT means wind from 180 degrees at 15 knots with what?
steps: G25 is a gust to 25 knots.

dd.trap: Thinking the direction is where it blows to. It is where it comes from.

cards.t: FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC get cloudier. The three digits are height in hundreds of feet. BKN040 = 4,000 ft.

dd.why: A METAR sky group has a cloud amount and a height. FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC mean few, scattered, broken, overcast, so they get cloudier. The three digits are the base height in hundreds of feet, so you add two zeros. Pilots care about low cloud decks (ceilings).
dd.pic: Draw a ladder with FEW, SCT, BKN, OVC from bottom to top for more cloud. Draw a cloud base at 4,000 ft.
dd.analogy: Like a restaurant seat count: few, scattered, broken, full. It stops working because sky cover is not discrete.
ways: Cloud amount, then height in hundreds of feet.
BKN040 = 40 x 100 = 4,000 ft, broken. OVC008 = 800 ft, overcast.
Add two zeros to the number.

ex.q: In a METAR, what does BKN040 mean?
steps: 040 is the height in hundreds of feet.

dd.trap: Reading 040 as 40 feet. Multiply by 100.
dd.tip: Add two zeros to get the base.

cards.t: 27/22 means 27 °C and dew point 22 °C. An M means minus.

dd.why: METAR temperature groups are in Celsius, temperature first and dew point second, separated by a slash. If the number is below zero, an M replaces the minus sign. So M01 means minus 1. A small gap between temperature and dew point means humid air.
dd.pic: Draw a thermometer with zero marked. Put M on the part below zero.
dd.analogy: The M is like a minus sign dressed in a letter. It stops working because normal numbers do not use letters.
ways: First number is temperature, second is dew point.

ex.q: A METAR temperature group reads 02/M01. What are the temperature and dew point?
steps: Left of the slash is temperature: 02.
Leading zero just fills space, so 2 C.
Right of the slash is dew point: M01.

dd.trap: Reading M as meters or missing. It means minus.

cards.t: A2985 = 29.85 inches of mercury.

dd.why: The altimeter group tells pressure in inches of mercury. It starts with A, then four digits. Put a decimal after the first two digits. This is pressure adjusted to sea level, so pilots set their altimeters.
dd.pic: Write A2985. Draw an arrow that inserts a dot between 29 and 85.
dd.analogy: Like 2985 cents being $29.85. It stops working because here the unit is inches of mercury.
ways: A then four digits, decimal after two.

ex.q: What pressure does A3005 show?
steps: Put a decimal after two digits: 30.05.

dd.trap: Reading it as millibars. It is inches of mercury.
dd.tip: A for altimeter, two digits then dot.

cards.t: 850 mb = low moisture. 700 mb = steering. 500 mb = troughs and ridges. 300 mb = jet stream.

dd.why: Weather charts at fixed pressure levels show different jobs. 850 mb is about 1.5 km up and shows low-level moisture. 700 mb is about 3 km and shows steering. 500 mb is about 5.5 km and shows troughs and ridges. 300 mb is about 9 km and shows the jet stream. Pressure drops as you go up.
dd.pic: Draw a vertical line with four marks: 850, 700, 500, 300. Label each job.
dd.analogy: Floors of a building, each with a different job. It stops working because floors are fixed in height.
ways: 850 mb about 1.5 km, 700 about 3 km, 500 about 5.5 km, 300 about 9 km.

ex.q: Which pressure level is usually used to locate the jet stream?

dd.trap: Using 850 for the jet.

cards.t: A plot of wind at each height. A long curved path means strong shear. Clockwise turning with height helps supercells.

dd.why: A hodograph plots the wind at each height as a point on a graph, joined by a line. A long path means the wind changes a lot with height, so shear is strong. A clockwise curve helps supercells because it supports rotating updrafts.
dd.pic: Draw axes. Plot dots at increasing height, join them in a curve going clockwise.
dd.analogy: A map of a hike: a long winding path means a lot of change. It stops working because wind has direction too.
ways: Wind 10 kt at surface to 60 kt aloft is 50 kt change.

ex.q: Why does a long path on a hodograph mean strong shear?
steps: Each point is wind at a height.
Answer: wind changes a lot with height.

dd.trap: Thinking a short path is bad.

cards.t: Temperature solid. Dew point dashed. Lines close = moist or cloudy. Far apart = dry.

dd.why: A sounding is a balloon's profile of the air. Temperature is a solid line and dew point is a dashed line. Where the lines are close, the air is moist or cloudy. Where they are far apart, the air is dry.
dd.pic: Draw two lines on a chart, close together at one level and far apart at another.
dd.analogy: Two friends walking: close together means they are alike. It stops working because air isn't friendly.
ways: Close is moist, far is dry.
T 20, Td 19 is saturated-ish. T 20, Td 0 is dry.

ex.q: On a sounding, a wide gap between temperature and dew point means the layer is what?

dd.trap: Thinking wide is moist.

cards.t: A layer where temperature rises with height. Very stable. It can act as a cap that holds storms back.

lab.hook: Normally air cools with height. An inversion is a warm layer above cooler air.
lab.out: Surface {t0} °C. Normal cooling is about 6.5 °C per km.

dd.why: An inversion is a layer where temperature rises with height, the opposite of normal. A warm layer on top of cooler air means rising parcels become cooler than their surroundings and stop. It is very stable, so it can cap storms. If the cap breaks, storms explode.
dd.pic: Draw a temperature line going up, then bending to the right for a short stretch.
dd.analogy: A lid on a pot. It stops working because the cap can leak.
ways: Temperature rises 22 C at 900 m to 25 C at 1000 m.

ex.q: A sounding layer where temperature increases with height is called what?

dd.trap: Thinking inversions are unstable.

cards.t: Same skills as Stüve. The lines are just tilted to spread them out. (States/Nationals)

dd.why: A Skew-T uses the same data as a Stüve. The temperature lines are tilted to the right to spread out the data and make the plots easier to read. So the skills are the same.
dd.pic: Draw a square grid, then tilt its lines.
dd.analogy: Like looking at a poster from an angle. It stops working because tilt changes shape.

ex.q: Skew-T diagrams differ from Stüve diagrams mainly because what?
steps: Answer: its temperature lines are tilted.

dd.trap: Thinking they use different data.

cards.t: Height where a rising parcel makes cloud. Lower LCL means lower cloud base and higher tornado risk.

lab.hook: A rising air parcel cools until it reaches its dew point. Clouds begin there.
lab.note: {=125*(t-td)|0} m. A bigger gap between T and Td means a higher cloud base.

pre.q: Dry air (dew point far below the temperature) makes cloud bases that are…
pre.why: A big T − Td gap means air must rise farther before it saturates.

dd.why: The LCL is the height where a rising parcel becomes saturated and forms cloud. The gap between temperature and dew point tells how far it must rise. About 125 m for every degree C of gap. A lower LCL means a lower cloud base, which favors tornadoes.
dd.pic: Draw a parcel rising from the ground to a cloud base at the LCL.
dd.analogy: Like a balloon cooling until it fogs. It stops working because it is an approximation.

ex.q: Surface temperature is 30 C and dew point is 18 C. What is the LCL?

dd.trap: Using T + Td.

cards.t: Storm fuel in J/kg. Under 1000 marginal. 1000–2500 moderate. 2500–4000 strong. Over 4000 extreme.

dd.why: CAPE is the energy stored for storms, in joules per kilogram. It measures how much a rising parcel would speed up. Under 1000 is marginal, 1000 to 2500 moderate, 2500 to 4000 strong, over 4000 extreme.
dd.pic: Draw a sounding with a shaded area between parcel and environment.
dd.analogy: A fuel tank gauge. It stops working because CAPE is not used up.

ex.q: CAPE of 300 J/kg is best described as what?

dd.trap: Thinking CAPE alone makes a storm.
dd.tip: CAPE is cake: more is stronger.

cards.t: Moisture, instability, lift, and shear. Miss one and storms struggle.

dd.why: Storms need four things. Moisture is the fuel. Instability lets air rise by itself. Lift (a front or dryline) starts the rise. Shear organizes the storm. If one is missing, the storm fails.
dd.pic: Draw four boxes in a row and a storm. Cross out one box and a weak storm.
dd.analogy: A pizza needs dough, sauce, cheese, oven. Missing one and it fails. It stops working because storms are not bakeable.

ex.q: Name the four ingredients for severe storms.
steps: Answer: moisture, instability, lift, and shear.

dd.trap: Thinking you only need heat.

cards.t: Fast river of air aloft. It steers storms and adds energy.

dd.why: The jet stream is a fast stream of air aloft. It steers storms and adds shear. It also helps by pulling air up. The dryline is separate: storms start there because it gives lift, with moist air meeting dry air in the afternoon when heating triggers rising.
dd.pic: Draw a long arrow high above the map with a wiggly shape and storms below.
dd.analogy: A river carrying leaves. It stops working because the jet is air.
ways: Jet speed can exceed 100 mph, up to 200.

ex.q: Why do storms often start along a dryline in the afternoon?
steps: Answer: lift from the boundary plus daytime heating.

dd.trap: Thinking the jet is on the ground.
dd.tip: Jet is high, steers the sky.

cards.t: Cold front: fast and sharp storms. Warm front: wide steady rain. Occluded: cold catches warm. Stationary: stalled.

dd.why: Fronts are the edges of air masses. A cold front moves fast, with cold air shoving under warm air, so lift is sharp and storms form in a narrow line. A warm front slopes gently, so air rises slowly over a wide area, giving steady rain. Occluded: cold catches warm. Stationary: stalled.
dd.pic: Draw a steep cold wedge and a shallow warm slope.
dd.analogy: A bulldozer (cold front) vs. a ramp (warm front). It stops working because fronts move.
ways: Cold is steep, warm is gentle.
Cold front slope about 1:50. Warm front about 1:200.

ex.q: Why do cold fronts bring narrow bands of intense storms but warm fronts wide, steady rain?
steps: Answer: steep fast lift versus gentle slow lift.

dd.trap: Mixing up the slopes.
dd.tip: Cold is a cliff, warm is a ramp.

cards.t: Boundary between moist and dry air. It is about moisture, not temperature. Common on the Plains.

dd.why: The dryline is a boundary between moist air and dry air, not warm and cold. On the Plains in spring, moist Gulf air is on the east and dry desert air is on the west. Moist air is lighter, so it rides over, and storms often form on the moist side.
dd.pic: Draw a map with a line. East side moist (green), west side dry (brown).
dd.analogy: A damp towel next to a dry towel. It stops working because air mixes.
ways: Dew point 65 on one side, 35 on the other.

ex.q: On the Great Plains in spring, the dryline usually has moist air to its what?
steps: Gulf moisture comes from the south and east.

dd.trap: Thinking it separates hot and cold.

cards.t: Wind changing with height. It lets updraft and downdraft work apart. Direction change starts rotation.

lab.hook: Wind that changes with height tilts and twists storms.

s.t: Imagine wind near the ground blowing slowly from the east.
Higher up, the wind blows fast from the west.
That change with height is wind shear. A rising updraft gets tilted and twists, so it can spin into a rotating storm.

lab.take: Shear + instability + moisture + a trigger = severe storms.

dd.why: Wind shear is wind changing with height. It tilts the updraft so rain falls apart from it. Then the storm lives longer. A change in direction creates spin. Strong shear organizes storms such as supercells.
dd.pic: Draw a tilted storm with rain falling beside the updraft.
dd.analogy: A tilted chimney: smoke goes up while ash falls aside. It stops working because storms are bigger.
ways: Shear 40 kt or more favors supercells.

ex.q: Does strong wind shear tend to organize thunderstorms or tear them apart?

dd.trap: Thinking shear always kills storms. Weak storms may.

cards.t: A narrow stream of heavy water vapor. Can drop extreme rain at landfall.

dd.why: An atmospheric river is a long narrow band of water vapor in the sky. When it runs into mountains, air is forced up and the moisture falls as heavy rain or snow. That is why landfall can bring floods.
dd.pic: Draw a long ribbon from the ocean to a coast with mountains.
dd.analogy: A fire hose of moisture. It stops working because vapor is invisible.
ways: Can carry more than the Mississippi's flow.

ex.q: What is an atmospheric river?
steps: Answer: a narrow stream of heavy water vapor.

dd.trap: Thinking it is in the ocean.

cards.t: Long fetch and warm water give storms energy. Storms leave a cooler wake. Mountains can trigger, weaken, or redirect storms.

dd.why: Fetch is the distance wind blows over open water. Longer fetch builds bigger waves. Warm water feeds storms. Storms churn up cooler water behind them. Mountains can lift, block, or turn storms.
dd.pic: Draw a long arrow across open water and bigger waves at the end.
dd.analogy: A runway: more room, more speed. It stops working because wind is not a vehicle.

ex.q: What is fetch?
steps: Answer: the distance wind blows over open water.

dd.trap: Thinking fetch is time.

cards.t: The thunderstorm cloud. It can bring every type of severe weather.

dd.why: Cumulonimbus is the only cloud that makes thunderstorms. Warm moist air rises strongly, cools, and keeps growing upward until it hits the stable layer (the tropopause) and spreads into an anvil. Because the updraft is so deep and strong, it can carry hail, build charge for lightning, and make strong winds. That is why it can bring every type of severe weather.
dd.pic: Draw a tall tower with a flat anvil top and a dark flat base. Put arrows going up in the center, and rain and hail falling from the base.
dd.analogy: A boiling pot with a lid on: steam rises hard, hits the lid, and spreads sideways. The pot is the ground, steam is the updraft, the lid is the stable layer, the sideways steam is the anvil. It stops working because the atmosphere has no actual lid.
ways: Cb tops can pass 12 km (about 40,000 ft) while bases sit near 1 to 2 km.

ex.q: Which cloud is the thunderstorm cloud?
steps: Names: cumulus (puffy), nimbus (rain), so cumulo-nimbus is puffy plus rain.
Stratus is a flat layer and cirrus is thin, high ice.
Only cumulonimbus is tall and makes lightning.

dd.trap: Picking cumulus. Cumulus is fair-weather puffs. The 'nimbus' part means rain.

cards.t: A lowered, often rotating base under the main updraft. A key tornado warning sign.

dd.why: A wall cloud forms where rain-cooled air gets pulled into the updraft. That air is humid, so it condenses at a lower height than the rest of the cloud base. The result is a lowered section. If it rotates and is beneath the main updraft, the storm is organizing rotation near the ground. That is why it is a key warning sign for a tornado.
dd.pic: Draw a big flat cloud base. Under one spot, draw a lower block hanging down like a step. Add a curved arrow showing it turning.
dd.analogy: A tent with one pole pushed up from underneath so the fabric droops down beside it. Mapping: the updraft is the pole, the lowered cloth is the wall cloud. It stops working because a wall cloud rotates and fabric does not.
ways: Wall cloud: lowered, often rotating base under the main updraft.
Normal base 1,500 m. Wall cloud base may sit 300 to 500 m lower.
Lowered AND rotating AND under the updraft = take cover.

ex.q: A lowered, often rotating cloud base under the main updraft is a what?
steps: Find the location: under the updraft, not at the edge.
It is lowered from the normal base.
Not a shelf cloud, which is at the front edge.

dd.trap: Mixing wall and shelf clouds. Wall: under the updraft, may rotate. Shelf: along the front edge, does not rotate.
dd.tip: A WALL stands where the storm breathes IN.

cards.t: A wedge along the leading edge. It marks the gust front.

dd.why: A shelf cloud forms where the storm's cool outflow slides under warm moist air. The warm air is forced up fast and condenses, forming a wedge. The cool air racing out is the gust front. So the shelf marks the leading edge of strong winds. It looks scary but is not rotating like a wall cloud.
dd.pic: Draw the ground and a storm to the right. Draw a long low wedge-shaped cloud pointing left with an arrow showing cold air rushing out.
dd.analogy: A snowplow shoving snow ahead of itself. Mapping: the plow is the cool air, the pushed snow is warm air lifted into cloud. It stops working because snow is not warm.
ways: Shelf cloud: wedge on the leading edge, marks the gust front.
Gust front winds can reach 58 mph or more in severe storms.

ex.q: A wedge-shaped low cloud on a storm's leading edge usually marks what?
steps: Leading edge: the front of the storm.
Cool outflow edge is the gust front.
So the shelf cloud is over the gust front.

dd.trap: Calling it a tornado sign. Shelf clouds mean wind, not a funnel.

cards.t: Rotating cone from the storm base. Not on the ground yet.

dd.why: A funnel cloud is a rotating cone of condensed water droplets. Low pressure in the spinning air cools it, so water vapor condenses into a visible cone. If it does not touch the ground, it is not called a tornado. If it touches, it is. A thin funnel can quickly reach the ground, so treat it seriously.
dd.pic: Draw a storm base. Hang a pointed cone from it. Stop the tip in the air. Draw a ground line below. Then draw the tip touching to show a tornado.
dd.analogy: A spinning top balanced on your finger: the spin is the rotation, the finger is the ground. Not touching = funnel cloud. Touching = tornado. It stops working because real funnels are air, not solid.
ways: Funnel cloud = rotating cone not touching the ground.
Funnel cloud: 0 ft contact. Tornado: ground contact at 1 ft or more of debris/damage.

ex.q: A rotating cone-shaped cloud hanging from a storm but not touching the ground is a what?
steps: No contact means not a tornado yet.

dd.trap: Calling every funnel a tornado. Contact with ground is the test.
dd.tip: Funnel in the air, tornado on the ground.

cards.t: Pouches under an anvil. Often seen as a storm weakens.

dd.why: Mammatus are pouches that hang under an anvil. Sinking air is cooler than the air around it, and it sinks in lumps. The lumps hold cloud droplets, so they show as pouches. They often show up when the storm is weakening, but the storm can still be dangerous. They are not a tornado sign.
dd.pic: Draw a big flat anvil. Under it draw rows of round bumps like cow udders or bubble wrap, hanging down.
dd.analogy: Bubbles of bubble wrap or sagging balloons under a table. Mapping: each balloon is a sinking lump of cloud. It stops working because balloons are filled, but mammatus are made of sinking air.
ways: Each pouch is about 1 to 3 km wide and lasts about 10 minutes.

ex.q: Pouch-like cloud shapes under an anvil are called what?
steps: They hang from the anvil base.
Not wall clouds, which are lower rotating blocks.

dd.trap: Thinking mammatus mean a tornado is coming. They do not. They show sinking air.
dd.tip: MAMMA-tus look like MAMA's soft pouches.

cards.t: A long period with far too little precipitation. Water runs short.

dd.why: Drought is not just no rain today. It is a long stretch of less moisture than normal. First rain runs short (meteorological). Then soil dries and crops suffer (agricultural). Then streams and reservoirs run low (hydrological). Each type builds on the one before. Water takes time to drain, so reservoirs show the problem last.
dd.pic: Draw three stacked boxes: sky with no rain, field with dry cracked soil, river with low water. Arrows go down from one to the next.
dd.analogy: A bank account. Rain is income, soil is your wallet, reservoir is savings. If income stops, the wallet empties first, savings last. It stops working because savings can be refilled quickly if a big storm hits.
ways: Drought: far too little precipitation for a long time.
If normal is 4 in/month and you get 1 in/month, you are short 3 in each month; after 6 months, 18 in short.

ex.q: Name the type of drought when streams, lakes, and reservoirs run low.
steps: Streams and reservoirs hold water on the surface.
Low water bodies point to the third type.
Check: it shows up last in a long drought.

dd.trap: Mixing up the types. Agricultural is about soil and crops. Hydrological is about rivers and reservoirs.
dd.tip: Hydro = water you can see in rivers.

cards.t: A long period of unusually high temperatures.

s.t: A strong high-pressure system parks over a region.
Sinking air under the high warms and clears skies.
Sunshine heats the ground all day and the heat builds for days.

dd.why: A heat wave is a long run of unusually high temperatures. Heat is most dangerous when nights stay warm, because your body does not get a break to cool down. Humid air adds to it, because sweat evaporates more slowly. Cities hold heat in pavement and buildings. The danger comes from body heat piling up day after day.
dd.pic: Draw a thermometer line across 5 days. Show daytime highs as peaks and nights as valleys that stay above 75 F. Add a person under a hot sun.
dd.analogy: A phone that never gets to charge. Daytime heat drains you. Cool nights recharge you. Hot nights mean no recharge. It stops working because bodies cannot be plugged in.
ways: Hot days plus hot nights give the body no recovery.
Day 1 high 100, low 80. Day 2 high 102, low 82. Body never drops below stress.
Warm nights make heat waves deadly.

ex.q: Overnight temperatures stay high during a heat wave. Why is this dangerous?
steps: Normally nights cool the body and buildings.
If it stays hot, no cooling happens.
Risk of heat illness rises, especially for kids and older adults.
Answer: the body cannot recover, so heat stress adds up.

dd.trap: Thinking only the afternoon high matters. The night low matters too.

cards.t: A blocking high-pressure ridge. It parks over a region and pushes storms away.

dd.why: A blocking ridge is a big area of high pressure that stalls. Sinking air under a high warms and dries, so clouds do not form. The ridge also acts like a rock in a stream, pushing storms around it. Under the ridge it stays sunny and hot, and soil dries. Dry soil heats faster, so the heat strengthens the ridge.
dd.pic: Draw a big H on a map. Draw storm arrows bending around it. Under the H, write 'sinking, dry, hot'.
dd.analogy: A big rock in a river. Water flows around it, leaving a calm spot behind. The rock is the ridge, water is storms. It stops working because rock is solid and the ridge changes over days.
ways: A stalled high pushes storms away and gives sinking, dry air.
A ridge may sit for 7 to 14 days. 14 days with no rain is a drought start.

ex.q: Which pattern often causes both drought and heat waves?
steps: Look for something that stops rain and adds heat.
If it stalls, it is blocking.

dd.trap: Linking drought to low pressure. Lows bring rising air and clouds.
dd.tip: High and dry, low and wet.

cards.t: Crop loss, water limits, wildfire risk, and heat illness.

dd.why: Drought and heat hurt in four ways. Crops lack water and fail. Cities limit water use. Dry plants and soil burn easily, so wildfires spread. Bodies overheat, causing cramps, exhaustion, and heat stroke. All four trace back to too little water and too much heat. Drinking water helps because sweat is your body's cooling system.
dd.pic: Draw four icons around a sun: wilted plant, faucet with an X, flame, and a sweating person.
dd.analogy: A car engine overheating. Water is the coolant, heat is the work. Low coolant means breakdown. It stops working because you can drink more water but a car cannot.
ways: Crop loss, water limits, fire risk, heat illness.
On a hot day you can lose over 1 liter of sweat per hour; drink often, not just when thirsty.
Drink water before you feel thirsty.

ex.q: What should you drink more of during a heat wave?
steps: Choose water, not sugary or caffeinated drinks.

dd.trap: Waiting until thirsty. Thirst shows up late.

cards.t: Collision-coalescence: small drops bump and merge into raindrops.

s.t: Water vapor condenses onto tiny particles, making cloud droplets.
Bigger droplets fall faster and collide with smaller ones.
Droplets merge (coalescence) until they are heavy enough to fall as rain.

dd.why: In warm clouds there is no ice. Cloud droplets are tiny and float. Bigger ones fall faster, hit smaller ones, and merge. This is collision-coalescence. As they grow they fall faster and gather more, until they are heavy enough to fall as rain. It needs a tall, wet cloud.
dd.pic: Draw a big drop falling through a bunch of tiny dots, swallowing them and getting bigger.
dd.analogy: A snowball rolling downhill picking up snow. It stops working because droplets merge in a collision, not stick.
ways: Cloud droplet about 0.02 mm. Raindrop about 2 mm. That is about 100 times wider.

ex.q: Which process lets cloud droplets merge into raindrops in warm clouds?

dd.trap: Using Bergeron for warm clouds. Bergeron needs ice.

cards.t: Bergeron process: ice crystals grow while supercooled droplets shrink.

dd.why: In cold clouds, both ice crystals and supercooled droplets (liquid below 0 C) exist. Air has more vapor than ice needs, and less than droplets need. So vapor leaves droplets and sticks on ice. Ice crystals grow while droplets shrink. When the crystals get heavy they fall.
dd.pic: Draw a small crystal with tiny droplets around it. Draw arrows from droplets to the crystal. Make the crystal bigger.
dd.analogy: A playground where one kid hogs the toys. The crystal hogs the water vapor. It stops working because toys are not made of gas.
ways: Crystal grows from 0.1 mm to over 1 mm while droplets evaporate.

ex.q: In the Bergeron process, ice crystals grow because what?
steps: Vapor pressure over ice is lower.
Answer: vapor leaves droplets and deposits on ice.

dd.trap: Thinking both grow. The droplets shrink.
dd.tip: Bergeron: ice gets big, drops go away.

cards.t: Riming: drops freeze onto ice, making graupel and hail. Aggregation: ice crystals stick to make snowflakes.

dd.why: Two ways to grow ice. Riming: supercooled drops hit ice and freeze on contact, making graupel and, in strong updrafts, hail. Aggregation: ice crystals bump and stick, which makes snowflakes. Snowflakes are clumps of crystals. Aggregation works best near 0 C where crystals are sticky.
dd.pic: Draw a pellet with small bumps from frozen drops (riming). Draw a snowflake made of several joined crystals (aggregation).
dd.analogy: Riming is paint spraying on a wall. Aggregation is gluing stickers together. It stops working because ice is not sticky like glue.
ways: Riming adds frozen drops. Aggregation sticks crystals.
Hail grows in many layers, each layer from a rimed drop trip.
Riming makes graupel and hail, aggregation makes snow.

ex.q: Snowflakes mostly form by what?

dd.trap: Mixing them. Riming involves liquid drops.

cards.t: Snow: cold all the way. Sleet: refreezes in a cold layer near the ground. Freezing rain: falls as liquid, freezes on contact.

dd.why: The kind of precipitation depends on the temperature layers from the cloud to the ground. All cold: snow. A warm layer aloft that melts snow, then a cold layer near the ground that refreezes it: sleet. A warm layer all the way down with a thin cold layer at the ground: freezing rain, which freezes on contact. Freezing rain is dangerous because it coats everything with ice.
dd.pic: Draw three columns from the cloud to the ground. Shade cold and warm layers. Add snow, ice pellets, and a drop on a branch.
dd.analogy: Like a sandwich: warm filling in the middle changes what happens. It stops working because the layers can change quickly.
ways: Cold throughout is snow. Melt then refreeze is sleet. Melt then freeze on contact is freezing rain.
Surface at -2 C with warm air aloft means freezing rain is possible.

ex.q: Freezing rain is dangerous because it does what?
steps: Ice builds on roads and lines.
Answer: it coats roads and power lines with ice.

dd.trap: Mixing sleet and freezing rain. Sleet bounces as pellets.

cards.t: Pea ¼ in. Penny ¾. Quarter 1 in (severe). Golf ball 1¾. Baseball 2¾. Bigger means stronger updraft.

dd.why: Hail grows when updrafts hold ice in the cloud. Bigger hail needs a stronger updraft to hold it up. Severe hail is 1 inch or more. Size comparisons help: pea 1/4, penny 3/4, quarter 1, golf ball 1 3/4, baseball 2 3/4 inches.
dd.pic: Draw five circles in size order. Label each with the object.
dd.analogy: A balloon held up by a fan: a bigger balloon needs a stronger fan. It stops working because hail is heavy.

ex.q: Hail with a diameter of about 1 inch is the size of which coin?

dd.trap: Picking a penny. A penny is 3/4 inch, not severe.

cards.t: Flash: minutes to hours. River: days. Urban: drains overwhelmed. Heavy rain on burn scars makes debris flows.

dd.why: Floods differ by speed and cause. Flash floods come in minutes to hours from intense rain. River floods rise over days as water collects. Urban floods happen when drains are overwhelmed. Burn scars repel water, so rain runs off fast and can cause debris flows.
dd.pic: Draw a timeline: minutes-hours (flash), days (river). Add a city street with a full drain and a burned slope with a mudflow.
dd.analogy: A bathtub: tap fast fills quickly (flash), slow fills over time (river). It stops working because tubs have a drain control.
ways: Flash is fast, river is slow.

ex.q: Which type of flood develops within minutes to hours of heavy rain?

dd.trap: Calling a river flood a flash flood.

cards.t: Intensity versus duration. Short bursts are more intense. Rarer storms plot higher. Chance per year = 1 ÷ return period.

dd.why: IDF curves link rainfall intensity (inches per hour), duration, and frequency. Short bursts can be very intense, but over longer times the average intensity drops. Rarer storms (100-year) plot higher than common ones. Chance per year is 1 divided by the return period.
dd.pic: Draw a graph with duration on the bottom and intensity on the side. Draw two curves falling to the right, 100-year above 10-year.
dd.analogy: Sprinting vs jogging: you can sprint fast for a short time, but not for a long time. It stops working because rain is not effort.
ways: Longer storms have lower average intensity.
100-year storm has a 1/100 = 1 percent chance each year. 10-year has 10 percent.

ex.q: An IDF curve for a 100-year storm shows that as duration gets longer, intensity does what?

dd.trap: Thinking a 100-year storm happens once every 100 years exactly. It is a 1 percent chance each year.

cards.t: Ice and graupel collide. Light ice rises (positive). Heavy graupel falls (negative). The base ends up mostly negative.

s.t: Ice crystals and hail collide inside the storm.
Heavier particles gain negative charge and sink; lighter ones gain positive and rise.
Charges separate. Lightning is the spark that rebalances them.

dd.why: Charge forms where ice and graupel (soft hail pellets) collide inside the cloud. Light ice crystals get carried up and end up positive. Heavier graupel falls and ends up negative. So the top is mostly positive and the middle and base are mostly negative. Lightning is the discharge that evens it out.
dd.pic: Draw a tall cloud. Put plus signs near the top, minus signs near the bottom. Draw rising arrows with tiny ice crystals and falling arrows with big pellets.
dd.analogy: Rubbing a balloon on hair. Rubbing moves charge. Mapping: balloon is graupel, hair is ice. It stops working because the cloud has billions of particles.
ways: Collisions separate charge. Top positive, base negative.
Cloud potential can reach millions of volts.
Light goes up (+), heavy goes down (-).

ex.q: Where is the main positive charge in a typical thunderstorm?
steps: Answer: in the upper part of the cloud.

dd.trap: Thinking the base is positive. It is mostly negative.

cards.t: Cloud-to-ground. Intracloud. Cloud-to-cloud. Cloud-to-air.

dd.why: Lightning is named by where it goes. Cloud-to-ground hits the earth. Intracloud stays inside one cloud. Cloud-to-cloud jumps between clouds. Cloud-to-air shoots into clear air. Most flashes stay in the cloud because the opposite charges are closer inside the cloud than the ground.
dd.pic: Draw two clouds. Draw four bolts: one to the ground, one inside a cloud, one between clouds, one out the side into the air.
dd.analogy: Sparks between objects. A spark jumps the shortest path. It stops working because lightning picks branches.
ways: Four types: CG, IC, CC, CA.
About 75 percent of flashes do not reach the ground.
Most lightning never reaches the ground.

ex.q: Most lightning flashes stay where?
steps: Opposite charges are within the cloud.
Short path inside the cloud is easiest.
So most flashes stay in the cloud.

dd.trap: Thinking most lightning hits the ground. Most does not.

cards.t: Seconds from flash to thunder ÷ 5 = miles away.

dd.why: Light reaches you almost instantly. Sound travels about 1 mile in 5 seconds. So the gap between flash and thunder tells distance. Divide seconds by 5 for miles. It is an estimate, not exact.
dd.pic: Draw a bolt and a person. Draw a line between them with a clock showing seconds. Write 5 s = 1 mi.
dd.analogy: A stadium: you see the pitcher throw, then hear the bat crack later. Mapping: light is sight, sound is the delay. It stops working because it is not exact in wind.
ways: 30 seconds or less means go inside.

ex.q: The flash-to-bang time is 10 seconds. About how many miles away is the lightning?
steps: Sound travels about 1 mile per 5 seconds.

dd.trap: Dividing by 3 (that is for kilometers). Miles use 5.

cards.t: Networks of sensors time the signal to find each strike.

dd.why: Lightning sends out a radio pulse. Sensors at different places hear it at slightly different times. Computers use the time differences to find where it came from. More sensors give better accuracy. It is like triangulation.
dd.pic: Draw three towers around a dot. Draw circles from each tower that cross at the dot.
dd.analogy: Three friends hear a shout at different moments and can work out where it came from. It stops working because lightning is far faster.
ways: Time differences between sensors locate strikes.
Radio travels about 300,000 km per second, so timing must be in microseconds.

ex.q: Lightning detection systems find strikes mainly by what?
steps: Answer: timing the signal at several sensors.

dd.trap: Thinking they use cameras only. Radio timing is the main method.

cards.t: Hail 1 inch or bigger, wind 58 mph or more, or a tornado.

dd.why: The National Weather Service calls a thunderstorm severe if it makes hail 1 inch or bigger, wind 58 mph or more, or a tornado. These thresholds mark damage: 1-inch hail dents cars and 58 mph wind breaks branches. Heavy rain or lightning alone do not make a storm severe.
dd.pic: Draw a quarter, a gust arrow marked 58, and a funnel. Label them 'any one'.
dd.analogy: A speeding ticket: you cross a line and it counts. It stops working because storms are not tickets.

ex.q: NWS criteria for a severe thunderstorm include hail at least how big?

dd.trap: Using 3/4 inch.

cards.t: One short-lived storm.

dd.why: A single-cell storm has one updraft. Rain forms, falls, and drags air down. The downdraft cuts off the warm updraft, so it dies in about an hour. With weak shear, rain falls into the updraft and kills it.
dd.pic: Draw a cell with an up arrow, then a rain shaft over the arrow, then fading.
dd.analogy: A candle with a cup placed over it. It stops working because storms are bigger.

ex.q: Why does a single-cell pulse storm die in about an hour?
steps: Answer: its downdraft cuts off the updraft.

dd.trap: Thinking they run out of water.

cards.t: A cluster or line. New cells keep forming.

dd.why: A multicell cluster has many cells at different stages. Outflow from old cells lifts air to start new cells. So the group lasts for hours even if each cell dies in an hour. Lines of cells can bring wind and flooding.
dd.pic: Draw three storms side by side: young, mature, old.
dd.analogy: A relay race: runners change but the team keeps going. It stops working because cells are not people.
ways: Each cell about 1 hour, cluster several hours.

ex.q: A cluster of cells at different stages that keep forming new storms is what?

dd.trap: Calling it a supercell.

cards.t: One long-lived storm with a rotating updraft called a mesocyclone. Makes the strongest tornadoes.

dd.why: A supercell has one long-lived rotating updraft called a mesocyclone. Shear separates the updraft from the downdraft, so the storm keeps running. The rotation makes it capable of large hail and the strongest tornadoes.
dd.pic: Draw a tilted giant cloud with a swirl in the middle labeled mesocyclone.
dd.analogy: A hurricane in miniature. It stops working because they form differently.

ex.q: A very strong, long-lived thunderstorm forms with a rotating updraft. Which is most likely to produce a strong tornado?

dd.trap: Thinking MCC makes the strongest tornadoes.

cards.t: A big, round, long-lived cluster of storms.

dd.why: An MCC (mesoscale convective complex) is a huge, round cluster of storms. It forms at night over the Plains, can last 12 hours, and brings heavy rain. It is organized and has a big cold cloud shield on satellite.
dd.pic: Draw a big round cold cloud on a satellite.
dd.analogy: A big family reunion. It stops working because storms leave.
ways: Area over 100,000 sq km, lasting 6 hours or more.

ex.q: A large, long-lived, organized cluster of thunderstorms covering a big area is what?

dd.trap: Calling it a supercell.

cards.t: Cumulus: updraft only. Mature: updraft and downdraft, worst weather. Dissipating: downdraft only.

lab.hook: Follow a thunderstorm from birth to death.

s.t: Cumulus stage: warm air rises in an updraft. Clouds grow upward.
Mature stage: rain and hail fall, creating a downdraft beside the updraft. This is the strongest stage.
Dissipating: the downdraft cuts off the warm updraft. The storm weakens and rains out.

lab.take: A storm dies when its own cold downdraft cuts off the updraft.

dd.why: A thunderstorm has three stages. Cumulus: updraft only, cloud grows. Mature: updraft and downdraft side by side, the worst weather. Dissipating: downdraft only, the storm fades. The downdraft cuts the supply.
dd.pic: Draw three clouds: up arrows only, up and down arrows, down arrows only.
dd.analogy: A life: growing, adult, retired. It stops working because storms don't age by years.

ex.q: Which stage has both an updraft and a downdraft?

dd.trap: Picking cumulus.

cards.t: Any storm wind damage that is not from rotation. The most common wind report.

dd.why: Thunderstorm winds come from two sources: rotation (a tornado) or air that rushes straight along the ground. Straight-line wind is the second kind. Rain-cooled air is heavy, so it sinks, hits the ground, and spreads out in a line. The damage path points the same way, like a bowling lane. Tornado damage instead twists and swirls around a center. Straight-line wind is the most common storm wind report because every strong storm can make it, but only a few make tornadoes.
dd.pic: Draw a storm cloud. Under it, draw arrows going down, then bending flat along the ground in one direction. Draw trees all lying with their tops pointing the same way.
dd.analogy: Think of a glass of water dumped on a table. The water hits and spreads out in all directions in a line from the splash. The storm's cold air is the water, the ground is the table. Unlike a spill, the storm wind can be 60 to 100 mph and last minutes.
ways: Wind damage with no spin is straight-line wind.
Fallen trees: 10 pointing east, 0 pointing other ways = straight-line. Trees pointing every direction in a small spot = rotation.
Same direction means straight-line. Swirly means tornado.

ex.q: A neighborhood has 12 fallen trees, all pointing north-east, and no rotation seen on radar. What caused it?
steps: Look at the tree directions: all the same way.
Same direction means the wind pushed in one straight path.
No rotation on radar rules out a tornado.
Rain-cooled air sank and spread out along the ground.

dd.trap: Thinking any storm wind damage is a tornado. Check the pattern: parallel means straight-line, twisted means tornado.
dd.tip: Straight trees fall in a straight line: straight-line wind.

cards.t: A downdraft that hits the ground and spreads out.

lab.hook: A downburst is a column of sinking air.

s.t: Rain and hail drag air downward.
Air hits the ground and spreads out in all directions.
The spreading air causes damaging straight-line winds.

dd.why: A downburst starts when rain and hail drag air down inside a storm. Falling rain also cools the air as water evaporates, which makes it denser than the air around it. Dense air sinks fast. When it hits the ground it cannot go further down, so it fans out sideways in all directions. That outward burst is what knocks things over. Without the ground to stop it, it would just keep falling and there would be no sideways blast.
dd.pic: Draw a storm cloud. Below it draw a thick arrow pointing down. At the ground, draw arrows curving out to the left and right like a starburst. Label the spot 'impact'.
dd.analogy: A water balloon dropped on the floor: the water falls down, hits, then splashes out sideways. The downdraft is the falling balloon, the ground is the floor, the spreading outflow is the splash. A real downburst can be invisible when the air is dry and no rain reaches the ground.
ways: A downdraft that hits the ground and spreads out is a downburst.
Air goes down at maybe 30 mph, then spreads outward at 60+ mph near the ground.
Side view: arrow down, then arrows flat in both directions along the ground.

ex.q: A downdraft hits the ground and winds spread outward. What is it called?
steps: Notice the air goes down first.
Then it spreads outward in all directions.
That full pattern defines a downburst.

dd.trap: Mixing it up with a tornado. A tornado rotates and pulls inward; a downburst blows outward.

cards.t: Microburst: under 4 km wide. Macroburst: 4 km or more.

dd.why: Size is the only difference between the two. A microburst is a small downburst, under 4 km wide. The small size makes the wind very strong in a tiny area and it can last just a few minutes. A macroburst is 4 km or more wide and can last longer. The word micro means small and macro means large, so you can remember the sizes from the Greek parts of the words.
dd.pic: Draw a circle 4 km wide on a grid. Draw a small circle inside it for a microburst and a big one reaching past it for a macroburst. Label the line '4 km'.
dd.analogy: A sprinkler head versus a fire hose: both spray water out, but one covers a small patch and one covers a big area. Microburst is the small spray, macroburst the big one. Real winds differ in strength too, not just size.
ways: Under 4 km is micro. 4 km or more is macro.
3 km wide = microburst. 4 km wide = macroburst. 10 km wide = macroburst.
Four kilometers is the dividing line.

ex.q: A downburst spreads over an area 7 km wide. Micro or macro?
steps: Compare 7 km with the 4 km cutoff.
Four or more km means macroburst.

dd.trap: Calling exactly 4 km a microburst. The rule says 4 km or more is macro.
dd.tip: Micro is mini; macro is massive.

lessons.title: Gust front · Squall line and derecho

cards.t: The leading edge of cool outflow. It can show as a shelf cloud.

dd.why: Rain-cooled air sinks and spreads out under a storm. The edge of this cool pool is the gust front. It pushes into the warm air in front of the storm like a snow plow. Warm air is lifted by the cool wedge. When the lifted air cools enough, a cloud forms along the edge. That low, wedge-shaped cloud is the shelf cloud. The gust front arrives before the rain, so a sudden wind shift and temperature drop tells you a storm is near.
dd.pic: Draw the ground and a storm on the right. Draw a low blob of cool air with a sloping front edge. Draw an arrow of warm air rising over the slope and a shelf cloud on top of the edge.
dd.analogy: A snow plow pushes snow ahead of it. The cool outflow is the plow, warm air is the snow being shoved up. The plow stops pushing when it runs out of power, and a gust front fades the same way.
ways: Gust front: leading edge of cool outflow. Shelf cloud: wedge cloud on top of it.
Before: 90 F, calm. At front: wind jumps to 50 mph, temperature falls to 75 F.
Wind and cool air arrive first; the rain follows.

ex.q: A low, wedge-shaped cloud sits on the front edge of a storm. What is it?
steps: Notice the cloud is low and wedge-shaped.
It sits at the front edge of outflow.
Warm air lifted by the gust front makes it.
That cloud type is a shelf cloud.

dd.trap: Confusing a shelf cloud with a wall cloud. Shelf clouds are on the front edge and spread wide; wall clouds hang lower under the storm base and can rotate.
dd.tip: Shelf cloud: a shelf over the front.

cards.t: Squall line: organized line of storms. Derecho: long-lived windstorm with hundreds of miles of damage.

dd.why: A squall line is a row of storms that formed in a line. When the storms push cool air out in one strong, shared surge, the line can race ahead. The line can bend into a bow shape. The strongest wind blows from the middle of the bow. If the line lasts a long time and causes damage over hundreds of miles, it is called a derecho. A derecho keeps going because its cool outflow keeps lifting new warm air, which feeds new storms.
dd.pic: Draw a long line of storm cells across a map from left to right. Bend the middle forward into a bow. Draw arrows pointing straight out from the middle and a long damage path trailing behind.
dd.analogy: A line of dominoes: one falling hits the next, so the whole row keeps going. Each storm is a domino pushing air that triggers the next. A derecho is a very long row that keeps falling for hours. Dominoes run out of row; storms run out of warm, moist air.
ways: Squall line: storms in a line. Derecho: long-lived, wide windstorm.
Damage swath of 400+ miles and wind gusts of 58 mph or more are signs of a derecho.
A squall line is the group. A derecho is the extreme version.

ex.q: A fast-moving band of storms damages trees across 450 miles with winds over 60 mph. Name it.
steps: The storms move as a band.
The damage is long: 450 miles, in the hundreds.
The wind is strong and straight-line.
A long-lived windstorm like this is a derecho.

dd.trap: Thinking every squall line is a derecho. Most are not; a derecho needs a long path of damage.

cards.t: Air speeds up as it sinks down a mountain. No thunderstorm needed.

dd.why: Downslope wind needs no storm. Air flows over a mountain, then sinks down the far side. Sinking air gets squeezed by higher pressure, which heats it. It warms by about 5.5 F for every 1,000 ft it drops when dry. Gravity and a pressure difference speed it up as it goes down the slope. In a thunderstorm downdraft, air is heavy from rain and cool from evaporation, so gravity pulls it quickly toward the ground.
dd.pic: Draw a mountain. Draw arrows rising up the left side and plunging down the right side, getting longer as they go. Label the bottom 'warm, dry, gusty'.
dd.analogy: A kid sliding down a playground slide speeds up as they go. The air is the kid, the slope is the slide. Unlike a slide, air also warms as it descends.
ways: Air sinking down a mountain speeds up and warms.
Drop 3,000 ft: dry air warms about 16.5 F (3 x 5.5).
Heavier or colder than surroundings means it sinks fast.

ex.q: Dry air drops 2,000 ft down a slope. About how much does it warm at 5.5 F per 1,000 ft?
steps: Drop is 2,000 ft, which is 2 thousands.

dd.trap: Saying you need a thunderstorm for strong sinking wind. Mountains alone can do it.
dd.tip: Down the slope, speed and warm both grow.

cards.t: Bow echo = derecho or damaging wind. Fine line = gust front. Bowing segment = strongest wind on a squall line.

dd.why: Radar sees rain and hail, not wind. But wind shapes where the rain goes. When a squall line surges forward in the middle, radar shows a bow-shaped echo. That bow means fast winds pushing the line ahead, so the middle is the most damaging. A fine line is a thin streak where outflow lifts air and dust or bugs; it marks a gust front. Learn the shape and you can guess the wind.
dd.pic: Draw a straight line on a radar screen, then the same line with its middle bulged forward like an archer's bow. Mark the strongest wind at the bulge. Draw a thin dotted line ahead of storms and label it gust front.
dd.analogy: A rope held by two people: if the middle is pushed, it bows out. The storm line is the rope, the fast wind is the push. Unlike rope, the radar bow is formed by air, not a hand.
ways: Bow echo means strong wind. Fine line means gust front.
Bowing segment gusts: often 60 to 80 mph. Other parts of line: weaker.
Straight line = normal. Bowed line = strong wind.

ex.q: On radar a line of storms bows out in the middle. Where is the wind strongest?
steps: Find the bowing part of the line.
The outward push is where air is fastest.
So winds are strongest at the bow.

dd.trap: Looking only at color. The shape of the echo tells you about wind.

cards.t: A violently rotating column touching the ground and a cloud. A waterspout is the same thing over water.

dd.why: A tornado needs two things at once: spinning air and contact with both a cloud base and the ground. The spin comes from wind shear that is tilted upright by a storm updraft. Squeezing the spinning air into a narrow column makes it spin faster, like a skater pulling in her arms. A waterspout is the same kind of column over water.
dd.pic: Draw a storm cloud. Draw a narrow column from the cloud base to the ground and add a curved arrow around it. Draw the same column over a lake and label it waterspout.
dd.analogy: A skater spinning: arms in means faster spin. Arms are the wide spinning air, the pulled-in position is the tight tornado. It stops working because a skater has a solid body.
ways: Rotating column touching ground and cloud.
Tornado width ranges from about 50 ft to over 1 mile.

ex.q: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air that touches what?
steps: It must connect to a cloud.
That separates it from a funnel cloud.
Answer: the ground and a cloud base.

dd.trap: Calling a funnel cloud a tornado. Check for ground contact.

cards.t: Late afternoon, spring, Plains and Southeast. But it can happen any time.

dd.why: Tornadoes need warm, humid air and a spinning storm. In spring, warm Gulf air meets cold air from the north over the Plains. Late afternoon is when the ground is hottest, so air is most unstable. The Plains and Southeast get the most. But the ingredients can appear any month, so tornadoes are possible any time.
dd.pic: Draw a U.S. map. Shade the Plains and Southeast. Draw a clock showing 4 to 6 pm.
dd.analogy: A pot of water reaching a boil after a while. Heating takes time, so the peak comes late. It stops working because storms need lift too.
ways: Spring, late afternoon, Plains and Southeast, but any time.
Peak hour is about 4 to 6 pm local time.
Hot afternoon, warm moist air, danger.

ex.q: What time of day do tornadoes most often occur?
steps: Hottest time is mid to late afternoon.

dd.trap: Believing tornadoes only happen in spring afternoons.

lab.hook: The Enhanced Fujita scale rates damage, not size.

dd.why: The EF scale rates a tornado by the damage it causes, then gives an estimated wind speed. EF0 is 65 to 85 mph, EF1 86 to 110, EF2 111 to 135, EF3 136 to 165, EF4 166 to 200, EF5 over 200. Because rating comes after the fact, it is an estimate. Each step means worse damage.
dd.pic: Draw six steps going up. Label each with EF number and range.
dd.analogy: Like grading a test after it is done. It stops working because the tornado does the damage, not the grade.
ways: EF3 and up is violent-ish, EF4 and EF5 are devastating.

ex.q: A tornado's estimated peak wind is 160 mph. What is its EF rating?

dd.trap: Picking EF4 because 160 feels high. Use the ranges.

cards.t: Before 1 Feb 2007: Fujita (F). On or after: Enhanced Fujita (EF). Both rate damage.

dd.why: The original Fujita (F) scale was used before 1 Feb 2007. The Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale started on that date. Both rate tornado damage, not the wind directly. EF uses more damage indicators and updated wind estimates. So date decides.
dd.pic: Draw a timeline with a line at Feb 1, 2007. Label F on the left and EF on the right.
dd.analogy: A video game patch: before the patch the old rules, after the new ones. It stops working because the scale did not replace history.
ways: F before, EF on or after.

ex.q: Which scale is used for tornadoes occurring after February 1, 2007?

dd.trap: Using F for recent ones.

cards.t: A reflectivity hook wrapping around the mesocyclone.

dd.why: A hook echo is a shape on radar reflectivity where rain and hail wrap around the rotating part of a supercell (the mesocyclone). It looks like a fishhook. It shows that the storm is rotating. A tornado is often near the tip of the hook.
dd.pic: Draw a blob of radar color with a curved tail wrapping around a small circle at the lower right.
dd.analogy: Cream swirled into coffee. It stops working because hook echoes are drops.
ways: Hook is often 2 to 5 miles long.
Hook plus low CC means debris.

ex.q: What does a hook echo on reflectivity wrap around?

dd.trap: Thinking the hook is the tornado. The tornado is near its tip.

cards.t: Strong inbound and outbound velocity side by side. Intense rotation.

dd.why: A tornado vortex signature (TVS) shows on velocity radar as strong inbound (green) winds right beside strong outbound (red) winds. Next to each other means air is spinning tightly. It is a sign of intense rotation.
dd.pic: Draw a radar dot. Draw a tiny green blob touching a tiny red blob. Draw a circle arrow around them.
dd.analogy: A merry-go-round seen from the side: one edge comes toward you, the other goes away. It stops working because radar sees only one slice.
ways: A pair like -50 kt and +50 kt side by side is 100 kt of shear.

ex.q: On Doppler velocity radar, a tight pair of inbound and outbound winds next to each other shows what?

dd.trap: Thinking it is two storms.

cards.t: Low correlation coefficient inside the hook. Debris is in the air.

dd.why: When a tornado lifts debris, the radar pulse hits many odd shapes: boards, leaves, dirt. They do not look alike, so correlation coefficient falls. A low CC spot inside the hook is a debris ball. It means the tornado is on the ground doing damage.
dd.pic: Draw the hook echo with a small blue-colored dot at the tip labeled low CC.
dd.analogy: A bag of mixed candy compared with a bag of identical candy. It stops working because candy is not flying.
ways: Rain CC about 0.98. Debris often below 0.8.
Low CC in a hook is a debris signature.

ex.q: Why does correlation coefficient drop inside a debris ball?
steps: Answer: debris targets are mixed in size and shape.

dd.trap: Thinking low CC means light rain.

cards.t: Hurricane, typhoon, and cyclone are one storm type named by ocean.

dd.why: Hurricane, typhoon, and cyclone are the same kind of storm. The names are just location labels. Atlantic and Northeast Pacific: hurricane. Northwest Pacific: typhoon. Indian Ocean and South Pacific: cyclone. A spinning ocean storm with warm core is what they all are. Only the map region changes the word.
dd.pic: Draw a world map with three colored zones: Atlantic and east Pacific (hurricane), west Pacific (typhoon), Indian Ocean and southern oceans (cyclone).
dd.analogy: Soda is called 'pop', 'soda', or 'coke' depending on where you live. Same drink, different words. Mapping: the drink is the storm, the word is the region. It stops working because soda names are slang, while storm names are official.
ways: Same storm, different names by ocean.
Winds at 74 mph or more qualify in every ocean for hurricane-strength.

ex.q: A hurricane, a typhoon, and a cyclone are what?
steps: Check what stays the same: the physics.
Answer: the same type of storm (tropical cyclone).

dd.trap: Thinking typhoons are stronger. They are not a different type.

cards.t: Invest, depression, tropical storm (39–73 mph), hurricane (74+), major hurricane (Cat 3+).

dd.why: A tropical storm system grows in steps as winds speed up. An invest is a disturbance being watched. Depression is under 39 mph. Tropical storm is 39 to 73 mph and gets a name. Hurricane is 74 mph or more. Major hurricane is Category 3 and up, 111 mph or more. More wind means more damage because force grows faster than wind speed.
dd.pic: Draw a staircase going up. Label steps with Invest, TD, TS (39-73), Hurricane (74+), Major (111+).
dd.analogy: Leveling up in a video game. Each level needs more points (wind). It stops working because storms can also skip levels or fall back.
ways: Under 39: depression. 39-73: tropical storm. 74+: hurricane. 111+: major.

ex.q: A tropical storm has winds of 65 mph. How many mph more are needed to be a hurricane (74 mph)?

dd.trap: Subtracting from 73. Hurricane is 74 and up.
dd.tip: 39 and 74: 'Thirty-nine, seventy-four, the storm gets a name and then a roar.'

dd.why: The Saffir-Simpson scale sorts hurricanes by sustained wind into five categories. It rates wind only, not surge or rain. Each step up brings much more damage because wind force grows faster than wind speed, roughly with its square. A Cat 5 can destroy homes.
dd.pic: Draw five bars rising like a bar chart. Under each write the category and mph: 74-95, 96-110, 111-129, 130-156, 157+.
dd.analogy: A bike speed scale: walk, jog, run, sprint, rocket. Each speed hits harder. It stops working because storms also differ in size and rain.

ex.q: A hurricane has sustained winds of 105 mph. Which category?
steps: Find where 105 fits in the ranges.

dd.trap: Rounding up to the next category. Use the ranges exactly.

cards.t: Warm water (26.5 °C+), moisture, low shear, away from the equator.

dd.why: A hurricane is a heat engine. Warm ocean water gives heat and moisture. At 26.5 C or warmer, evaporation is strong enough to feed the storm. Low wind shear lets the storm stack straight up. Away from the equator is needed because the Coriolis force (spin from Earth) is too weak there to start rotation.
dd.pic: Draw a bowl of warm ocean. Arrows rise from it. Add a vertical column showing calm winds aloft. Mark the equator with an X where spin is missing.
dd.analogy: A campfire needs wood, air, and a spark. Missing one and it dies. Mapping: warm water is the wood, low shear is steady air, Coriolis is the spark. It stops working because a fire is chemical.
ways: Warm water, moisture, low shear, away from equator.

ex.q: A hurricane needs warm ocean water. About what temperature, in C, is the minimum?
steps: Colder water gives too little fuel.
So the minimum is about 26.5 C.

dd.trap: Thinking 20 C is enough. It is not.

cards.t: Eye: calm. Eyewall: worst wind and rain. Spiral bands: showers, tornadoes.

dd.why: A hurricane has parts with different jobs. The eye is the calm center where air sinks. Around it the eyewall has the strongest wind and rain because air rises hard there. Spiral bands farther out bring showers and sometimes tornadoes. So the worst weather is the ring around the calm, not the calm itself.
dd.pic: Draw a circle target. Center: eye, calm. First ring: eyewall, worst. Spirals outward: bands.
dd.analogy: A donut. The hole is the eye, the dough is the eyewall, sprinkles are the bands. It stops working because donuts are not rotating.
ways: Calm eye, fierce eyewall, bands with showers and tornadoes.
Eye width is often 20 to 40 miles.

ex.q: Spiral bands in a hurricane can sometimes produce what?
steps: Spin in the bands can make small tornadoes.

dd.trap: Thinking the eye is the most dangerous. It is calm, but the eyewall around it is not.

cards.t: Water pushed onshore. Bigger with strong, large, slow storms and shallow coasts. Often the deadliest hazard.

dd.why: Storm surge is water pushed onshore by wind. Big storms push more water. Slow storms push longer. Shallow coasts let water pile up higher. Surge is often the deadliest hazard because water is heavy and floods homes fast. It is not a tide, and it is not rain.
dd.pic: Draw a side view of a coast sloping gently. Draw wind arrows pushing a wave of water up the slope and over a house.
dd.analogy: Blowing on a bowl of soup: the soup piles on one side. Mapping: your breath is wind, the soup is the sea. It stops working because real surge also includes low pressure.
ways: Wind pushes ocean water onto land.
Cat 4 surge can reach 13 to 18 ft above normal tide.
Strong + big + slow + shallow = high surge.

ex.q: Storm surge is what?
steps: Surge is a rise in water level.
It is caused by wind pushing water.
It is not rain or tide.
Answer: water pushed onshore by a storm's winds.

dd.trap: Confusing surge with rain flooding. Surge comes from the sea.

cards.t: Land, wind shear, dry air, and cooler water all weaken a storm.

dd.why: Hurricanes weaken when fuel runs out or something tears them apart. Land cuts off warm water and adds friction. Wind shear tilts the storm. Dry air dries it out. Cooler water gives less heat. Without moisture and heat from the ocean, the engine stalls.
dd.pic: Draw a hurricane over water and then over land. Add an X on the arrow from the ocean to the storm when over land.
dd.analogy: A car running out of gas. Land is an empty tank. It stops working because a hurricane may still drop heavy rain after losing wind.
ways: Winds can drop 25 percent within about 24 hours over land.

ex.q: How does a hurricane weaken over land: it loses its supply of what?
steps: So moisture and heat are cut.
Answer: warm, moist ocean air (moisture and heat).

dd.trap: Thinking weakening means no danger. Rain and flooding can last.

cards.t: Wind or gusts of 35 mph or more, snow in the air, and visibility under ¼ mile. All for at least 3 hours.

dd.why: A blizzard is about wind and visibility, not how much snow falls. Needed: wind or gusts of 35 mph or more, snow in the air, and visibility under 1/4 mile, for at least 3 hours. Wind picks up snow and fills the air, making a whiteout. Without strong wind, snow falls straight down and you can see further. All three parts must happen together for 3 hours.
dd.pic: Draw a road with flat white ground. Add a wind arrow marked 35 mph. Draw snow filling the air so a car 1/4 mile away disappears. Put a clock showing 3 hours.
dd.analogy: A snow globe: shake it and you cannot see through. The wind is the shake. The globe stops swirling after a moment, but a blizzard keeps going for hours.
ways: Strong wind + snow in air + low visibility, for 3 hours.
40 mph wind, 1/8 mile visibility, 4 hours = blizzard. 25 mph, 1/8 mile, 4 hours = not.

ex.q: Wind gusts 38 mph, visibility 1/8 mile in blowing snow, for 4 hours. Blizzard?
steps: Time of 4 hours is at least 3.

dd.trap: Thinking heavy snow makes a blizzard. A light snowfall with strong wind can qualify; heavy snow with calm wind cannot.

cards.t: Wind blowing old snow can meet the blizzard test.

dd.why: Blowing snow counts. Wind can lift old snow off the ground and fill the air. That drops visibility the same as new snow. So the test only asks for wind, snow in the air, and low visibility. It does not care where the snow came from. A clear, sunny sky can still have a ground blizzard.
dd.pic: Draw a sunny sky with no clouds. On the ground draw wind arrows kicking up a cloud of old snow. Label it 'ground blizzard'.
dd.analogy: A broom sweeping dust: the dust was already there but it fills the air. Wind is the broom and old snow is the dust. The broom can't sweep up more than is there; if the ground is bare, no blizzard.
ways: Old snow blown by wind can meet the blizzard test.
0 inches of new snow, 40 mph wind, visibility 1/8 mile for 3 hours: still a blizzard.
Needed: wind, snow in air, low view. Not needed: new snow.

ex.q: Which is NOT required for a blizzard: wind, low visibility, or new snowfall?
steps: List the required items: wind, snow in air, low visibility.
Check each option against the list.
New snowfall is not on the list.

dd.trap: Believing it must be snowing. It does not have to be.

cards.t: Big East Coast storm. Northeast winds. Snow, wind, and coastal flooding.

dd.why: A nor'easter is a big storm along the East Coast with winds from the northeast. The winds push ocean water toward the coast for days. Water piles up, and slow-moving storms mean it lasts through several high tides. Each high tide sits on the extra water, so flooding repeats. Add heavy snow or rain and strong gusts, and it is a major event.
dd.pic: Draw the East Coast on the right and ocean on the left. Draw a low-pressure circle offshore with wind arrows from the northeast toward the coast. Show water piled against shore.
dd.analogy: A bathtub being pushed by a hand: pushing water to one end raises it there. Wind is the hand, the coast the tub end. Unlike a tub, tides rise and fall on top, so flooding comes in waves.
ways: Northeast winds, big storm, snow, wind, coastal floods.
Normal high tide plus 3 ft storm surge = flooding at each high tide for 2 days.
Slow storm plus repeated high tides means long flooding.

ex.q: Storm surge adds 3 ft for 3 days at 2 high tides per day. How many high tides are affected?

dd.trap: Thinking the flooding ends after the first high tide. A slow storm keeps pushing water.
dd.tip: Nor'easter: wind from the northeast, tides keep the flood.

cards.t: Cold air over warm open lake water makes narrow heavy snow bands downwind.

dd.why: Cold air moves over warm open lake water. The lake heats and moistens the bottom of the air. Warm moist air rises, forms clouds, and drops snow. Wind carries the snow downwind so it falls in narrow bands along the shore. The bigger the temperature difference between lake and air, the heavier the snow. If the lake freezes, the supply stops.
dd.pic: Draw a lake with wind arrows blowing across it. Draw wavy arrows rising off the water and a thick cloud band downwind. Shade the shore underneath with heavy snow.
dd.analogy: A pot of hot water in a cold room: steam rises off the top. The lake is the pot, cold air is the room. The pot cools if you don't reheat it, but a big lake stays warm for weeks.
ways: Cold air plus warm lake equals snow bands downwind.
Lake 45 F, air 15 F: difference 30 F. Bigger difference, more snow.
Needs open water that is warmer than the air.

ex.q: Lake water is 40 F and air is 10 F. What is the difference?
steps: Answer: 30 F; a large difference, good for snow.

dd.trap: Thinking it snows everywhere equally. It falls in narrow bands downwind.
dd.tip: Warm lake, cold air: snow over there.

cards.t: Freezing rain coats everything. ¼ inch can break lines and branches.

dd.why: Freezing rain falls as liquid, then freezes on contact with surfaces below 32 F. It coats lines, trees, and roads with a layer of ice. Even 1/4 inch can add hundreds of pounds to a power line and break branches. Sleet bounces and does not stick, so it builds little weight. That is why freezing rain is worse for power lines. A cold layer near the ground freezes the drops on touching.
dd.pic: Draw a power line with a thick tube of ice around it. Draw raindrops falling and freezing where they touch. Draw a sleeping tree branch bending under the ice.
dd.analogy: A glaze on a donut: liquid sugar coats the donut and hardens. Freezing rain is the glaze, objects are the donut. The glaze is sweet; ice is dangerous.
ways: Freezing rain coats everything with ice.
1/4 inch of ice on lines can bring down trees and wires.

ex.q: Which builds heavier ice on power lines: sleet or freezing rain?
steps: Sleet is ice pellets that bounce.
Freezing rain stays liquid until it touches.
It then spreads and freezes in a layer.

dd.trap: Thinking sleet and freezing rain are the same. Sleet bounces, freezing rain coats.

cards.t: Conditions favorable. Get ready.

dd.why: A watch means the ingredients are in place for a hazard, but it has not happened yet. You have time to prepare. Know where you will go, charge phones, and watch the sky. Think of it as a heads-up.
dd.pic: Draw a clock with a long time to go and a person packing a bag.
dd.analogy: Like a coach saying the weather might be bad for the game, so bring a jacket. It stops working because watches cover large areas.
ways: A watch can cover 6 to 8 hours and many counties.

ex.q: A tornado watch means what?
steps: Answer: conditions are favorable for tornadoes; be ready.

dd.trap: Treating a watch as no danger. Stay alert.

cards.t: Happening or about to. Act now.

dd.why: A warning means the hazard is happening or about to. Radar or spotters have seen it. Warnings cover small areas and short times, so you must act at once. Go to shelter right now.
dd.pic: Draw a small polygon on a map with a red border and a person running to a shelter.
dd.analogy: A fire alarm: you leave now. It stops working because alarms may be false.
ways: Warning means it is here. Act.
Tornado warnings often last 30 to 45 minutes and cover a small area.

ex.q: A tornado warning means what?
steps: Warning means it is happening or about to.
