Answer: a tornado is occurring or imminent; take shelter now.

dd.trap: Waiting to see it. Act when warned.

cards.t: Less serious but still disruptive.

dd.why: An advisory covers conditions that are less serious but can still cause trouble, such as light snow or dense fog. They are not life-threatening for most but can cause crashes or delays. Take care.
dd.pic: Draw a yellow caution sign next to a slippery road.
dd.analogy: A yellow traffic light: slow down. It stops working because advisories are for specific hazards.
ways: Winter weather advisory may be 2 to 4 inches of snow.

ex.q: Which is more serious: a watch, an advisory, or a warning?

dd.trap: Ignoring advisories.

cards.t: Lowest floor, interior room, away from windows.

dd.why: Tornado winds break windows and throw debris. The safest spot is low, in the middle, and away from glass. Walls around you stop flying debris. Lower floors are less exposed than upper floors.
dd.pic: Draw a house. Mark the lowest floor, the center room with an X, and windows with an X.
dd.analogy: Like hiding in the middle of a hallway during a school drill. It stops working because homes differ.
ways: Lowest floor, interior room, away from windows.
Put 2 walls between you and outside.
Get low, get in, get away from glass.

ex.q: Where is the safest place in a house during a tornado warning?
steps: Go low: basement or lowest floor.
Answer: lowest floor, interior room, no windows.

dd.trap: Opening windows. This does nothing.

cards.t: Follow evacuation orders. Surge is often the deadliest part.

dd.why: Hurricanes bring surge, wind, and rain. Surge is often the deadliest, and you cannot outlast it at home in a surge zone. Officials order evacuations by zone. Follow them early because roads fill up.
dd.pic: Draw a coast map with zones A, B, C moving inland and an arrow going away from the coast.
dd.analogy: Like a school fire drill where the teacher tells your class when to move. It stops working because storms change.
ways: Evacuate 48 to 72 hours before landfall if ordered.

ex.q: In a hurricane evacuation, you should follow orders from whom?

dd.trap: Staying because the wind seems fine. Surge is the main danger.

cards.t: Flood: go high, never drive through water. Lightning: get indoors or into a hard-topped car.

dd.why: Floods and lightning each have a rule. Water 6 inches deep can knock you down and 12 inches can float a car. Lightning can strike miles from the storm. A hard-topped car or a building is safe.
dd.pic: Draw a car in water with an X and a building with a check mark.
dd.analogy: A slippery slide: easy to start, hard to stop. It stops working because water is dangerous.
ways: Turn Around, Don't Drown. When thunder roars, go indoors.
6 inches can knock you down. 12 inches floats a car.

ex.q: Complete the NWS slogan about flooded roads: Turn Around, ___.

dd.trap: Trying to cross shallow water.

cards.t: weather.gov, spc.noaa.gov for storms, nhc.noaa.gov for tropics.

dd.why: Good sources are official and fast. Weather.gov is the NWS site, spc.noaa.gov covers storms, nhc.noaa.gov covers tropical storms. NOAA Weather Radio works without internet or cell service, so it can wake you with alerts.
dd.pic: Draw a radio with an alert light and three website boxes.
dd.analogy: Like a smoke alarm that runs on batteries. It stops working because radios need batteries.

ex.q: A NOAA Weather Radio is useful because it what?
steps: Answer: gives alerts even when power or cell service is out.

dd.trap: Trusting social media alone.
dd.tip: Radio when the grid is out.

cards.t: Use generators outside. Stay away from downed lines. Power loss can cause carbon monoxide danger.

dd.why: After storms, hidden dangers remain. Downed lines can still be live. Generators make carbon monoxide, an invisible poison gas, so they must stay outside, away from windows. Cold or dark homes tempt people to bring them in. Never do it.
dd.pic: Draw a house with a generator outside 20 feet away and an X for indoors.
dd.analogy: Like a car in a closed garage. It stops working because generators are louder.
ways: Generator outside, away from doors and windows.
Place at least 20 feet from the house.

ex.q: After an ice storm, why is a portable generator used outside only?

dd.trap: Running it in the garage.

cards.t: Galveston 1900, Andrew 1992, Katrina 2005, Sandy 2012, Ida 2021, Ian 2022, Hilary 2023, Helene 2024, Erin 2025, Melissa 2025.

dd.why: Hurricane case studies are really about telling a hurricane from other disasters. Each name on this list is a tropical storm that grew over warm ocean and then hit land. The big harm came from wind, storm surge, and rain together. Galveston 1900 is the deadliest U.S. natural disaster on record, from surge before warnings existed. Later storms show how forecasts and building rules changed outcomes.
dd.pic: Draw a simple U.S. map with the Gulf and Atlantic coasts. Put a dot for each place: Galveston, New Orleans (Katrina), New York and New Jersey (Sandy), Houston area (Hilary is West Coast, so draw it near Southern California). Label each dot with its year.
dd.analogy: Think of a list of famous football games. You do not replay every play, you just remember the game, the year, and why it mattered. Here the 'game' is a storm and 'why it mattered' is the damage type. The analogy stops working because storms are natural and no team plans them.
ways: Hurricane list means the event was a tropical cyclone, not a blizzard or tornado outbreak.
Galveston 1900, Andrew 1992, Katrina 2005, Sandy 2012, Ida 2021, Ian 2022, Hilary 2023, Helene 2024, Erin 2025, Melissa 2025. That is 10 names, spanning 125 years.
Name plus year plus 'ocean storm with surge' = hurricane case.

ex.q: Hurricane Katrina (2005) caused major flooding in which U.S. city?
steps: Katrina is on the hurricane list, so think Gulf Coast.
Recall the surge and broken levees (flood walls) in 2005.
The levees failed in New Orleans, Louisiana.
Check: flooding came from surge, a hurricane hazard.

dd.trap: Mixing up the lists. Students put Storm of the Century (1993) with hurricanes because it sounds huge. Ask: did it form over warm tropical ocean? If it is a winter storm, it goes on the other list.
dd.tip: Hurricanes on the first list all had a name or came from the sea: Gal-Katrina-Sandy-Ida-Ian.

cards.t: Blizzard of March 1888. Dust Bowl 1930s. Xenia tornado 1974. April 2011 outbreaks. Great Flood 1993. Storm of the Century 1993.

dd.why: These events are big weather disasters that were not hurricanes. Each has a different cause, so the type tells you the clues. A blizzard needs wind and snow. A drought needs weeks of no rain. A tornado outbreak needs lots of warm, humid, sheared air. Knowing the cause lets you name the event from data without memorizing every detail.
dd.pic: Make a 6-row chart. Left column: event name and year. Right column: one picture word, like snowflake, dust cloud, funnel, rain cloud, river, big winter storm. Draw a tiny icon for each.
dd.analogy: Like sorting school supplies into bins: pencils, glue, markers. Each event goes in its own bin by what it is made of. The analogy stops because real events can mix, such as a storm with both snow and flooding.
ways: Blizzard 1888 = snow and wind. Dust Bowl = drought. Xenia 1974 = tornado.
1888, 1930s, 1974, 2011, 1993, 1993: six events from three centuries' worth of eras (1800s and 1900s and 2000s).
Ask: what fell or blew? Snow, dust, wind funnel, rain, river water.

ex.q: The Storm of the Century (March 1993) was a huge winter storm. Which type of event is it?
steps: It is on the non-hurricane list.
It brought heavy snow, high wind, and cold to the eastern U.S.
So it is a winter storm, not a tropical cyclone.

dd.trap: Thinking 'Storm of the Century' means a hurricane. The name is just a nickname. The type comes from the clues: cold air, snow, and wind.
dd.tip: B-D-X-A-G-S: Blizzard, Dust, Xenia, April, Great flood, Storm.

cards.t: The rules say you analyze data given. Know what type each event was.

dd.why: The rules give you data and ask you to analyze it. So you do not need a dictionary of dates. You only need to know what kind of event each one was. A type tells you what the data should look like: wind speeds for hurricanes, snow depth for blizzards, rainfall for floods.
dd.pic: Draw a funnel. Wide top says 'event data'. Middle says 'clues'. Narrow bottom says 'type of event'.
dd.analogy: A detective does not memorize every crime, just the patterns. Clues point to a kind of crime. Here clues point to a kind of storm. The analogy stops because detectives need proof, and weather data gives probabilities.
ways: Know the type of each event, not the story.
Wind 130 mph = hurricane Cat 4. Snow 24 inches with 40 mph wind = blizzard.

ex.q: A report shows months of heavy rain and the Missouri and Mississippi rivers over their banks in 1993. What type?
steps: List the clues: months of rain, two big rivers.
Heavy rain over a long time points to flooding.
Rivers rising is a river flood, not a flash flood.
Match to the list: Great Flood of 1993.

dd.trap: Memorizing every date and detail. Practice spotting clues instead.

cards.t: 1) Name the storm type. 2) List the clues. 3) Use the right scale or signature. 4) Check the date against cutoffs.

dd.why: This is a four-step habit for any case question. Naming the storm type narrows what scale or tool applies. Clues tell you what data matter. The right scale gives a rating. The date matters because scales changed: the Fujita scale before 1 Feb 2007 and the Enhanced Fujita after. Skipping the date check is how people choose the wrong scale.
dd.pic: Draw four boxes in a row with arrows: Type, Clues, Scale, Date. Put a small calendar icon on the last box.
dd.analogy: Like a recipe: pick the dish, check ingredients, use the right pan, check the oven temperature. Each step prevents a different mistake. It stops working because recipes are fixed and storms vary.
ways: Name it, list clues, pick the scale, check the date.
Tornado on 2011-04-27: 2011 is after Feb 1, 2007, so use EF. Tornado on 1974-04-03: before, so use F.

ex.q: A tornado hit on 3 April 1974 with peak wind estimated 170 mph. Which scale applies, and what is the rule?
steps: Step 2: clue is wind damage estimate.
Step 3: tornado scales are F or EF.
Step 4: 1974 is before 1 Feb 2007, so use the original Fujita scale.

dd.trap: Using EF for old tornadoes. Always compare the date to 1 Feb 2007 first.
dd.tip: Name, Clues, Scale, Date: N-C-S-D, 'Never Check Stale Dates'.

cards.t: Long drought plus plowed soil gave huge dust storms on the Plains.

dd.why: The Dust Bowl was not a single storm. Drought dried the soil. Farmers had plowed up the native prairie grass whose roots held the dirt. With no roots and no rain, strong winds lifted the soil into huge dust storms. Cause: drought plus bare, plowed ground plus wind. Remove any one and it would have been much milder.
dd.pic: Draw a flat field with no plants. Draw wavy arrows lifting brown specks into a tall brown wall. Add a dry sun above.
dd.analogy: A bare table dusted with flour: blow and it flies. If you cover it with a cloth (grass), it stays. Mapping: flour is topsoil, cloth is grass roots, your breath is wind. It stops working because the Dust Bowl lasted years across many states.
ways: Long dry spell plus loose soil plus wind equals dust storms.
Years of drought in the 1930s. Rain near 0 for months means soil moisture near 0, so soil is loose.

ex.q: Which historic event was mainly a long drought with massive dust storms on the Plains?
steps: Clue: dust storms on the Plains.
The event is the Dust Bowl.

dd.trap: Calling it a hurricane or tornado because dust walls look like storms. Check for drought first.

cards.t: Months of heavy rain flooded the Mississippi and Missouri rivers.

dd.why: In 1993 the Midwest got rain for months, not just one big storm. Soil filled up, so extra rain ran straight to rivers. The Mississippi and Missouri rose over banks and levees for weeks. Cause: a long wet pattern with storm after storm over the same region. Because the pattern lasted so long, it is a river flood, not a flash flood.
dd.pic: Draw two rivers joining on a map of the Midwest (Missouri from the west, Mississippi down the middle). Shade a wide blue band along them.
dd.analogy: A sink with the tap on and a clogged drain. The tap is steady rain and the sink is the river basin. It overflows slowly. It stops working because rain also soaks into soil first.
ways: Months of heavy rain made big rivers flood.
1993 summer: rain on top of full soil. If 2 in/week falls for 8 weeks, that is 16 in on already wet ground.
River floods take days to weeks.

ex.q: The Great Flood of 1993 mainly affected which river basins?
steps: Recall the cause: months of heavy rain.
Rain was over the central U.S.
Rivers draining that area are the Mississippi and Missouri.
Floods were along those rivers and their tributaries.
Answer: upper Mississippi and Missouri river basins.

dd.trap: Calling it a flash flood. A flash flood takes minutes to hours. This took weeks.
